## BARIATRIC SURGERY, OBESITY AND WEIGHT LOSS - ROOM B5____________________

## OP039 INTRAGASTRIC BALLOON-INDUCED WEIGHT LOSS PRIOR TO SURGERY IN SUPER-OBESE PATIENTS – A SINGLE CENTER EXPERIENCE
I. Mocanu1, A. Laranjo1, S. Pires1, N. Veloso1, I. Medeiros1, M. Rocha2, S. Silva2, M. Amaro2, M. Carvalho2

1Gastroenterology, Hospital Espirito Santo de Évora, Évora/Portugal

2Surgery, Hospital Espirito Santo de Évora, Évora/Portugal

Contact E-mail Address:
irina.mocanu.24@gmail.com

Introduction: Bariatric surgery remains the most effective treatment for morbid obesity, and laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (LRYGB) continues to be the preferred operation. However, extreme obesity increases morbi-mortality in bariatric surgery. In super-obese patients (BMI > 50Kg/m2), pre-operative weight loss can be achieved with minimally invasive endoscopic intragastric balloon (IGB) placement.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to explore the potential benefits of preoperative IGB on the outcomes of LRYGB in super-obesity. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of the patients with a BMI > 50Kg/m2 treated at our obesity center between 2008 and 2016 with LRYGB alone (controls) or with prior placement of an IGB (cases). Clinical success of IGB was considered a body weight loss (BWL) of ≥10% and surgical success – an excess body weight loss (EBWL) ≥50% by the second year of post-operative follow-up (FU).
Results: 133 patients were included (82% females, mean age 45.8years, 85% with comorbidities): 46 cases Vs. 87 controls. Cases were significantly more overweight than controls (BMI 57.5 vs. 53Kg/m2; p < 0.05, excess body weight 83.7 vs. 70.2 Kg; p < 0.01). The median time of IGB therapy was 196.8 days with 100% technical success rate in placement and removal of the device. 16 patients (34, 8%) had any complaint during IGB treatment (nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain) and in two (4%) of these, the IGB was removed before the scheduled date. Average weight effects of IGB were: weight loss: 27kg, BWL: 18.1%, BMI loss 10.7kg/m2 and EBWL of 32.6%, with a clinical success rate for IGB of 87%. 71, 7% of cases had more than 25% EBWL at time of removal. 26.1% improved fitness for surgery as assessed by ASA score (drop from III to II) and 6.5% reported improvement in comorbidities during IGB treatment. The average delay from removal of IGB to surgery was 139 days, with a mean weight increase of 4.9kg. At time of surgery, average BMI was lower in cases than controls (48.6 vs. 53kg/m2, p < 0.01). There were no records of major surgical complications. Average EBWL effect of LRYGB in cases vs. controls was: 46.6 vs. 53% (p < 0.05) at 6 months, 56.9 vs. 70% (p < 0.05) at 12 months and 51.2 vs 73.8% (p < 0.05) at 2 years after surgery. When initial excess body weight was compared, EBWL in controls maintained superiority over the cases (73.8% vs. 64%, p < 0.05) at 24 months. 74.4% (n = 99) had a post-surgical FU of more than 2 years and of these, 81% had reached a clinical success (EBWL ≥ 50%). At most recent post-surgical FU (average 42.8 months), there was no difference between the two groups in total EBWL (63.7 vs. 66.5, p > 0.05). 57.8% (n = 77) reported improvement in comorbidities after surgery. Dyslipidemia, type II diabetes and joint pain were the comorbidities that most frequently improved.
Conclusion: IGB is a safe and effective method to promote weight loss in super-obese patients awaiting bariatric surgery, with subsequent improvement in anesthetic risk in a quarter of patients. Prior to surgery, patients submitted to IGB had lower BMI, despite initially being more overweight and at last post-surgical follow-up, there was no statistical difference in EBWL between the two groups. Another variable that has been previously demonstrated to improve with IGB was surgery time. We decided not to analyze this due to the long timespan of the study and the inherent improvement of the technical skills during these nine years, which could deliver biased results.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP040 EROSIVE ESOPHAGITIS IS PREVALENT AND PREDICTABLE BY PRE-OPERATIVE GERDQ QUESTIONNAIRE IN OBESE INDIVIDUALS AND IS ASSOCIATED WITH THE NEED FOR CONTINUED PPI USE AFTER LAPAROSCOPIC SLEEVE GASTRECTOMY
A.I. Sharara, H. H. Rimmani, A.I. Al Abbas, B. Safadi, R. H. Shayto, H. Aridi, Y. Shaib, R. Alami

Internal Medicine, American University of Beirut Medical Center, Beirut/Lebanon

Contact E-mail Address:
husseinrimmani@gmail.com

Introduction: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is common in obese individuals and following laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). There is limited information on the true prevalence, risk factors, and outcome of GERD before and after LSG.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to prospectively evaluate the prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux disease in obese patients considered for bariatric surgery and to identify risk and predictive factors for erosive esophagitis (EE) and continued PPI therapy post-LSG.
Methods: Consecutive patients undergoing routine esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) prior to bariatric surgery were enrolled after informed consent. Patients completed the GERDQ and Nocturnal GERD Symptom Severity and Impact Questionnaires (N-GSSIQ). Demographic data included gender, age, BMI, waist circumference, and use of PPI or H2-antagonists. Endoscopic data included presence of erosive esophagitis (EE), hiatal hernia (HH), and gastroesophageal flap valve endoscopic grading (Hill grade). Patients were assessed 6 months post-LSG for BMI, GERDQ, and need for PPI.
Results: 175 consecutive patients have been recruited to date (76 males and 99 females). The mean age was 38.4 ± 11.7 and mean BMI was 40.0 ± 6.1, nearly equally divided between BMI ≤ or >40. Forty four patients (25.1%) were on PPIs at baseline. EE was documented in 48 of 131 patients on no PPI (36.6%). The total prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux (EE + PPI users) was 52.6%. On multivariate analysis, presence of HH and a high GERDQ score (38) were significantly associated with EE (p = 0.025 and <0.001 respectively). Patients with high probability GERDQ scores had a significantly higher prevalence of EE compared to low scorers (45.8% vs. 21.6%, p = 0.001). EE was more common in males vs. females (40.8% vs. 24.2%, p = 0.019) and in patients with HH vs. those without (48.4% vs. 27.8%, p = 0.025). BMI (≤40 vs. >40) and WC were not associated with the presence of EE. Logistic regression analysis showed that GERDQ scores of ≥8 was the only independent risk factor for EE (OR 3.077, 95% CI 1.58–5.96). Forty-seven patients had LSG and completed the follow-up assessment. At 6 months post-LSG, mean BMI declined to 29.8 ± 4.3 (D = -11.05) and 15 of 47 patients (31.9%) required continued PPI therapy to control their symptoms. EE on baseline EGD was the only factor associated with need for continued PPI use (58.8% in EE patients vs. 16.7% without EE; p = 0.003). BMI, HH repair, baseline PPI use were not predictive of continued post-operative PPI use.
Conclusion: Gastroesophageal reflux disease is very prevalent in obese patients considered for bariatric surgery. A high GERDQ score correlates with the presence of erosive disease in this population. The presence of erosive esophagitis, but not PPI use pre-operatively is highly predictive of the need for continued PPI requirement post-laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP041 DEFECTS IN ENTEROENDOCRINE CELL DEVELOPMENT IN MORBIDLY OBESE HUMANS ARE NORMALIZED AFTER SLEEVE GASTRECTOMY
A.C. Meyer-Gerspach1, A. W. Moran2, B. K. Wölnerhanssen1, G. Burdyga2, R. Peterli3, M. Manz4, M. Thumshirn4, K. Daly2, C. Beglinger1, S. P. Shirazi-Beechey2

1Department Of Research, Clara Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

2Institute Of Integrative Biology, University of Liverpool, Liverpool/United Kingdom

3Department Of Surgery, Clara Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

4Department Of Gastroenterology, Clara Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

Contact E-mail Address:
ac.meyergerspach@gmail.com

Introduction: Morbidly obese patients exhibit impaired secretion of gastrointestinal peptides that may contribute to the development of obesity and its associated conditions. Bariatric surgery induces an increase in gastrointestinal peptide release. The mechanisms associated with these changes are unclear. A better understanding of the underlying mechanisms may contribute to the development of non-invasive therapeutic strategies.
Aims & Methods: Gastric and duodenal tissues were endoscopically collected from lean controls and morbidly obese subjects before and 3 months after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). Gastrointestinal peptides were measured after a standardized nutrient drink pre- and post- LSG. Tissue morphology was determined by morphometric analysis. Tissue expression levels of chromogranin A, gut hormones, α-defensin, mucin 2 and Na+/glucose co-transporter 1 (SGLT1) were assessed by combination of immunohistochemistry, western blotting and quantitative PCR. Protein abundance of transcription factors (Hes1, HATH1, NeuroD1, and Ngn3) were determined by western blotting.
Results: In the obese, the total number of enteroendocrine cells (EEC) containing gastrointestinal peptides was significantly reduced (p < 0.001); they were restored post-LSG (p < 0.001). This profile matched the levels of circulating gastrointestinal peptides (p < 0.001, respectively). A significant increase in SGLT1 (p < 0.05) expression was detected in the obese duodenum. Expression levels of transcription factors required for differentiation of absorptive and secretory cell lineages were reduced (p < 0.05, respectively).
Conclusion: In conclusion, in obesity, there is a deregulation of developmental programming of intestinal epithelial cell lineages. The programing is restored post-surgery leading to an increase in secretion of gut hormones and reduced blood glucose levels.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP042 A WEIGHT LOSS INTERVENTION REDUCES BOWEL SYMPTOMS: A PROSPECTIVE STUDY IN SUBJECTS WITH MORBID OBESITY
M. Aasbrenn1, S. Lydersen2, P. Gronaas Farup1

1Department Of Cancer Research And Molecular Medicine, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim/Norway

2Regional Centre For Child And Youth Mental Health And Child Welfare, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim/Norway

Contact E-mail Address:
Martin.Aasbrenn@gmail.com

Introduction: Low-grade inflammation and dietary habits are possible explanations for the high prevalence of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in subjects with morbid obesity.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to study changes in bowel symptoms, BMI, physical and mental health and a selection of blood tests during a weight loss intervention, and to study the associations between the changes in bowel symptoms and the other variables. Subjects referred to a hospital for treatment of morbid obesity were included. The intervention included personalized advice on lifestyle (regular, healthy meals and physical activity) and frequent group-based follow-up for six months. IBS was diagnosed with the Rome III criteria. Bowel symptoms were assessed with the irritable bowel syndrome symptom severity scale (IBS-SSS) and gastrointestinal symptom rating scale for IBS (GSRS-IBS). Health was assessed with eight questionnaires including WHO-5 Well-Being Index for emotional well-being and the Sense of Humor Questionnaire. CRP, lactoferrin, neopterin, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein, cholesterol, HbA1c, thyroid stimulating hormone, T4 and vitamins B1, B6, B12 and D were measured in the blood.
Results: Eighty-eight subjects (71(81%) females) with mean age 44 years (SD 8) were included. BMI was reduced from 42 (SD 4) to 39 (SD 4) kg/m2 (p < 0.001). The prevalence of IBS was 24/88 (27%) before and 17/88 (19%) after the intervention (p = 0.19). The IBS-SSS was reduced from 116 (SD 104) to 81 (SD 84) (p = 0.001). The GSRS-IBS was reduced from 1.8 (SD 0.8) to 1.6 (SD 0.6) (p = 0.006). Scores on GSRS-IBS subscales changed significantly: Bloating, diarrhoea and satiety decreased while constipation increased. The markers of low-grade inflammation and most of the other health scores and blood tests improved significantly. The reduction in IBS-SSS was negatively associated with reduction in BMI (partial correlation (pc) = −0.29, p = 0.012) and associated with improved sense of humor (pc = −0.30, p = 0.012). The reduction in GSRS-IBS was associated with improvement in emotional well-being (pc = −0.23, p = 0.038) and increased vitamin D (pc = −0.29, p = 0.010). Neither the changes in IBS-SSS nor GSRS-IBS were significantly associated with changes in the inflammatory markers, the other health scores or blood tests.
Conclusion: The bowel symptoms were markedly reduced during the weight loss intervention, but the reduction was not associated with the changes in low-grade inflammation. These results weaken the hypothesis that low-grade inflammation from adipose tissue is the cause of the high prevalence of IBS in subjects with obesity. Dietary habits (size of meals, fat intake) or psychosocial factors are alternative explanations.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP043 DYNAMICS OF DECREASE OF ABDOMINAL FAT AFTER BARIATRIC SURGERY: A NONINVASIVE ASSESSMENT OVER 24 MONTHS BY MRI
A.C. Meyer-Gerspach1, B. K. Wölnerhanssen1, D. Nabers2, M. Moor3, S. Borgwardt4, R. Peterli5, C. Beglinger1, O. Bieri3

1Department Of Research, Clara Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

2Division Of Medical And Biological Informatics, German Cancer Research Center, Heidelberg/Germany

3Department Of Radiology, University Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

4Department Of Psychiatry, University Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

5Department Of Surgery, Clara Hospital Basel, Basel/Switzerland

Contact E-mail Address:
ac.meyergerspach@gmail.com

Introduction: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is characterized by atherogenic dyslipidemia. NAFLD patients are at an increased risk for both cardiac and non-cardiac vascular diseases. The effect of bariatric surgery on fat distribution in the liver has so far been studied with liver biopsies and single voxel MR techniques. The objective of this study was to assess liver fat fraction (LFF), subcutaneous (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) using MRI in combination with blood lipids to monitor the efficiency of bariatric surgery.
Aims & Methods: In 15 morbidly obese patients an iterative decomposition of water and fat with echo asymmetry and least-squares estimation (IDEAL) approach was used for whole liver fat quantification in combination with a 2-point Dixon technique for volumetric fat imaging of adipose tissue pre- and 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery. SAT and VAT adipose tissue volumes were assessed from fat images and separated by statistical shape models. Serum: total cholesterol, HDL, LDL and TG were measured.
Results: LFF, SAT and VAT volumes decreased postoperatively with a good phenomenological description using an exponential model of form. t is the time (in days) after intervention, A = [A1, A2, …, A11] refers to the individual patient specific LFF, SAT or VAT volumes, in combination with a global time constant TLFF,VAT,SAT for each measure. The LFF reduced the fastest, (time constant: TLFF = 96 ± 28 d), followed by SAT (TSAT = 140 ± 18 d), and VAT (TVAT = 170 ± 21 d). LFF measures showed a clear correlation with total cholesterol, cholesterol/HDL ratio and LDL (each: p < 0.001) and a trend for HDL (p = 0.006). Decrease in VAT and SAT did not correlate with blood lipids.
Conclusion: In conclusion, the decrease of body fat after bariatric surgery follows a distinct time pattern: liver fat decreases fastest followed by subcutaneous and last visceral fat, and decrease in liver fat correlates with changes in blood lipids.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP044 FINAL RESULTS OF MULTI-CENTER, PROSPECTIVE, CONTROLLED TRIAL OF THE DUODENO-JEJUNAL BYPASS LINER FOR THE TREATMENT OF TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS IN OBESE PATIENTS: EFFICACY AND FACTORS PREDICTING A SUBOPTIMAL EFFECT
M. Benes, P. Drastich, T. Hucl, J. Spicak

Department Of Hepatogastroenterology, Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine, Prague/Czech Republic

Contact E-mail Address:
marek.benes@ikem.cz

Introduction: The global increase in obesity incidence results in an increase of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Surgical treatment has proven to be effective; however, it carries a high risk of complications. The duodenal-jejunal bypass liner (EndoBarrier®, GI Dynamics, EB) is an endoscopic implant that mimics the intestinal bypass portion of the Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass. It results in weight loss and improvements in glucose control in obese patients with T2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
Aims & Methods: This is a final report of a prospective, controlled, multicentre study aimed to determine the effectiveness of EB and to identify factors associated with a sub-optimal outcome of EB.
Results: Seventy subjects (45 with an implant, 25 controls) were included in the study. The groups were comparable with respect to age, gender, BMI (mean 41.7 vs. 39.5 kg/m2), T2DM duration (7.8 vs. 8.3 years), HbA1c level (88 vs 86 mmol/mol) and T2DM treatment. In the EB group, all devices were successfully implanted. Only 6 devices had to be explanted prior to the end of the 10 months study period (bleeding, dislocation and need for ERCP because of choledocholithiasis). The mean procedure time was 17 minutes for an implantation and 16 minutes for an explantation. At 10 months there was significantly greater weight loss and %EWL (19% vs. 7% and 43 vs. 12) and significantly improved long-term compensation of T2DM marker HbA1c (decreased by 25 vs. 10 mmol/mol) in the EB group. T2DM medicinal treatment could be reduced in more device subjects than controls. There was no serious adverse event. Mild abdominal pain and nausea after implantation were experienced by 60% of patients during first 14 days after implantation, 30% of patients during the first month and 10% of patiens after one month. Lower initial BMI and lower body height were identified as negative prognostic factors for pain, but positive for efficacy of EB.
Conclusion: The EB is safe when implanted for 10 months, and results in significant weight loss and HbA1c reduction. This suggests that this novel device is a candidate for the primary therapy of morbid obesity and T2DM. Lower initial BMI and lower body height could be negative prognostic factor for pain, but positive for efficacy.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## ABSTRACTS ON FIRE: ADVANCES IN ENDOSCOPIC RESECTION OF EARLY COLORECTAL NEOPLASIA - HOTSPOT____________________

## OP045 UNDERWATER ENDOSCOPIC COLORECTAL POLYP RESECTION IS A SAFER AND MORE EFFECTIVE TECHNIQUE THAN GAS INSUFFLATION POLYPECTOMY FOR EVERYDAY CLINICAL PRACTICE
M. Liggi1, S. Cadoni2, P. Gallittu2, D. Mura1, M. Koo3

1Digestive Endoscopy Unit, Sirai Hospital, Carbonia/Italy

2Digestive Endoscopy Unit, CTO Hospital, Iglesias/Italy

3Dalla Lana School Of Public Health, University Of Toronto, Department of Medical Research, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan, Toronto/Canada/ON

Contact E-mail Address:
liggim@gmail.com

Introduction: Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) is a well-established technique for resecting flat or sessile benign colon polyps. Underwater endoscopic mucosal resection (UEMR) is a novel technique that eschews submucosal injection. Reports about the feasibility, efficacy and safety of the technique were limited to small series of single and/or tertiary-care referral centers.
Aims & Methods: To demonstrate that underwater polypectomy (UWP, here includes UEMR) can be efficaciously and safely used in routine clinical practice also by endoscopists with various levels of expertise (2 experts; 2 fellows). Main outcomes: en bloc resection rate, R0 resection rate, residual or recurrent adenoma (RRA) at follow-up (median 14 months) of piecemeal resections of flat and sessile lesions ≥10 mm, and adverse events. Analyses were also conducted with stratification by the colonoscopists’ expertise. Colonoscopy records maintained at our two community hospitals in Italy about UWP, traditional EMR for flat and sessile lesions ≥6 mm and for resections of pedunculated polyps ≥6 mm performed from 01/2015 to 12/2016 were included in the current retrospective analysis. Data on UWP and gas insufflation polypectomy (GIP) were compared.
Results: Table 1 shows that a total of 318 polypectomies (195 UWP and 186 GIP) were performed. Demographic and procedural data were comparable, as well as the distribution, morphology and histology of resected lesions. Pathology record median size (interquartile range, IQR) in the UWP group (10 mm; 7–15) vs. the GIP group (10 mm; 17–12.5) was comparable. Median (IQR) resection time was significantly shorter in the UWP group (1.5 minutes; 0.8–3.8) than in the GIP group (3.4 minutes; 2.5–5.4) (p < 0.001), respectively. En bloc and R0 resections, as well as RRA proportions, irrespective of polyp morphology and size, were comparable. Immediate bleeding for pedunculated lesions was significantly lower in the UWP than in the GIP group: 3.4% vs. 13.5%, p = 0.031. No post-polypectomy syndrome or perforation cases occurred. Analyses according to colonoscopist expertise showed that fellows performed 41% of UWP and 61.8% of GIP. Polyp morphology, size, en bloc and R0 resections were comparable between study groups and with those of experts. Fellows’ UWP resection times for flat and sessile lesions (1.1 minutes; IQR 0.7–3.3) and for pedunculated lesions (0.8 minutes; IQR 0.6–1.1) were significantly shorter than experts’ [3.3 minutes; IQR 2.0–6.0 (p = 0.006) and 3.3 minutes; IQR 2.0–8.0 (p < 0.001), respectively] and than GIP resection times (3.5 minutes; IQR 2.8–6.7 and 3.5 minutes; IQR 2.6–5.0, respectively; both p < 0.001). UWP of pedunculated lesions performed by fellows showed significantly less immediate bleeding that GIP (0% vs 17.8%; p = 0.006).
Conclusion: Compared with GIP, UWP (including UEMR) achieved comparable proportions of en bloc and R0 resections, and RRA; with a significantly shorter resection time (all polyps) and lower bleeding episodes (pedunculated polyps) despite different colonoscopists’ expertise. This evidence suggests that UWP can be easily and safely used in routine clinical practice, also by not very expert colonoscopists. Its use should be encouraged.

 Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP046 HAS THE SAFETY OF COLORECTAL ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION BEEN MAINTAINED EVEN IN THE REGIONAL GENERAL HOSPITAL IN JAPAN?: A MULTICENTER PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY
Y. Hiraga, S. Tanaka, S. Oka, K. Boda, S. Nagata, M. Kunihiro, R. Higashi, T. Kuwai, A. Furudoi, K. Nakadoi, H. Kanao, M. Terasaki, H. Okanobu, M. Higashiyama, K. Chayama

Hiroshima Endoscopy Research Group, Hiroshima/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
penguist@ktb.biglobe.ne.jp

Introduction: In Japan since April 2012, colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) has been covered under health insurance, and now it has certainly become one of the treatment options of early colorectal neoplasms. There are a lot of reports of good outcomes of colorectal ESD, but that were performed by very skillful experts at advanced high-volume centers.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to investigate the clinical outcomes of colorectal ESD performed in our region, Hiroshima prefecture in Japan, included many non-specialized general hospitals. We recruited prospectively 1126 consecutive patients (681 male, mean age 69 years) with 1118 colorectal tumors resected by ESD at 26 hospitals (1 academic center and 25 community hospitals) in Hiroshima prefecture between August 2013 and June 2016. We categorized the 26 hospitals into high- (Group H) or low-volume centers (Group L), based on the median number (80 lesions) of ESD performed during the study period. We compared the groups with respect to the clinicopathological characteristics of the lesions and the clinical outcomes of ESD.
Results: Regarding the clinicopathological characteristics of 1118 tumors, 594 (50%) were located in the right colon, 253 (21%) in the left colon, and 341 (29%) in the rectum. The average tumor size was 30 mm (range 5–120 mm). Laterally spreading tumors of the granular type (LST-G), LST of the non-granular type (-NG) and polypoid type were 500 lesions (42%), 433 (36%) and 255 (22%), respectively. Histologically, there were 531 (45%) intramucosal carcinomas (Tis), 81 (7%) shallow submucosal invasive cancers (<1000 µm; T1a), 144 (12%) deep submucosal invasive cancers (>1000 µm; T1b) and 432 (36%) dysplasias. 198 (17%) tumors had severe submucosal fibrosis and 484 tumors (41%) had the poor scope operability. As for the procedural outcomes of ESD, the mean procedure time was 90 minutes (range 5–660 minutes), and the ratios of the en bloc resection, histological complete resection and R0 resection were 95% (1133/1188), 93% (1101/1188) and 83% (986/1188), respectively. The delayed bleeding and perforation during procedure occurred in each 2% (24/1188), 4% (42/1188, included 3 patients shifted to surgery). There were no significant differences between the groups in relation to the sex ratio, the patients’ average age, the ratio of taking antithrombotic drugs, the mean tumor size, the tumors’ locations and the mean procedure times. The ratios of additional ESD after endoscopic resection, of polypoid lesions, of severe submucosal fibrosis and of poor scope operability were significantly higher in Group H compared with that in Group L. The histological complete resection rates were significantly higher in Group H than in Group L, but the en bloc resection rate and the adverse events rates were not.
Conclusion: In our region, the safety of colorectal ESD has been maintained, because we appropriately choose the lesions which ourselves should do according to the skill level of each institutions after having judged the degree of procedure difficulty of them.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP047 WHAT ARE THE RESULTS OF RECTAL ESD IN FRANCE: A LARGE RETROSPECTIVE MULTICENTRE STUDY IN EXPERTS CENTERS
J. Albouys1, M. Guillaumot2, V. Lepilliez3, S. Chaussade4, M. Pioche5, S. Leblanc6, M. Barret2, R. Legros1, F. Prat7, J. Rivory5, D. Sautereau8, T. Ponchon9, J. Jacques8

1CHU Limoges, Limoges/France

2Gastroenterology, Cochin Hospital, Paris/France

3Hopital prive Jean Mermoz, Lyon/France

4Service De Gastro-entérologie, CHU Cochin Dept. de Gastroenterologie, Paris/France

Introduction: Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection has become the standard of care for large superficial rectal precancerous and cancerous lesions. Despite increasing practice in the western world, few European studies have been reported. First French results were far from those reported by Japanese teams: En bloc resection: 64%; R0 resection: 53%. Since these first results, experts teams have trained with animal models and in Japanese centers. We report here the largest European retrospective multicenter study of four French leading teams in rectal ESD.
Aims & Methods: We performed a retrospective multicenter study of all cases of rectal ESD performed for precancerous or superficial cancerous lesions in four French teams that performed more than 150 ESDs in the last 5 years. All these teams had individual databases of their cases of rectal ESDs that were merged. Primary Endpoint was to evaluate the En bloc, R0 and curative resection rate. Secondary endpoints were: -evaluation of risk factors for non R0 resection -evaluation of risk factors for non en bloc resection -evaluation of the effect of learning curve (before and after 40 ESDs) on the results
Results: 349 rectal ESDs were performed between 01/06/2010 and 31/12/2016. Descriptive results: male 49%, mean size of the specimen: 56.4 mm, mean duration of procedure 118.9 min, mean speed of ESD: 23.9 mm2/min, perforation rate: 6%, post procedural bleeding rate: 6.3%, secondary surgery 6.6% (0% for a complication; 95% for a failure or pathological risk factor or lymph node metastasis; 5% for ulcerative colitis). Pathological analysis: low grade dysplasia in 22%, high grade dysplasia in 32, 4%, intra-mucosal carcinoma in 29%, superficial submucosal carcinoma in 6, 3%, deep submucosal carcinoma in 4.6% and T2 adenocarcinoma in 2.3%. Only 5 patients (1.5%) had a recurrent disease during endoscopic follow up: 2 that had an ESD failure and a piece-meal resection, 2 that had low-grade dysplasia in lateral margin and one high-grade dysplasia lesion R0 resected. Primary Endpoint: En bloc resection rate: 95.3%, R0 resection rate: 73%, curative resection rate: 68.5% Secondary endpoints: -non en bloc resection was associated with a longer procedure duration (221 vs 113 min, p = 0.002); a lower speed (12.9 vs 24.2 mm2/min, p = 0.0005); a higher perforation rate (21.05% vs 5.2%, p = 0.005); a higher rate of secondary surgery (21% vs 5.2% p = 0.02) and a higher rate of recurrent disease (10.5% vs 0.9%, p = 0.02) -non R0 resection was associated with a longer procedure duration (165.2 vs 105 min, p = 0.002)); a lower speed (17.4 vs 25.9 mm2/min, p = 0.0005); a higher rate of non exclusive ESD (17.2% vs 1.7%, p = ….) and and a higher rate of recurrent disease (4.3% vs 0.4%, p = 0.02) -the beginning of the learning curve (<40 ESDs whatever the location) was associated with a longer procedure duration (167 vs 107 min, p = 1.2 × 10−6); a lower speed (15.49 vs 25.83 mm2/min, p = 1.6 × 10−6), a higher rate of post procedural bleeding (13.3% vs 4.4%, p = 0.004) a lower rate of deep sm or T2 adenocarcinoma (0% vs 5% and 0% vs 2.%, p = 0.05), a lower rate of secondary surgery (0% vs 8.4%, p = 0.009) and longer hospital stay (3.76 vs 2.82 days, p = 0.0001)

 Conclusion: ESD allows a high en bloc and R0 resection in rectal lesions with a low recurrence rate in French expert teams. French experts centres are able to report results close to those of Japanese experts when an adequate training has been performed. This retrospective study represent the largest study of rectal ESD in the western world.

## OP048 EFFICACY OF TRACTION-ASSISTED COLORECTAL ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION USING CLIP AND THREAD: A PROSPECTIVE RANDOMIZED STUDY
Y. Yamasaki1, Y. Takeuchi2, N. Uedo2, T. Kanesaka2, R. Ishihara2, H. Okada1, H. Iishi2

1Department Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Okayama University Graduate School of Medicine, Okayama/Japan

2Department Of Gastrointestinal Oncology, Osaka International Cancer Institute, Osaka/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
yasshifive@yahoo.co.jp

Introduction: Colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is still challenging because of its technical difficulties, long procedure time, and high risk of adverse events. To facilitate colorectal ESD, we developed a novel simplified traction method “traction assisted colorectal ESD using clip and thread (TAC-ESD)” [1, 2]. Here, we conducted a prospective randomized controlled trial to fully evaluate the efficacy of TAC-ESD.
Aims & Methods: Patients with superficial colorectal neoplasms (SCNs) >20 mm were enrolled and randomly assigned to conventional-ESD group or TAC-ESD group. SCNs < 50 mm were treated by 2 intermediates, and SCNs > 50 mm were treated by 2 experts. Primary endpoint was the procedure time. Secondary endpoints were successful rate of TAC-ESD, self-completion rate by the intermediates, and adverse events. Procedural success of TAC-ESD was defined as successful sustained application of clip and thread until the end of procedure. In the colon, TAC-ESD was performed as follows. Before the endoscope was inserted, a 3–0 polyester surgical thread 0.25 mm in diameter (Natsume Seisakusho Co., Ltd, Tokyo, Japan) was inserted into its accessory channel by grasping the thread with hemostatic forceps, and pulling it up through the working channel. Then the ends of the thread were tied together outside the endoscope. After that, the endoscope was inserted as usual and the actual ESD procedure started. After submucosal injection, the mucosa was incised on the anal side of the lesion. Next, the thread was cut externally at the hand control end of the endoscope and the accessory channel end of the thread tied to the teeth of the clip (HX-610-090; Olympus, Tokyo) attached to an applicator. At this stage, it was important not to fully open the clip. The clip and thread were then retracted into the applicator and the applicator inserted into the accessory channel. The clip was fully opened in the colon and used to grasp the anal side of the specimen, after which the thread was pulled gently by hand to provide good visibility of the submucosal layer. Finally, the submucosal layer was dissected easily under direct visualization [1]. In the rectum, TAC-ESD was performed as follows. First, a polyester thread was tied to the teeth of a clip, which was attached to an applicator. The clip and thread was then retracted into the applicator as in preparation. Next, the endoscope was inserted into the rectum. After a mucosal incision on the anal side of the lesion was performed, the endoscope was withdrawn outside of the rectum. The applicator was inserted into the accessory channel of the endoscope, and the thread was pulled back up through the working channel. Then, the endoscope was reinserted into the rectum. The clip was fully opened within the rectum and used to grasp the anal side of the lesion. Since then, the procedure was same as above [2].
Results: In total, 42 SCNs in conventional-ESD group and 42 SCNs in TAC-ESD group were analyzed between August 2015 and October 2016. The procedure time (median [range]) in TAC-ESD group was significantly shorter than in conventional-ESD group (40 [11–86] min vs. 70 [30–180] min, respectively; P < 0.0001). In subgroup analyses, the procedure time was significantly shorter in TAC-ESD group than in conventional-ESD group for both colonic (37 [21–86] min vs. 68 [30–180] min, respectively; P < 0.0001) and rectal (44 [11–84] min vs. 73 [32–120] min, respectively; P = 0.02) lesions. Successful rate of TAC-ESD was 95% (40/42). The self-completion rate by the intermediates was significantly higher in TAC-ESD group than in conventional-ESD group (100% [39/39] vs. 90% [36/40], respectively; P = 0.04). There were 1 intra-operative perforation in conventional-ESD group, and 1 delayed perforation in TAC-ESD group.
Conclusion: TAC-ESD reduced the procedure time and raised the self-completion rate without increasing adverse events.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.
References
1. Yamasaki Y, Takeuchi Y, Uedo N et al. Traction-assisted colonic endoscopic submucosal dissection using clip and line: a feasibility study. Endosc Int Open. 2016; 4: E51-5.
2. Yamasaki Y, Takeuchi Y, Uedo N et al. Feasibility of Simple Traction Technique for Rectal Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection. Dig Dis Sci. 2016; 61:2127–31.

## OP049 EFFICACY OF ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION USING THE “CLIP-FLAP METHOD” FOR COLORECTAL TUMORS
K. Yamamoto1, S. Hayashi2, H. Saiki1, T. Nishida2, N. Tatsumi1, T. Michida3, T. Ito1

1Department Of Gastroenterology, Japan Community Healthcare Organization Osaka Hospital, Osaka/Japan

2Department Of Gastroenterology, Toyonaka Municipal Hospital, Osaka/Japan

3Teikyo University Medical Center, Chiba/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
yamamoto-kts@umin.ac.jp

Introduction: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is technically challenging because of poor visualization and instability in the operative field. Although mucosal flap formation improves visualization of the cutting area, it is difficult to achieve, especially in colorectal ESD. To facilitate mucosal flap creation, we developed the “clip-flap method” using the endoclip as a substitute for the mucosal flap until the flap is completed (K. Yamamoto, et al. Endoscopy 2012·2015).
Aims & Methods: We retrospectively studied 497 cases in which ESD for superficial colorectal tumors was performed between August 2008 and April 2017. The primary object lesions were large laterally spreading tumor. We compared the treatment outcomes after the adoption of the clip-flap method (Clipflap-ESD: 377 cases) with those before the adoption of the clip-flap method (Conventional-ESD: 120 cases) to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the clip-flap method. Furthermore, we investigated the cases for which clip-flap method was especially effective in difficult lesions. The procedure of the clip-flap method is as follows. The lesions were moved upward as far as possible against gravity following a postural change to take advantage of the counter-traction of gravity. After submucosal injection, the mucosa around the lesion on the anal side was incised with an adequate margin, and the submucosal layer was cut deeply. The edge of the exfoliated mucosa was clipped with an endoclip (EZ CLIP, HX-610-135; Olympus). The distal attachment was inserted under the endoclip, and then the submucosal layer was dissected with the endoknife. A single endoclip was generally used, and the cross pattern of endoclips, created by attaching one endoclip to another endoclip, was also used according to the situations. We mainly used a short-needle electrosurgical endoknife with a water-jet function (FlushKnifeBT; Fujifilm).
Results: Median tumor diameter, resected specimen diameter, procedure time, en bloc resection rate, and perforation rate of Conventional-ESD and Clipflap-ESD were 26 mm vs 27 mm, 32.5 mm vs 36 mm, 88.5 minutes vs 47 minutes, 90 % vs 97.1 %, and 4.2 % vs 1.6 %, respectively. The procedure time of Clipflap-ESD was statistically significantly shorter than that of Conventional-ESD (P < 0.01), and en bloc resection rate of Clipflap-ESD was significantly higher than that of Conventional-ESD (P < 0.01). Application rate of the clip-flap method in Clip-flap-ESD was 61.8 %. In all the cases which the clip-flap method was applied, the exfoliated mucosa was lifted by the endoclip attached to the exfoliated mucosa after the distal attachment was inserted under the endoclip, allowing for clear visualization and efficient dissection of the submucosal layer, and effective creation of the mucosal flap. In technically difficult lesions for ESD, the difficulties in the cases for which clip-flap method was especially effective caused poor elevation of submucosal layer despite after submucosal injection due to the presence of submucosal fibrosis or vessels (68.2%), and poor visualization of submucosal layer due to vertical approach (31.8%). Clip-flap method greatly improved the visualization of the cutting area even those challenging situations.
Conclusion: The clip-flap method facilitated the mucosal flap creation and its adoption allowed our treatment outcomes to be greatly improved. This study demonstrates that the clip-flap method is a simple, safe, and effective option for colorectal ESD. In technically difficult cases, the clip-flap method seems to be especially effective for poor elevation of submucosal layer due to the presence of submucosal fibrosis or vessels, and vertical approach for the lesions.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

2. Yamamoto K, Hayashi S, Saiki H, et al. Endoscopic submucosal dissection for large superficial colorectal tumors using the “clip-flap method.” Endoscopy 2015; 47:262–265.

## OP050 EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF ENDOSCOPIC FULL-THICKNESS RESECTION IN THE COLORECTUM WITH THE FTRD SYSTEM – INTERIM RESULTS OF A GERMAN REGISTRY
A. Schmidt1, B. Meier2, A. Fischer1, M. Wegener3, T. Wiedbrauck3, M. Repp4, G. Fitzel4, G. Hübner5, D. Albers6, B. Schumacher6, A. Erhardt7, K. Gutberlet8, A. Bielich9, D. Scholz9, M. Caselitz10, T. Frieling11, M. Breidert12, C. Rasch13, K. Fellermann14, K. Caca2

Introduction: The Full-Thickness Resection Device (FTRD) is an over-the-scope system approved for endoscopic full-thickness resection (EFTR) in the lower GI tract. Small retrospective studies and a recent prospective study have shown good efficacy and acceptable safety of the device. We present the interim analysis of the German multicenter registry.
Aims & Methods: The prospective multicenter German online registry was designed to generate “real-life” data on efficacy and safety of the device. Data of patients (n = 250) which was entered by 31 German centers between 09/2015 and 10/2016 was analysed.
Results: 250 FTRD procedures were registered. Major indications for EFTR were non-lifting adenomas (49%), early carcinomas (23%), adenomas at the appencical orifice (7%) and subepithelial tumors (6%). 173/250 lesions (69%) were located in the colon and 77/250 (31%) were located in the rectum. Median lesion size was 20 × 15 mm. Median procedure time was 45 min (5−150 min). R0 resection rate was 79%. Adverse events were recorded in 20/250 (8%) of cases including 8 perforations (3.2%; 5/8 were due to wrong sequence of procedural steps) and 7 minor bleedings (2.8%). Follow-up was available from 200 cases, median follow up time was 10 weeks (0.5−77). Residual or recurrent lesions were observed in 12% of cases.
Conclusion: The preliminary results of this registry show good efficacy and safety of EFTR with the FTRD System. These “real-life” results are consistent with previous studies.

## OP051 MINIMISING THE RISK OF DELAYED BLEEDING IN COLONIC ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION: IS THERE A ROLE FOR A NOVEL HAEMOSTATIC PEPTIDE?

Introduction: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is now an established technique to treat precancerous and early cancerous lesions in the colon. Delayed bleeding is a well-recognised complication following colonic ESD that can occur in up to 5% of patients. The risk of bleeding may be increased depending on the lesion size, location, anticoagulant use, age and co-morbidities. The endoscopic management of delayed bleeding conventionally includes electrocautery of visible vessels although there has been growing interest in topical haemostatic products that can be applied over the ESD resection site. Purastat® is a novel extracellular scaffold matrix that gels upon blood contact for haemostasis. It is hypothesised that it can reduce the risk of delayed bleeding when applied prophylactically over the ESD resection base.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to compare the rate of delayed bleeding in a cohort of patients who had received prophylactic application of Purastat® following colonic ESD with a control group where no bleeding prophylaxis was used. Methods: Data on the lesion size, location, age, gender and delayed bleed rate was collected from a cohort of patients who had received Purastat® prophylactically and compared to a recent historic control group. A delayed bleed was defined as a significant bleed occurring after the completion of ESD necessitating further intervention, hospital readmission or blood transfusion.
Results: There were 76 patients in the Purastat® group compared to 202 in the control cohort. The table below shows the patient demographics, location and size of lesions as well as delayed bleeding rates in both groups.

 Conclusion: This study has demonstrated that the rate of bleeding in colonic ESD was reduced by just over 50% in the group of patients receiving Purastat® prophylaxis. The risk of bleeding may be higher in large rectal lesions (>50 mm). The device was easy to use with complete coverage of the resection base achieved. Despite the limitation of this study with unmatched controls, the results do support its potential in reducing the risk of bleeding following colonic ESD. A prospective randomised controlled trial is required to evaluate its haemostatic efficacy in greater detail.

## OP052 ENEMA OF MESENCHYMAL STEM CELL CULTURE SUPERNATANT PREVENTS RECTAL STRICTURE FORMATION AFTER CIRCUMFERENTIAL ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION IN PIGS
M. Tsuda1, S. Ohnishi1, T. Mizushima1, S. Abiko1, Y. Shimizu2, N. Sakamoto1

1Department Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Hokkaido University Graduate School of Medicine, Sapporo/Japan

2Division Of Endoscopy, Hokkaido University Hospital, Sapporo/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
momoko0221tsuda@gmail.com

Introduction: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) for colorectal tumors has been widely accepted in the last decades as a minimally invasive treatment option with higher en bloc resections and a lower recurrence rate. Although stricture formation after ESD of large colorectal tumors has been reported, underlying mechanisms in developing stricture is not fully understood. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are a valuable cell source in regenerative medicine, and MSC culture supernatant (MSC-CS) has reportedly inhibited inflammation and fibrosis.
Aims & Methods: The aims of this study were to investigate whether circumferential ESD in the colorectum causes stricture formation, and to examine the effect of MSC-CS enema on post-ESD stricture. We performed circumferential ESD with 5 cm long axis in the rectum or distal colon in 20 kg pigs. We prepared MSC-CS gel by mixing MSC-CS with 5% carboxymethyl cellulose and administered into the rectum immediately after ESD from day 1 through day 4. We applied standard medium gel as a control group. We euthanized the pigs on day 22, measured the stricture rate, and performed histological analysis. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Hokkaido University.
Results: Severe stricture was observed in the rectum but not distal colon (Stricture rate: 60.7 ± 16.8% versus 16.1 ± 12.6%, P < 0.01, n = 4 in each group). Moreover, extensive fibrosis and hypertrophy of the muscularis propria were observed in the rectum, but not distal colon. In addition, the numbers of infiltrated neutrophils and activated myofibroblasts were significantly higher in the rectum than in the distal colon. Rectal stricture rate was significantly lower in the MSC-CS group compared with control group on day 22 (14.7 ± 0.6% versus 63.9 ± 27.4%, P < 0.05, n = 3 in each group). Furthermore, MSC-CS significantly attenuated the numbers of infiltrated neutrophils and activated myofibroblasts as well as fiber accumulation on day 22.
Conclusion: Stricture after circumferential ESD was developed only in the rectum, and associated with the activation of myofibroblasts and fiber accumulation. In addition, MSC-CS enema prevented the stricture formation after circumferential ESD in the rectum by suppressing the infiltration of neutrophils and following myofibroblast activation and fibrosis. MSC-CS enema would be a promising treatment to prevent post-ESD stricture.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP053 A NOVEL TEMPERATURE-RESPONSIVE, BIODEGRADABLE AND INJECTABLE COLLAGEN SOL FOR ENDOSCOPIC CLOSURE OF COLONIC PERFORATION HOLE: AN ANIMAL STUDY
T. Uraoka1, S. Kinoshita2, S. Yunoki3, T. Narita3, Y. Takatori2, H. Mori2, Y. Hirai2, S. Banno2, Y. Kubosawa2, Y. Sunata2, M. Shimoda4, N. Yahagi1

1Division Of Research And Development For Minimally Invasive Treatment, Cancer Center, Keio University, Tokyo/Japan

2Gastroenterology, National Hospital Organization Tokyo Medical Center, Tokyo/Japan

3Biotechnology Group, Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Technology Research Institute, Tokyo/Japan

4Department Of Pathology, Keio University, Tokyo/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
turaoka@a3.keio.jp

Introduction: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) can remove large size of early stage colorectal cancer en bloc; however, this procedure has a risk of intraprocedure perforation. Although an appropriate endoscopic closure using endoclipping is required, this technique is sometimes technically difficult. Recently, we have developed a biodegradable injectable collagen sol that forms liquid to gel formation in response to body temperature1.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to determine the feasibility of this novel injectable collagen sol for endoscopic closure of iatrogenic perforation hole. The ethics committee of our institution approved the use of four living 25–30 kg female pigs under the general anesthesia in this experiment. An ESD knife with an electric current made a 3–5 mm perforation hole in the colon at 30 to 40 cm from the anal verge resulting in the collapse of the colonic lumen. We performed two studies using 12 and 5 perforation holes on 4 and 3 pigs, respectively. Study 1: At the beginning of the collapse of the colon due to perforation, the 1.4–1.6% neutral collagen sol containing 4 mM of genipin was delivered to the perforation hole using an endoscopic catheter. When the colon was expanded by CO2 insufflation after one-minute pass, three endoclips were applied to the perforation area. Study 2: We only included the use of the collagen sol for endoscopic closure. Collagen sol which was adjusted based on the result of Study 1 was delivered to perforation holes in the same manner to Study 1. After confirming an expanded colon by CO2 insufflation after one-minute pass, an endoscope was withdrawn. All pigs were euthanized immediately after clipping and an hour after endoscopic evaluation in Study 1 and 2, respectively. A leak test was performed for every colon and we also evaluated histology of all perforation sites.
Results: In both studies, collagen sol was smoothly delivered to the target area and fixed as a gel on perforation hole in response to body temperature. Study 1: Although collagen gel was not fixed on two perforation holes, ten of 12 perforation holes were completely closed and then all endoclips were placed with composure. There was no leak from the perforation hole. Study 2: An endoscope confirmed complete closure of the perforation holes with collagen gel in the all pigs. There was also no leak from the perforation hole. Histology revealed a fixation of collagen gel as a thrombus agent in the perforation hole.
Conclusion: A novel temperature-responsive, biodegradable and injectable collagen sol may be used for endoscopic closure of intraprocedure perforation. Further studies are necessary to determine the clinical feasibility and safety of this collagen sol.

## OP054 EARLY MUCOSAL HEALING IN PATIENTS WITH MODERATE TO SEVERE ULCERATIVE COLITIS TREATED WITH GOLIMUMAB PREDICTS FAVORABLE OUTCOMES: DATA FROM THE REAL-LIFE BE-SMART COHORT

Introduction: Golimumab (GOL) is registered for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis (UC). Data on the use of GOL in daily clinical practice are limited. Currently, it is unclear which factors are predictive for a favorable outcome.
Aims & Methods: The aim of the study is to evaluate the mid-term outcome of GOL in patients with moderate-to-severe UC and to determine predictors of favourable outcome. Patients included in the SMART study (NCT02155335) were evaluated for their mid-term outcome. Demographic data, disease characteristics and medical history were recorded retrospectively. Data on disease activity based on total MAYO score, previous and concomitant medication, GOL dosing, mucosal healing (Mayo 0 or 1), adverse events (colectomy, hospitalization) and biomarkers (C-reactive protein, fecal calprotectin, hemoglobin and albumin) were collected at baseline, week 2, 6, 14, 26 and 52. The primary endpoint was steroid-free GOL continuation at week 26.
Results: Eight out of 100 patients from the SMART study had to be excluded (low baseline disease activity, misdiagnosis, loss of follow-up). From the 92 patients (42% female, median age 41 years, median disease duration 5 years) 4% were active smokers, 25% had extensive colitis, and 38% had an endoscopic Mayo score of 3 at baseline. The median (IQR) baseline Mayo score was 9 (8–10). While 76% of patients had previously failed immunomodulators (IMM), the majority (87%) were anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) naive. GOL was started in combination with IMM and steroids in 38% and 64%, respectively. The median (IQR) follow-up on GOL therapy was 36 (12–106) weeks. Twenty six weeks after GOL induction, 38 patients (41%) were steroid-free and still on GOL, of whom 6 required GOL dose optimization. Short-term mucosal healing (STMH) at week 14 could be evaluated in 52% of the patients and was achieved in half of them. In multivariate analysis, only concomitant systemic steroids (p = 0.044) were predictive of STMH. Patients with STMH more frequently achieved the primary endpoint [67% vs. 29%, OR 4.86 (95%CI 1.43–16.50), p = 0.011]. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 26 (23–30) months, 78% needed a therapeutic intervention and 63% discontinued GOL. STMH was significantly associated with intervention free survival (p = 0.030) and prolonged treatment of GOL (p = 0.002).
Conclusion: Real-life data confirm the effectiveness of GOL on the mid-term in moderate to severe UC, although therapeutic interventions are needed frequently. Short-term mucosal healing predicts a favorable outcome.

## OP055 PREDICTION OF CLINICAL OUTCOMES IN CROHN’S DISEASE BY USING CONFOCAL LASER ENDOMICROSCOPY: A PROSPECTIVE MULTICENTER STUDY
G.E. Tontini1, J. Mudter2, M. Vieth3, C. Günther2, V. Milani4, R. Atreya5, T. Rath5, A. Nägel2, G. Hatem6, G.C. Sturniolo6, M. Vecchi1, M.F. Neurath2, P. R. Galle7, A. Buda8, H. Neumann9

1Gastroenterology And Digestive Endoscopy Unit, IRCCS Policlinico San Donato, San Donato Milanese/Italy

2Department Of Medicine I, University of Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen/Germany

3Abt. Pathologie, Klinikum Bayreuth Abt. Pathology, Bayreuth/Germany

4IRCCS Policlinico San Donato, San Donato Milanese/Italy

5Medical Department I, University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Erlangen/Germany

6Department Of Surgical, Oncological, And Gastroenterological Sciences, University of Padua, Padua/Italy

7First Medical Department, University Medical Center Mainz, Mainz/Germany

8Gastroenterology And Digestive Endoscopy Unit, Ospedale di Feltre, Feltre/Italy

9Universitätsmedizin Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Mainz/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
gianeugeniotontini@libero.it

Introduction: Emerging evidence clearly shows that the precise assessment of prognostic factors is of pivotal importance for early intervention and treat-to-target strategies in Crohn’s disease (CD) patients. Confocal Laser Endomicroscopy (CLE) is an advance endoscopic imaging technique that enables on demand in vivo characterization of mucosal architectural changes during ongoing endoscopy.
Aims & Methods: We prospectively assessed the value of CLE for the prediction of relevant clinical outcome parameters in CD. Patients undergoing colonoscopy for disease assessment were consecutively included in this multicentre study at two referral IBD units (Erlangen, Germany and Padua, Italy). CLE imaging focused on two highly reproducible histological hallmarks of colonic inflammation: focal cryptitis and crypt architectural abnormality [1]. We have evaluated whether CLE, CD endoscopic index of severity (CDEIS), serum C-reactive protein (CRP) and CD activity index (CDAI) were associated with the risk of medical treatment escalation, transmural complications, and CD-related hospitalisation or surgery during a four-year follow-up.
Results: Forty-nine patients (53% men, 39 years [IQR = 30–47years]) met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Among them, the baseline (CRP) was ≥5 mg/L in 47%, CDEIS was ≥3 in 75%, and CDAI was >150 in 51%. Focal cryptitis and crypt architectural abnormality were observed in 63% of them (i.e., positive CLE group). Patients with positive CLE at baseline showed an increased incidence of medical treatment escalation (P < 0.001, RR = 3.27) and transmural lesions (P = 0.025, RR = 1.70), while patients with high level of CRP with CD-related hospitalisation and surgery (P = 0.020, RR = 2.71) at one-year follow-up. No association was found over the one-year follow-up, and for CDEIS as well as CDAI at any time.

 Conclusion: This prospective multicenter study confirms that CLE can reveal CD-related features of mucosal inflammation during ongoing endoscopy, threby predicting two higly reproducible histopathological hallmarks of active large-bowel mucosal inflammation. In addition, the CLE assessment allows for early prediction of relevant clinical outcomes related to CD such as the need for treatment escalation and the risk of transmural complications at one-year follow-up. Further studies should now address whether this promising prognostic tool could refine the timing of treatment strategies in patients suffering from CD.

1. Tontini GE, Mudter J, Vieth M, et al. Confocal laser endomicroscopy for the differential diagnosis of ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease: a pilot study. Endoscopy 2015;47(5):437–43.

## OP056 HISTOLOGICAL PREDICTORS OF RELAPSE IN ULCERATIVE COLITIS: WHICH FEATURES MATTER MOST?
B. Gonzalez Suarez1, E. U. Yee2, T. Zenlea1, L. Rosenberg1, K.S. Nande1, J. D. Goldsmith2, A. C. Moss1

1Gastroenterology Department, Center for Inflammatory Bowel Disease, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston/United States of America/MA

2Department Of Pathology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston/United States of America/MA

Contact E-mail Address:
bgonzals@clinic.ub.es

Introduction: Histological scores used in Ulcerative Colitis (UC) contain many morphological features. The comparative association of the individual score components with clinical relapse has not been validated to date. Our goal was to compare components of the Geboes Scale and their association with clinical relapse over 12 months.
Aims & Methods: Patients with UC in clinical and endoscopic remission (Mayo score < 1) had their Geboes Scale determined at baseline by an experienced GI pathologist. They were then prospectively followed after colonoscopy and relapse was evaluated 12 months later. We categorized Geboes Scale as a continuous variable to generate a ROC Curve and establish a cut-off point predictive for relapse.
Results: We included 89 patients in clinical and endoscopic remission. Biopsies on the Geboes Scale were scored >3.1 in 29% of subjects at enrollment. Fourteen patients (16%) developed relapse after 12 months of follow-up. All individual components of the Geboes Scale were significantly associated with relapse, except the presence of eosinophils, in univariate analysis. However, in a multivariate analysis, only the presence of crypt destruction was an independent predictive factor for relapse (p < 0.00001). Using the Geboes Scale to generate an ROC curve, the AUC was 0.73, and the optimal sensitivity and specificity (71% and 68%) for clinical relapse over 12 months was at a cutoff of 1.2 (5.5 when converted to a continuous scale).
Conclusion: Most components of the Geboes Scale associate with risk of clinical relapse, but only crypt destruction is independently associated with this outcome. This may allow development of more simple histological scores of prognostic importance.

## OP057 DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION OF THE “MINI INDEX” (MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION -NON INVASIVE INDEX) FOR CROHN’S DISEASE ON A LARGE PROSPECTIVE PEDIATRIC COHORT
A. Ben Shoham1, M. A. Cozijnsen2, B. Kang3, B. Choe3, Y.H. Choe4, R. K. Russell5, F. M. Ruemmele6, J. C. Escher2, L. De Ridder2, S. Koletzko7, J. Martin De Carpi8, J. S. Hyams9, T. D. Walters10, A. M. Griffiths10, D. Turner1

1Shaare Zedek Medical Center, Jerusalem/Israel

2Erasmus, Rotterdam/Netherlands

3Kyungpook, Seoul/Korea, Democratic People's Republic of

4Samsung, Seoul/Korea, Democratic People's Republic of

5Royal Hospital, Glasgow/United Kingdom

6Hôpital Necker, Paris/France

7Dr. von Hauner Children’s Hospital, München/Germany

8Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, Barcelona/Spain

9Connecticut Children’s Medical Center, Hartford, United States of America/CT

10SickKids, Toronto/Canada/ON

Contact E-mail Address:
turnerd@szmc.org.il

Introduction: Mucosal healing (MH) has become an important therapeutic goal in Crohn’s disease (CD). Repeated assessments by ileocolonoscopy are less feasible, especially in children. The Pediatric Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (PCDAI) does not correlate well with mucosal inflammation. We aimed to develop and validate a multi-item index, based on clinical and laboratory parameters, which could reflect MH in clinical trials as well as for clinical practice.
Aims & Methods: This study utilized data from the prospective ImageKids study where children with CD underwent ileocolonoscopy concurrent with recording of explicit clinical and laboratory data, including fecal calprotectin (FC), at disease onset or thereafter. PCDAI items, laboratory tests and FC, were associated with the Simple Endoscopic Score for CD (SESCD) in a multivariate analysis and validated on an independent prospective cohort from Korea of children whose workup included ileocolonoscopy, clinical and lab assessment and FC. We employed a blended clinimetric judgmental and psychometric mathematical approach.
Results: The derivation and validation cohorts included 154 and 86 children, respectively (n = 240; age 14.6 ± 2.6 years; SES-CD 7.8 ± 8.2), of whom 24 (16%) and 56 (65%) had MH (i.e. SESCD < 3), respectively. In a multivariate regression analysis, the stool and weight items of the PCDAI, ESR and FC were associated with SESCD (all p < 0.05). Judgmentally, we removed the weight item and included CRP, to form a weighted categorized MINI index (Table). In the validation cohort the sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of the MINI to reflect MH using a cutoff of <8 was 91%, 67%, 84% and 80% (AUROC curve 0.90 (95%CI 0.84–0.96)). In the entire cohort (n = 216) the correlation between MINI and SESCD was r = 0.783 (p < 0.001).

 Conclusion: In children with ileocolonic CD, the MINI-index can reflect MH with a good accuracy. The likelihood of MH with a MINI<8 points is 84%.

## OP058 LITTLE BENEFIT OF ENDOSCOPIC-BASED THERAPEUTIC MANAGEMENT IN POSTOPERATIVE RECURRENT CROHN'S DISEASE: RESULTS OF A RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
P. Rivière1, S. Vermeire2, G. Van Assche2, P. Rutgeerts2, A. De Buck Van Overstraeten3, A. Wolthuis3, A. D'Hoore3, M. Ferrante2

1Gastroenterology, Bordeaux University Hospital, Bordeaux/France

2Department of Gastroenterology, University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven/Belgium

3Abdominal Surgery, University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven/Belgium

Contact E-mail Address:
riviere.paulin@gmail.com

Introduction: The Rutgeerts’ score (RS) is widely used to guide post-operative management of patients with Crohn’s disease (CD) undergoing a resection with ileo-colonic anastomosis. The modified RS differentiates lesions at the anastomosis with or without <5 isolated neo-terminal ileal erosions (i2a) from presence of ≥5 isolated neo-terminal ileal erosions with or without anastomotic lesions (i2b), but its clinical relevance has not been validated.
Aims & Methods: We investigated if clinical relapse (CR) and need for endoscopic dilatation (ED) or new surgical intervention (NSI) differ between i2a and i2b endoscopic recurrence (ER). Our secondary objective was to evaluate the effect of therapy modification based on endoscopic findings in patients with an i2a or i2b RS, or a RS > = i3. This was a single-center retrospective study, including all patients operated between 2000 and 2013 with a colonoscopy <12 months after ileo-colonic anastomosis and >3 years of follow-up after endoscopy. The modified RS was attributed based on the available endoscopic report and images. CR was defined as the occurrence of CD related symptoms along with objective signs of disease activity. Kaplan-Meier curves were plotted for time from index endoscopy to CR, ED and NSI and compared through Log rank tests.
Results: The study population consisted of 296 patients [123 males, median age 40 years]. At index endoscopy, 61 patients (20.6%) had a RS i0, 24 (8.1%) i1, 81 (27.4%) i2a, 69 (23.3%) i2b, 35 (11.8%) i3 and 26 (8.8%) i4. Medical treatment was optimized according to index colonoscopy in 4 (4.7%) patients with i0/i1 and 88 (41.7%) with > = i2a [Odds ratio 11.0 (95%CI 5.6–24.4), p < 0.001]. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 76 (48–113) months, CR, ED and NSI were observed in 150 (50.7%), 51 (17.2%) and 36 (12.2%) patients, respectively. Patients with i2a and i2b had a similar risk for CR, ED or NSI (Log Rank p = 0.19, p = 0.10 and p = 0.30, respectively). Also after exclusion of patients with immediate post-endoscopy treatment optimization, i2a and i2b scores were not predictive (Log Rank p = 0.22, p = 0.21 and p = 0.41, respectively). Probability of CR was higher in patients with an i3 or i4 compared to the others (Log Rank p < 0.001). A RS > = i2a [1.62 (1.06–2.50), p = 0.03], active smoking at endoscopy [1.61 (1.08–2.39), p = 0.02] and CRP >5 mg/l at endoscopy [1.76 (1.17–2.65), p = 0.01] were associated with CR during the follow-up in patients without clinical relapse at endoscopy. In patients with a RS = i2, initiation of an immunosuppressant or biological therapy after endoscopy was not associated with a different outcome in terms of CR or NSI (p = 0.59 and p = 0.66, respectively). Only a modest benefit in terms of CR was observed for patients with a RS = i3 or i4 when an immunosuppressant or biological therapy was introduced after endoscopy (p = 0.03), but the risk of NSI was not influenced (p = 0.14).
Conclusion: No difference was observed in terms of clinical relapse and need for endoscopic/surgical intervention between patients with i2a or i2b endoscopic recurrence after ileo-colonic resection with ileo-colonic anastomosis. In patients with a RS = i2, no effect on probability of clinical relapse or need for a new surgery was observed when an immunosuppressant or a biological treatment were initiated after the index endoscopy. Despite intensification of therapy based on endoscopic findings, outcomes of i3 and i4 patients remain poor in our cohort.

## OP059 TOFACITINIB FOR MAINTENANCE THERAPY IN PATIENTS WITH ACTIVE ULCERATIVE COLITIS IN THE PHASE 3 OCTAVE SUSTAIN TRIAL: RESULTS BY LOCAL AND CENTRAL ENDOSCOPIC ASSESSMENTS
B. G. Feagan1, S. Vermeire2, W. J. Sandborn3, W. Reinisch4, J. Panés5, D. Tarabar6, C. Su7, W. Niezychowski7, H. Zhang7, G. Friedman7, D. Woodworth7, B.E. Sands8

1Robarts Research Institute, Western University, London/Canada/ON

2Department Of Gastroenterology, University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven/Belgium

3Division Of Gastroenterology, University of California, La Jolla, San Diego/United States of America/CA

4Division Of Gastroenterology, McMaster University, Hamilton/Canada/ON

5Hospital Clinic de Barcelona, IDIBAPS, CIBERehd, Barcelona/Spain

6Clinic For Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Military Medical Academy, Belgrade/Serbia

7Pfizer Inc, Collegeville/United States of America/PA

8Dr. Henry D. Janowitz Division Of Gastroenterology, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York/United States of America/NY

Contact E-mail Address:
brian.feagan@robartsinc.com

Introduction: Tofacitinib is an oral, small molecule Janus kinase inhibitor that is being investigated for ulcerative colitis (UC). A Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance study (OCTAVE Sustain, NCT01458574) demonstrated the efficacy of tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg twice daily (BID) vs placebo in patients (pts) with moderate to severe UC.
Aims & Methods: We describe the clinical efficacy endpoints assessed by local endoscopy readings and previously reported results assessed by central readings. Pts who completed one of two studies (OCTAVE Induction 1, NCT01465763; OCTAVE Induction 2, NCT01458951) and achieved clinical response were eligible to participate in OCTAVE Sustain. Clinical response was defined by a decrease from induction study baseline in Mayo score of ≥3 points and ≥30%, with an accompanying decrease in rectal bleeding subscore ≥1 or an absolute rectal bleeding subscore ≤1. 593 pts were randomised (1:1:1) to receive placebo, tofacitinib 5 or 10 mg BID for 53 weeks (wks) in OCTAVE Sustain. Pts’ eligibility was assessed based on central endoscopic reading. Pts entering OCTAVE Sustain were permitted concomitant treatment with oral corticosteroids, although tapering was mandatory from study baseline. Concomitant treatment with immunosuppressants and biologics was prohibited. Efficacy endpoints assessed at Wk 52 included remission (primary endpoint: Mayo score ≤2, no individual subscore >1 and rectal bleeding subscore of 0), mucosal healing (Mayo endoscopic subscore ≤1) and clinical response.
Results: At Wk 52, remission was achieved by significantly more pts treated with tofacitinib 5 or 10 mg BID compared with placebo, as demonstrated by both central and local endoscopic readings (Table). Similar results were observed at Wk 52 with mucosal healing, clinical response and sustained, steroid-free remission among pts in remission at baseline. Efficacy assessed by local endoscopic readings was numerically greater than central readings, except for clinical response. There was good agreement between locally and centrally read endoscopic subscores (kappa = 0.6 [95% CI 0.5, 0.6]).

 Conclusion: Efficacy assessed by local endoscopic readings was numerically greater than efficacy assessed by central readings for tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg BID compared to placebo. Overall, local endoscopic readings were consistent with central readings. Both methods demonstrated that tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg BID were both more effective than placebo for maintenance therapy in pts with moderately to severely active UC.

## OP060 GLUTEN INGESTION AND INTRADERMAL INJECTION OF PEPTIDES THAT ACTIVATE GLUTEN-SPECIFIC CD4+ T CELLS ELICIT A CYTOKINE SIGNATURE DOMINATED BY INTERLEUKIN-2 IN CELIAC DISEASE
J. A. Tye-Din1, J. J. Dzuris2, A. K. Russell1, S. Wang2, K. E. Goldstein2, L. J. Williams2, R. P. Anderson2

1Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, Parkville/Australia

2ImmusanT, Cambridge/United States of America

Contact E-mail Address:
bob@immusant.com

Introduction: The explanation for symptoms experienced by celiac disease (CeD) patients within hours of gluten ingestion has puzzled researchers because the early onset seems incompatible with a T-cell mediated (delayed hypersensitivity) effect. We hypothesized the role for gluten-specific CD4+ T cells in gluten-responsive symptoms could be tested by comparing acute immune effects of ingesting gluten with intradermal injection of Nexvax2®, an experimental adjuvant-free therapeutic vaccine that is a mixture of three short peptides including immunodominant epitopes for gluten-specific CD4+ T cells.
Aims & Methods: To assess changes in circulating cytokines in CeD volunteers on GFD after eating gluten or after intradermal administration of Nexvax2. Methods: A time course assessment of 19 cytokines and chemokines in plasma and sera from adult HLA-DQ2.5+ CeD volunteers on a GFD were compared from two separate studies. The first was a double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge (DBPCFC) with ∼3 g wheat gluten flour compared to a matched gluten-free drink over 10 min. The second study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 clinical trial of Nexvax2 (Goel et al. Lancet Gastro Hepatol 2017) with plasma assessed after the first dose of Nexvax2 150 mg or normal saline i.d. in 0.1 mL. Chemokines (eotaxin, MIP-1β, eotaxin-3, TARC, IP-10, MIP-1α, MCP-1, MDC, MCP-4) and cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12p70, IL-13, TNF-α) were measured by the Meso Scale Discovery multiplex ELISA platform.
Results: Cytokine and chemokine assessments were performed in 19 subjects after DBPCFC (11 administered gluten, & 8 non-gluten), and in 14 subjects in the final “biopsy” cohort of the phase 1 study of Nexvax2 (7 administered Nexvax2, & 7 placebo). In the first 5 subjects after gluten ingestion, hourly profiling indicated IL-2 elevation from 2 h (median 5-fold rise compared to predose, range 1.1–117) and plateauing between 3 to 5 h (median maximal fold-change 21, range 2.6–94). Median fold increase in IL-8 was between 1.8 and 2.4 from 3 to 6 h (median maximal fold-change 2.5, range 1.3–28). Median fold increases were less than 2 for other cytokines and chemokines for all time points. Overall, serum assessed from before, and at 4 and 6 h showed median IL-2 fold change of 15 at 4 h after gluten (range: 1.9–39, n = 11) compared to 1.0 for non-gluten (0.5–1.6, n = 8; p < 0.0001 Mann Whitney). For IL-8, median fold change at 4 h after gluten was 2.4 (range: 1.0–8.4, n = 11) compared to 1.1 for placebo (0.7–1.3, n = 8; p = 0.012 Mann Whitney). Apart from IL-2 at 6 h, no other cytokines or chemokines showed median elevation above 2-fold at any time points after gluten ingestion. After Nexvax2, median fold changes at 2, 4 and 6 h post-dose in IL-2 were 14 (range: 1.3–68), 127 (range: 2.1–915), and 70 (range: 1.6–396), and in IL-8 were 1.6 (range: 0.9–2.8), 11 (range: 2.1–28), and 5.3 (range: 2.0–12). Weaker median fold rises of at least 2 were observed after Nexvax2 but not placebo in MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-10, IFN-γ, MIP-1β, IP-10, IL-4, eotaxin, and TNFα.
Conclusion: Il-2, a T-cell specific cytokine, dominates the cytokine signature present between 2–6 h after gluten ingestion or intradermal administration of Nexvax2. These findings suggest ingestion of gluten or injection of peptides activate T cells rapidly, and could account for symptoms triggered by gluten.

## OP061 BACTERIAL MODULATION OF INTESTINAL INNATE ACTIVATION INDUCED BY WHEAT AMYLASE TRYPSIN INHIBITORS (ATIS) IN NOD-DQ8 MICE
V.F. Zevallos1, J. McCarville2, A. Caminero2, E. Verdu2, D. Schuppan1

1Institute Of Translational Immunology, University of Mainz, Mainz/Germany

2Farncombe Family Digestive Health Research Institute, McMaster University, Hamilton/Canada/ON

Contact E-mail Address:
zevallos@uni-mainz.de

Introduction: Wheat alpha-amylase/trypsin inhibitors (ATIs) are nutritional activators of intestinal innate immunity via the toll like receptor 4 (TLR4)-MD2-CD14 complex in myeloid cells. We have observed that wheat ATIs enhance innate immune responses towards gluten in a host at risk, such as SPF NOD-DQ8 mice.
Aims & Methods: The aim of the study was to screen, identify and test bacterial strains with a capacity to degrade ATIs and therefore reduce their immune stimulatory activity in-vitro and in-vivo. Supernatants of a large group of intestinal bacterial species were incubated with ATI and degradation was monitored using Western blotting with polyclonal antibodies against the most prevalent ATI subtypes (CM3 and 0.19). The in vivo effects of two groups of bacteria with low and high ATI degrading capacities were assessed in by concomitant gavage with a single dose of ATIs in NOD-DQ8 mice on a gluten-free diet after 6 h.
Results: We identified commensal bacteria in vitro that have the capacity to degrade the main ATI subtypes. When the ATI-degrading bioactivity of those bacterial strains was tested in mice gavaged with ATIs, the bacteria combined or individually significantly reduced intestinal expression of TLR4-dependent proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, and serum levels of IL-6 when compared to mice that received the ATIs without the bacteria. Data were confirmed in myeloid cell cultures in vivo that were exposed to bacterial or control supernatants of ATIs with and without prior depletion of potential traits of LPS.
Conclusion: Some Lactobacillus strains have the capacity to modulate the innate inflammatory effects of ATIs in vitro and in vivo. Since wheat-ATIs are implicated in the pathogenesis of celiac disease as well as non-celiac wheat sensitivity (NCWS), including the modulation of autoimmunity, therapeutic intestinal colonization with ATI degrading bacteria may be an attractive therapeutic target.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP062 HLA-DQ:GLUTEN TETRAMER TEST IN BLOOD GIVES BETTER DETECTION OF CELIAC PATIENTS THAN BIOPSY AFTER 14-DAY GLUTEN CHALLENGE
V.K. Sarna1, G.I. Skodje2, H. M. Reims3, L. F. Risnes4, S. Dahal-Koirala4, L. Sollid4, K.E. A. Lundin5

1Immunology And Transfusion Medicine, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo/Norway

2Nutrition, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo/Norway

3Pathology, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo/Norway

4Centre For Immune Regulation, Oslo University Hospital and University of Oslo, Oslo/Norway

5Gastroenterology, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo/Norway

Contact E-mail Address:
v.sarna@hotmail.com

Introduction: Initiation of a gluten-free diet without proper diagnostic work-up of coeliac disease is a frequent and demanding problem. Recent guidelines suggest a gluten challenge of at least 14 days followed by duodenal biopsy to establish a diagnosis in such patients. The rate of false negative outcome of this approach remains unclear. We aimed to study responses to 14-day gluten challenge in subjects with treated coeliac disease.
Aims & Methods: We challenged 20 subjects with biopsy-verified coeliac disease, all in confirmed mucosal remission, for 14 days with 5.7 g per oral gluten daily. Duodenal biopsies were collected. Blood was analyzed by flow cytometry using HLA-DQ:gluten tetramers, and by multiplex assay for cytokine detection.
Results: Nineteen participants completed the challenge. Villous blunting appeared at end of challenge in five of 19 subjects. Villous height to crypt depth ratio reduced with at least 0.4 concomitantly with an increase in intraepithelial lymphocyte count of at least 50% in nine of 19 subjects. IL-8 concentration increased by more than 100% after four hours in seven of 19 subjects. Number of blood CD4+ effector-memory gut-homing HLA-DQ:gluten tetramer-binding T cells increased by more than 100% on day 6 in 12 of 15 evaluated participants.
Conclusion: A 14-day gluten challenge is not enough to trigger significant mucosal architectural changes in majority of coeliac disease patients (sensitivity ≈ 25 – 50%). Increase in CD4+ effector-memory gut-homing HLA-DQ:gluten tetramer-binding T cells in blood six days after gluten challenge is a more sensitive and less invasive biomarker that should be validated in a larger study. Registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov (NCT02464150).
