## OP092 CAN MESALAZINE AFFECT THE PROGNOSIS OF ACUTE PANCREATITIS?––EVIDENCE FROM THE INTESTINE
L. Huang, W. Yang, J. Li, Y. Tai, C. Ye, S. Tang, C. Tang

Department Of Gastroenterology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu/China

Contact E-mail Address:
melody224@163.com

Introduction: The intestine plays an important role in the development of acute pancreatitis (AP). Previous studies have indicated that controlling the intestinal inflammation, restoring the intestinal mucosal barrier function and improving intestinal micro-ecological environment may lessen the severity of AP and improve its prognosis. Mesalazine has been proved to effectively alleviate active intestinal inflammation and regulate intestinal flora. However, it is still unclear whether mesalazine has similar effect in AP. This study is to investigate whether mesalazine can affect the prognosis of AP and to find out its evidence from the intestine.
Aims & Methods: 70 patients with AP were randomly divided into conventional treatment group (n = 38) and mesalazine group (n = 32). Meanwhile, 20 healthy adults were recruited for the analysis of intestinal flora in the healthy control group. Histological score of duodenal inflammation was evaluated after hematoxylin-eosin staining. The expression of myeloperoxidase in the duodenal mucosa was semi-quantified by immunohistochemistry for evaluating the extent of neutrophil infiltration. Second-generation high-throughput sequencing was performed to detect intestinal flora. Circulating levels of proinflammatory cytokines (C-reactive protein, interleukin (IL)-6, tumor necrosis factor-α, IL-8) were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay on admission and the 9th day after admission. During hospitalization, the incidence of organ failure, septic complications and death were recorded as well.
Results: 1) Mesalazine alleviated the inflammatory changes of duodenum. Histological scores of duodenal inflammation and neutrophil infiltration in duodenal mucosa were much lower in mesalazine group than that of in conventional treatment group (P < 0.05). 2) Compared with healthy control group, the proportion of aggressive bacteria of conventional treatment group were significantly elevated (P < 0.05), while that of protective bacteria were decreased significantly (P < 0.05). After mesalazine administration, the proportion of aggressive bacteria were decreased significantly (P < 0.05), while that of protective bacteria were increased significantly (P < 0.05). 3) Compared with conventional treatment, mesalazine markedly increased the degree of decline in circulating proinflammatory factors (P < 0.05). 4) Mesalazine significantly reduced the incidence of organ failure (P < 0.05).
Conclusion: Mesalazine could improve the prognosis of AP patients to a certain extent, possibly by rebalancing intestinal bacterial composition, alleviating duodenal and systemic inflammation.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.
References
1. Frossard JL, Steer ML, Pastor CM. Acute pancreatitis. Lancet, 2008, 371: 143–152.
2. Llopis M, Antolin M, Carol M, et al. Lactobacillus casei downregulates commensals' inflammatory signals in Crohn's disease mucosa. Inflamm Bowel Dis, 2009, 15: 275–283.
3. Sokol H, Pigneur B, Watterlot L, et al. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii is an anti-inflammatory commensal bacterium identified by gut microbiota analysis of Crohn disease patients. Proc Natl Acad Sci, 2008, 105: 16731–16736.
4. Kaufman J, Griffiths TA, Surette MG, et al. Effects of mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid) on bacterial gene expression. Inflamm Bowel Dis, 2009, 15: 985–996.

## OP093 STATINS AND RISK OF ACUTE PANCREATITIS - A META-ANALYSIS OF OBSERVATIONAL STUDIES
G. Poropat1, L. Archibugi2, T. Korpela3, K. Cardenas-Jaen4, E. De-Madaria4, G. Capurso2

1Department Of Gastroenterology, University Hospital Rijeka, Rijeka/Croatia

2Digestive & Liver Disease Unit, Sant'Andrea Hospital, Faculty of Medicine and Psychology, University of Rome "La Sapienza", Rome/Italy

3Department Of Surgery, Helsinki University Hospital, University of Helsinki, Helsinki/Finland

4Gastroenterology Department, Alicante University General Hospital. ISABIAL-FISABIO Foundation, Alicante/Spain

Contact E-mail Address:
goran_poropat@yahoo.com

Introduction: Existing reports on the association between statins administration and the risk of developing acute pancreatitis (AP) are contradictory. Statins are widely perceived as potential etiological factors for AP, but more recent evidence suggests the opposite. The mechanisms of their possible benefit is still unclear, with experimental studies showing potential specific anti-inflammatory aspects. The latest meta-analysis on this topic evaluted only clinical trials, excluding observational studies and found a reduced risk of AP in statin users.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the association between the use of statins and the risk of developing AP. Medline, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for cohort (C) and case-control (C-C) studies in which statins are included as an intervention and AP as an outcome regardless of publication language. Two authors independently searched the literature and extracted data. Disagreements were solved by discussion and by decision of a third author. Eligible studies were selected according to the PRISMA statement. Pooled adjusted ORs with corresponding 95% CIs were calculated using random effects model. Publication bias was assessed through Begg and Mazumdar test. Heterogeneity was assessed by means of the I2 value.
Results: A total of 13 studies (7 CC, 6 C) contributed to the analysis. A total of 34,899 AP patients and 5,377,894 controls were included. The pooled prevalence of statin use was 9.8% (3411/34,899) among AP patients and 25% (1,357,175/53,77,894) among controls. The pooled adjusted OR for the 13 studies was 1.00 (95% CI 0.63–1.59; p = 0.99) with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 98%). In a sensitivity analysis for study design, case-control studies were associated to an increased risk (OR 1.33; 95% CI 1.20–1.47; p < 0.0001), but cohort studies were not (OR 0.69; 95% CI 0.37–1.31; p = 0.26). Similarly, in a sensitivity analysis for country of origin no association with the risk was seen for Western countries (OR 0.90; 95% CI 0.52–1.56; p = 0.71) while there was an increased risk in studies conducted in Asia (OR 1.39; 95% CI 1.10–1.75; p = 0.006). There was evidence of publication bias (Begg and Mazudmar Kendall’s tau = −0.549; p = 0.006) suggesting that studies showing an increased risk of AP associated with statin use were more likely to be published than studies with negative results.
Conclusion: The results of the first meta-analysis of observational studies for the association between statins use and AP suggest the absence of an increased risk in statin users. Evidence for an increased risk is limited to case-control studies, while cohort studies showed no global effect, similarly to previous data from controlled trials. Further research on the topic is needed to clarify whether statin type, dosage, lenght of use or etiology of AP might account for this difference.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP094 CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF PATHOGENIC CTRC, CFTR AND SPINK1 MUTATIONS IN CHILDHOOD-ONSET PANCREATITIS (DATA ANALYSIS FROM APPLE STUDY)
B. Nemeth1, A. Parniczky2, C. Pienar3, M. Sahin-Toth4, P. Hegyi5

1First Department Of Medicine, University of Szeged, Szeged/Hungary

2Heim Pal Children’s Hospital, Budapest/Hungary

3Pediatrics Department, "Victor Babes" University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Timisoara/Romania

4Center For Exocrine Disorders, Department Of Molecular And Cell Biology, Boston University Henry M. Goldman School of Dental Medicine, Boston/United States of America/MA

5Institute For Translational Medicine, University of Pecs, Pecs/Hungary

Contact E-mail Address:
nemeth.balazs@med.u-szeged.hu

Introduction: Increasing incidence of pancreatitis was observed in children in the past years. Genetic risk is a significant etiological factor in pediatric cases. Specific genetic testing became relatively widely available after the discovery of susceptibility genes. Mutations in the CTRC, CFTR and SPINK1 genes are overrepresented in pediatric pancreatitis. It is still unclear whether these mutations change the clinical onset and outcome in these patients.
Aims & Methods: Our aim was to perform genetic testing and investigation of genotype-phenotype associations in childhood-onset pancreatitis. Patients with childhood-onset pancreatitis (n = 121) were recruited by the Hungarian Pancreatitis Study Group. The clinical data of patients who carried known pathogenic mutation(s) in the CTRC (n = 41) or CFTR (n = 15) or SPINK1 (n = 13) genes were compared to those patients who did not have any known genetic risk factor (n = 62).
Results: Patients with pancreatitis who carried pathogenic CTRC or SPINK1 mutations more likely developed recurrent acute or chronic pancreatitis than those patients who did not have any genetic risk factor (48.7% or 70% vs. 8.8%, respectively). Additionally, average number of documented acute episodes was higher in patients carrying CTRC or SPINK1 mutation(s) compared to the control group (4.5 or 3.4 vs. 1.5, respectively). Age of onset and days spent in the hospital did not differ significantly between groups of patients carrying pathogenic mutation(s) (CTRC or CFTR or SPINK1) and patients without any known genetic risk factor.
Conclusion: Patients with childhood-onset pancreatitis more likely develop recurrent acute or chronic pancreatitis if they carry pathogenic CTRC or SPINK1 mutation(s). Moreover, they develop acute episodes more frequently compared to those patients who do not have genetic risk factor. Mutations in the CTRC orCFTR or SPINK1 genes do not influence the age of onset and the duration of hospitalization in children with pancreatitis.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP095 TOFACITINIB, AN ORAL JANUS KINASE INHIBITOR, IN THE TREATMENT OF ULCERATIVE COLITIS: OPEN-LABEL, LONG-TERM EXTENSION STUDY
G. R. Lichtenstein1, E.V. Loftus Jr2, S. Bloom3, N. Lawendy4, G. Friedman4, H. Zhang4, W. Wang4, A. J. Thorpe4, C. Nduaka4, C. Su4

1Division Of Gastroenterology, Perelman School of Medicine of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia/United States of America/PA

2Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester/United States of America/MN

3University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, London/United Kingdom

4Pfizer Inc, Collegeville/United States of America/PA

Contact E-mail Address:
stuart.bloom@uclh.nhs.uk

Introduction: Tofacitinib is an oral, small molecule Janus kinase inhibitor that is being investigated for ulcerative colitis (UC). The efficacy and safety of tofacitinib was demonstrated as induction and maintenance therapy in three Phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled studies (OCTAVE Induction 1, NCT01465763; OCTAVE Induction 2, NCT01458951; OCTAVE Sustain, NCT01458574) in patients (pts) with moderate to severe UC.1, 2
Aims & Methods: We present interim safety and efficacy data up to 3 years of treatment (as of 08 July 2016) from an ongoing Phase 3, multicentre, open-label, long-term extension study (OLE, NCT01470612) in pts who had completed or demonstrated treatment failure in OCTAVE Sustain, or who were non-responders after completing OCTAVE Induction 1 or 2. Eligibility for this study was determined based on Week (Wk) 8 data from OCTAVE Induction 1 & 2, or Wk 52 data (for completers) or early termination data from OCTAVE Sustain. Pts who were in remission at Wk 52 of OCTAVE Sustain were assigned to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily (BID); all others were assigned 10 mg BID. At Month 2, all pts underwent endoscopy, and non-responders from induction were mandated to withdraw if they did not show evidence of clinical response. Remission was defined by a Mayo score ≤2 with no individual subscore >1, and rectal bleeding subscore of 0. Binary efficacy endpoints were derived from Mayo score based on local-read endoscopic subscore.
Results: A total of 914 pts (5 mg BID, N = 156 [17.1%]; 10 mg BID, N = 758 [82.9%]) received at least one dose of study drug, of whom 381 (41.7%) discontinued (reasons included adverse events [AEs]: 23 [2.5%] and insufficient clinical response: 283 [31.0%]). The most frequent AE leading to discontinuation was worsening of UC. Serious and severe AEs occurred in 10.4% and 7.8% of pts, respectively (5 and 10 mg BID groups combined). The two most frequent treatment-emergent AE (TEAE) system organ classes in both dose groups were ‘infections and infestations’ and ‘gastrointestinal disorders’. The two most frequent TEAEs by preferred term were nasopharyngitis and worsening of UC. Serious infections AEs were reported in four (2.6%) and 14 (1.8%) pts in the 5 and 10 mg BID groups, respectively. Malignancies excluding non-melanoma skin cancer were reported in nine (1.2%) pts in the 10 mg BID group (with no clustering of malignancy type); none were reported in the 5 mg BID group. No new safety risks were identified. The available data ‘as observed’ for remission and mucosal healing at Months 2, 12 and 24 are shown in the Table.

## OP096 SAFETY AND EFFICACY OF LONG-TERM TREATMENT WITH OZANIMOD, AN ORAL S1P RECEPTOR MODULATOR, IN MODERATE TO SEVERE ULCERATIVE COLITIS: TOUCHSTONE EXTENSION 2-YEAR FOLLOW-UP
W. J. Sandborn1, B. G. Feagan2, G. D'Haens3, S. Hanauer4, D. C. Wolf5, S. Vermeire6, S. Ghosh7, C. Li8, D. Penenberg8, A. Petersen8, R. Aranda8, A. Olson8

1Division Of Gastroenterology, University of California, La Jolla, San Diego/United States of America/CA

2Robarts Research Institute, Western University, London/Canada/ON

3Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam/Netherlands

4Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago/United States of America/IL

5Atlanta Gastroentereology Associates, Atlanta/United States of America/GA

6Department Of Gastroenterology, University Hospitals Leuven, Leuven/Belgium

7Division Of Gastroenterology, Department Of Medicine, University of Calgary, Calgary/Canada

8Receptos, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Celgene, San Diego/United States of America/CA

Contact E-mail Address:
wsandborn@ucsd.edu

Introduction: Ozanimod, an oral, once-daily immunomodulator designed to selectively target S1P1R and S1P5R, has demonstrated clinical efficacy in ulcerative colitis (UC) for induction and maintenance therapy in the TOUCHSTONE trial (Sandborn NEJM 2016). The objective of the open-label extension (OLE) of the TOUCHSTONE trial is to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of daily 1 mg ozanimod in patients with moderate to severe UC who had initially participated in the TOUCHSTONE trial for up to 32 weeks.
Aims & Methods: A total of 197 patients were randomized (1:1:1) and treated with daily ozanimod 0.5 mg (n = 65), 1 mg (n = 67), or placebo (n = 65) in the TOUCHSTONE trial. Of the initial 197 patients randomized, 170 (86%) entered the OLE and received daily ozanimod 1 mg. As of the data cut-off in March 2017, 100 (58.8%) had efficacy evaluations reported through Week 92; of these 100 patients, 94 (55.3%) had received ozanimod 1 mg/day in the OLE for ≥2 years. Efficacy data are reported as observed through Week 92 and safety includes all events through the data cut-off of March 2017.
Results: At entry into the OLE, the partial Mayo Score (pMS) for patients on placebo, ozanimod 0.5 mg, and 1.0 mg was 4.6, 4.5, and 3.3 respectively, which improved significantly by OLE Week 8 (−2.3, −1.9 and −1.1), with the greatest improvement reported in patients who had received placebo or ozanimod 0.5 mg in the TOUCHSTONE trial. At the Week 92 visit in the OLE, 91/100 (91.0%) had little or no active disease based on the physician global assessment (PGA 0 or 1), 97/100 (97.0%) had little or no blood in their stools (rectal bleeding subscore [RBS] 0 or 1), 86/100 (86.0%) had no blood in the stools (RBS 0). Adverse events (AEs) and serious AEs were reported in 85 (50.0%) and 20 (11.1%) of patients respectively. The most common AEs (>2.0%) during OLE were UC flare, anaemia, nausea, upper respiratory tract infection, nasopharyngitis, back pain, arthralgia, headache, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) elevation and hypertension. The only serious AEs in ≥2 patients were anaemia, and ulcerative colitis flare. ALT and AST >3x upper limit of normal (ULN) occurred in 5 (2.9%) of the 170 patients in the OLE. All elevations were asymptomatic, <5xULN, transient, and resolving while receiving continued treatment.
Conclusion: Long-term treatment with ozanimod continues to be safe and well tolerated with good compliance and evidence of durable efficacy.

## OP097 VEDOLIZUMAB DEMONSTRATES EARLY SYMPTOMATIC IMPROVEMENT IN ULCERATIVE COLITIS: A GEMINI 1 POST HOC ANALYSIS
B. Feagan1, K. Lasch2, J. M. Khalid3, C. Cao2, A. M. Wojtowicz2, A. James3, J. Colombel4

1Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario, London/Canada/ON

2Takeda Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc., Deerfield/United States of America/IL

3Takeda Development Centre Europe, London/United Kingdom

4Department Of Gastroenterology, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York/United States of America/NY

Contact E-mail Address:
brian.feagan@robartsinc.com

Introduction: Vedolizumab (VDZ) achieves long-term clinical remission and mucosal healing in patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis (UC).1 Rapid symptomatic relief of rectal bleeding (RB) and stool frequency (SF) remain important treatment goals for patients and key indicators of remission for physicians in clinical practice. We aimed to characterize early symptomatic response with VDZ, specifically evaluating the timing of RB and SF improvement.
Aims & Methods: We assessed symptomatic improvement with VDZ through post hoc analysis of GEMINI 1 data. Patients with active UC were randomised to receive double-blind placebo (PBO) or VDZ at weeks (wks) 0 and 2 during the 6-wk induction phase (intent-to-treat population). Mayo clinic subscores of SF and RB were evaluated at 0, 2, 4, and 6 wks. Mean subscores and mean percent change from baseline (BL) were reported for the overall population and in those who were tumour necrosis factor antagonist (anti-TNF) naïve. The percentages of patients who reached SF subscore ≤1 and/or RB subscore of 0 were also determined.
Results: In anti-TNF-naïve patients, greater percentage decreases in mean SF subscores from BL were observed with VDZ than with PBO, reaching statistical significance at wks 4 and 6 as indicated by the non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals (Table). The same trends were observed in the overall population without reaching statistical significance. Similarly, a numerically greater percentage decrease from BL in RB subscore was observed with VDZ than with PBO, reaching statistical significance at wk 6 in both anti-TNF-naïve and overall populations. Significantly larger percentages of patients overall achieved SF subscore ≤1 or RB subscore of 0 with VDZ than with PBO at wk 6 and as early as wk 2 among the anti-TNF-naïve population (Table). A composite of SF subscore ≤1 and RB subscore of 0 was achieved in a significantly greater percentage of patients with VDZ than PBO at all time points (Table).

 Conclusion: Symptomatic improvements were achieved with VDZ as early as wk 2, with greater differences from PBO observed in anti-TNF-naïve patients. Taken together, these results highlight the rapid onset of VDZ in UC; however, assessing clinical efficacy at wk 14 and beyond for those who exhibit a more gradual response should be used to inform clinical practice.

## OP098 INDIGO NATURALIS IS EFFECTIVE FOR INDUCING CLINICAL REMISSION AND MUCOSAL HEALING IN PATIENTS WITH ULCERATIVE COLITIS (INDIGO STUDY)
M. Naganuma1, S. Sugimoto1, K. Mitsuyama2, T. Kobayashi3, N. Yoshimura4, K. Matsuoka5, T. Hisamatsu6, K. Watanabe7, T. Abe8, Y. Suzuki9, T. Hibi3, T. Kanai1

1Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Department Of Internal Medicine, Keio University, Tokyo/Japan

2Division Of Gastroenterology, Kurume University, Kurume/Japan

3Center For Advanced Ibd Research And Treatment, Kitasato University Kitasato Institute Hospital, Tokyo/Japan

4Dept. Of Internal Medicine, Central General Hospital Dept. of Medicine, Tokyo/Japan

5Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Tokyo/Japan

6Kyorin University, Tokyo/Japan

7Gastroenterology, Osaka City General Hospital, Osaka/Japan

8Department Of Preventive Medicine And Public Health, Biostatistics Unit At Clinical And Translational Research Centre, Keio University, Tokyo/Japan

9Internal Medicine, Toho Unversity Sakura Medical Centre Division of Gastroenterology, Sakura/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
maknaganuma@gmail.com

Introduction: By recent advances of immune-biological therapy for UC, the clinical outcomes of UC have been improved. However, intractable cases, in which mucosal regeneration is disturbed, cannot yet be treated well even by the most advanced anti-inflammatory biological therapies. Indigo naturalis (IN), contains highly concentrated aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) ligands, which has the effect for mucosal regeneration via AhR/interleukin−22. Therefore, IN may be effective for inducing mucosal healing in ulcerative colitis (UC). More recently, we reported the efficacy of IN for UC patients who were refractory to conventional treatments in a prospective study, and approximately 70% of patients had clinical response within 8 weeks after the treatment. However, there have been no double-blind trials which demonstrate the efficacy of IN and its appropriate doses are unclear.
Aims & Methods: In this study, we have evaluated the efficacy and safety of IN in terms of the dose dependency. This multicenter, double-blind trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of IN in 86 patients with active UC. An independent centre randomly allocated UC patients (Mayo score of ≥6) to four treatment groups to receive IN (daily dose, 0·5 g, 1·0 g, 2·0 g) or placebo in a 1:1:1:1 ratio. The primary efficacy endpoint (the rate of clinical response) and key secondary endpoints (the rates of clinical remission and mucosal healing) at 8 weeks of treatment were assessed in the full analysis set (FAS). For a longitudinal profile of Mayo scores and partial Mayo score, changes from baseline over 8 weeks were compared between treatment groups by means of a mixed-effects model for repeated measuresThis study is registered with UMIN Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN000021439).
Results: A total of 86 patients were enrolled. The proportion of steroid-dependent patients was 36.4, 56.5, 60.0, and 52.4% in patients receiving placebo, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 g daily of IN, respectively. Mean Mayo score at the week 0 was comparable among the 4 groups (8.2, 8.1, 8.5, and 8.3 in patients receiving placebo, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 g daily of IN, respectively). In the FAS population (n = 81), significant linear trend for the dose-response in clinical response rates was confirmed (placebo (n = 21): 14.3%, IN 0.5 g (n = 20): 80·0%, 1.0 g (n = 19): 79·5%, 2.0 g (n = 19): 89·5%, vs. placebo, P < 0·001). The dose-response in clinical remission rates showed significant linear trend (placebo: 4.8%, IN 0.5 g: 26.1%, P < 0.05, 1.0 g: 57.9%, P < 0.001, 2.0 g: 42.1%, P < 0·01). The mucosal healing rates were 14.3%, 65.0%, 63.2%, and 52.6%, in placebo, IN 0.5 g (P < 0.01), 1.0 g (P < 0.001), 2.0 g (P < 0.05) group, respectively. Patients receiving 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 g daily of IN had greater improvement in the Mayo score compared with patients receiving placebo at week 8 and partial Mayo score showed a gradual decrease in score in 2 weeks, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks in patients receiving IN. No serious adverse events were observed.
Conclusion: In this multi-centre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, we demonstrated that IN is tolerated and the efficacy was confirmed in patients receiving 0.5–2.0 g daily doses. IN may be able to use as an alternative induction therapy to steroids and as a therapy for refractory cases including chronic persistent type, especially cases with insufficient mucosal regeneration by immunosuppressants and anti-TNFα treatments.

## OP099 SUBMUCOSAL INJECTION OF THE RNA OLIGONUCLEOTIDE STNM01 IN ACTIVE ULCERATIVE COLITIS INDUCES MUCOSAL HEALING AND REVERSES TISSUE REMODELING
R. Atreya1, T. Kühbacher2, M. J. Waldner1, S. Hirschmann1, O. Drvarov2, R.A. Hashem2, C. Maaser3, T. Kucharzik4, J. Dinter5, J. Mertens6, C. Schramm5, B. Holler7, J. Mössner7, K. Suzuki8, N. Yokoyama8, S. Terai9, H. Yoneyama10, H. Asakura9, T. Hibi11, M. F. Neurath1

1Medical Department, University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Erlangen/Germany

2Asklepios Westklinikum, Hamburg/Germany

3Ambulanzzentrum Gastroenterologie, University Teaching Hospital Lüneburg, Lüneburg/Germany

4Department Of Internal Medicine And Gastroenterology, University Teaching Hospital Lüneburg, Lüneburg/Germany

5Uniklinik Köln, Köln/Germany

6Köln, Uniklinik Köln, Köln/Germany

7Department of Internal Medicine, Neurology and Dermatology, Division of Gastroenterology, University of Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany, Leipzig/Germany

8Niigata City General Hospital Dept. of Digestive Surgery, Niigata/Japan

9Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Graduate School of Medical and Dental Sciences, Niigata University, Niigata/Japan

10Stelic Institute & Co., Inc., Tokyo/Japan

11Center For Advanced IBD Research And Treatment, Kitasato University Kitasato Institute Hospital, Tokyo/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
raja.atreya@uk-erlangen.de

Introduction: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterized by mucosal inflammation and structural damage that is associated with matrix remodeling and tissue fibrosis. We had previously shown that carbohydrate sulfotransferase 15 (CHST15) that biosynthesizes sulfated matrix glycosaminoglycans is an important regulator of experimental colitis and gut fibrosis. Here, we evaluated the efficacy of the double-stranded RNA oligonucleotide STNM01, a specific blocker of CHST15, in refractory UC patients.
Aims & Methods: In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial, 24 patients with moderate-to-severe UC were randomized to receive a single endoscopic submucosal injection of 25 nM, 250 nM STNM01 or placebo.
Results: The primary endpoint, mucosal healing at weeks 2 or 4 was achieved by 62.5% in the STNM01 (250 nM) group compared to 28.6% in the placebo group (p = 0.018). Clinical remission at these time points was reached by 50.0% in the STNM01 (250 nM) and 14.3% in the placebo groups (p = 0.050). There was significant histological improvement according to the Geboes score in the STNM01 (250 nM) group (p < 0.01). There were no statistical differences between the lower dose STNM01 (25 nM) and placebo groups. STNM01 application was well tolerated. Immunostaining demonstrated significant inhibition of CHST15 expression in STNM01 (250 nM) treated patients. Functionally, STNM01 inhibited sulfation of L-selectin ligand on inflammation-associated high endothelial venule-like vessels, suppressed hydrogen sulfide-producing enzymes and inhibited pre-established fibrosis.
Conclusion: In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that targeting CHST15 by submucosal injection of the CHST15 blocker STNM01 could allow refractory UC patients to achieve mucosal healing and clinical remission. Local application of STNM01 would thus be a unique novel therapeutic approach for reversal of tissue remodeling in refractory UC.

## OP100 EARLY RELAPSE OF ULCERATIVE COLITIS AFTER DISCONTINUATION OF TREATMENT IN PATIENTS RESPONDING TO GOLIMUMAB
P. J. Hamlin1, S. Sebastian2, P. Irving3, D. R. Gaya4, C. Wheeler5, A. Rose6, G. Gillespie6, C. S. J. Probert7

1Department Of Gastroenterology, Leeds Teaching Hospitals Trust, Leeds/United Kingdom

2Hull Royal Infirmary, Hull/United Kingdom

3Dept. Of Gastroenterology, Guy's and St Thomas' Hospital, London/United Kingdom

4Gastroenterology Unit, Glasgow Royal Infirmary, Glasgow/United Kingdom

5Medical Affairs, MSD, Hoddesdon/United Kingdom

6MSD Sharp & Dohme Division of Immunology, Hoddesdon/United Kingdom

7Gastroenterology Research Unit, Cellular And Molecular Physiology, University of Liverpool, Liverpool/United Kingdom

Contact E-mail Address:
chris.probert@liverpool.ac.uk

Introduction: GO-COLITIS (NCT02092285; 2013−004583-56) is a phase 4, multicentre, open-label, single-arm trial in the UK assessing efficacy of golimumab (GLM) in induction and maintenance of clinical response in patients with moderate to severe ulcerative colitis (UC) despite conventional treatment. Data from the 12-week follow-up of patients in clinical response at week 54 is presented here.
Aims & Methods: 141/205 (68.8%) anti-TNF naive adults with UC ≥3 months responded to induction therapy with subcutaneous GLM at week 6, according to partial Mayo score (PMS)1 and were eligible to receive GLM maintenance of 50 mg or 100 mg (based on body weight) every 4 weeks for a total of 54 weeks. At the end of 54 weeks, their physician reviewed their treatment choosing to either continue with GLM or discontinue GLM treatment. PMS response was assessed at week 30, 54 and 66 (defined as decrease in PMS of ≥2 points and ≥30% from baseline, plus a decrease in rectal bleeding subscore of ≥1 point or absolute rectal bleeding score ≤1). 52/140 (37.1%) responders were monitored for sustained efficacy and safety at week 66 (12 weeks after study end). During this period concomitant medications were permitted at the discretion of the treating physician.
Results: 60/140 patients continued GLM maintenance treatment through week 54; 52/140 were responders at week 54. Of these 21 continued GLM treatment while 31 discontinued GLM treatment at week 54 (Table). All patients continuing GLM treatment (21/21) remained in clinical response at week 66. Of the patients who discontinued GLM at week 54, 27/31 (87%) patients maintained clinical response at week 66.

 Conclusion: 100% of patients who continued on GLM treatment between weeks 54 and 66 continued to respond; of the patients who discontinued GLM treatment at week 54, early relapse (i.e. relapsed within 12 weeks of stopping GLM treatment) was seen in 4/31 (13%). These are the first data on the effect of GLM withdrawal after 1 year in patients with moderate to severe UC responding to treatment. Further studies are required to evaluate the percentage of patients remaining in response at 6 months, or later, following anti-TNF treatment discontinuation in responding patients after 1 year of treatment.

## ALCOHOLIC LIVER DISEASE: ANYTHING NEW? - ROOM A2____________________

## OP101 TARGETING LIVER INFLAMMATION USING MINCLE-TARGETED LIPOSOMES AS A NOVEL DRUG DELIVERY SYSTEM
M. Szachniewicz1, M. Bartneck2, F. Tacke3, R. Bansal1

1Targeted Therapeutics, Department Of Biomaterials Science And Technology, MIRA Institute, University of Twente, Enschede/Netherlands

2Department Of Medicine Iii, University Hospital RWTH Aachen, Aachen/Germany

3Dept Of Medicine Iii, University Hospital Aachen - Dept of Medicine III, University Hospital Aachen; Aachen/DE, Aachen/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
r.bansal@utwente.nl

Introduction: Inflammatory macrophages (Mϕs) play a critical role in the development of liver inflammation. Hepatocellular damage, instigated by hepatitis viral infections, alcohol abuse or metabolic syndrome, results in the recruitment and activation of inflammatory cells mainly Mϕs in the liver. The inflammatory Mϕs initiates the process of liver injury progressing from liver fibrosis to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Therefore, selective targeted inhibition of the inflammatory macrophages would be a promising approach to attenuate liver inflammation or liver fibrosis. Anti-inflammatory therapies targeting Mϕs has shown to be highly efficacious in many disorders. Currently there is no therapy available for the treatment of liver fibrosis therefore there is an unmet need to develop a efficacious therapy with minimal side effects for the treatment of progressive disease. We identified Mincle receptor as a prospective target for pro-inflammatory subset (M1) of Mϕs for the development of effective inflammatory macrophage specific drug delivery system.
Aims & Methods: In this study, we developed a novel delivery system i.e. Mincle-targeted liposomes to achieve M1-specific uptake and to selectively deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to inhibit M1 Mϕs thereby ameliorating liver inflammation. Specificity and significance of Mincle receptor was evaluated in vitro in murine and human M1 Mϕs, in vivo in CCl4-induced acute liver inflammation using immunostainings and quantitative PCR. Diverse Mincle-targeted liposomes were synthesized and characterized using dynamic light scattering (DLS). M1-specific uptake in murine and primary human Mϕs was analyzed using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). We used prednisolone as an anti-inflammatory drug to inhibit inflammatory M1 macrophages. Prednisolone encapsulated mincle-targeted liposomes were generated, characterized and tested for efficacy in vitro in murine RAW macrophages, primary BMDMs, primary human Kupffer cells and in vivo in acute CCl4-induced liver injury mouse model.
Results: Significant up-regulation of Mincle receptor was confirmed in murine and human M1 Mϕs in vitro, in vivo in liver fibrosis mouse models and human fibrotic liver tissues. siRNA mediated knockdown (70% inhibition) of Mincle receptor in M1 Mϕ resulted in reduced inflammatory markers (TNFα and IL1β) and Mincle co-receptor. Mincle-targeted liposomes showed favorable size, stability and drug entrapment efficiency. We used prednisolone as an anti-inflammatory drug as a model drug to inhibit inflammatory M1 macrophages. We tested these liposomes in different mouse macrophage cell lines, primary bone marrow derived macrophages and in primary human macrophages for efficacy and M1-specific uptake. Significantly, targeted liposomes showed M1-specific uptake, while liposomes without targeting moiety showed comparatively reduced internalization at different time points. Furthermore, targeted liposomes demonstrated significantly reduced uptake in M2 restorative Mϕs. No significant uptake in other cells was observed. Antibody blocking of Mincle receptor significantly inhibited uptake in M1 Mϕ strongly suggesting Mincle-mediated mechanism of uptake. Prednisolone-encapsulated Mincle targeted liposomes showed significant reduction in M1-specific markers and inflammatory markers in vitro in RAW cells, in primary murine BMDMs and human kupffer cells. In vivo in acute CCl4-induced liver inflammation mouse model, prednisolone-encapsulated Mincle-targeted liposomes demonstrated specific liver uptake, highly significant attenuation in intra-hepatic inflammation, macrophage infiltration and reduction in fibrotic parameters as compared to free prednisolone and non-targeted liposomes.
Conclusion: This study presents a highly novel targeting approach of specifically targeting inflammatory macrophages with increased therapeutic efficacy while off-target effects on healthy tissues and other cell types can be avoided. These inflammatory macrophage targeted liposomes therefore holds great promise for diagnosis and therapeutic treatment of liver fibrosis and other inflammatory diseases.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP102 IGA ANTIBODIES AGAINST FILAMENTOUS-ACTIN ARE FREQUENTLY DETECTED IN PATIENTS WITH CIRRHOSIS AND INDICATE A PROGRESSIVE DISEASE COURSE
T. Tornai1, B. Balogh1, N. Sipeki1, Z. Vitalis1, I. Tornai1, P. Antal-Szalmas1, G.L. Norman2, T. Bruns3, M. Papp1

1Division Of Gastroenterology, University of Debrecen, Faculty of Medicine, Institute of Medicine, Debrecen/Hungary

2Inova Diagnostics, San Diego/United States of America/CA

3Department Of Internal Medicine IV, University Hospital Jena, Jena/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
papp.maria@med.unideb.hu

Introduction: Gut barrier failure and the consequential pathological bacterial translocation (BT) are characteristic features of cirrhosis and play an important role in the progression of liver disease. We hypothesized that serological hallmarks of gut barrier dysfunction are associated with accelerated progression of liver disease in cirrhosis and the development of specific complications and liver-related death.
Aims & Methods: Sera from 260 stable outpatients with cirrhosis (male: 129, age: 56 ± 11 yrs, alcohol: 167 [64.2%]) and from 155 healthy subjects were assayed for the presence of antibodies against filamentous-actin [AAA IgA and IgG] and gliadin [AGA IgA and IgG]) and for intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP) by ELISA. Association of gut failure markers with disease specific characteristics was assessed at baseline and the course of liver disease was evaluated in a 5-year follow-up observational study for decompensating events (ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy and/or bacterial infection) and liver-related death. BT was assessed based on the presence of anti-microbial antibodies (anti-OMP Plus IgA and/or endotoxin core IgA antibody [EndoCab]).
Results: Elevated concentrations of the gut failure markers IgA-AAA (62.7 vs. 4.4%) and IgA-AGA (27.7 vs. 2.6%) were more often observed in cirrhosis as compared to healthy controls (p < 0.001 for both). In addition, serum I-FABP was increased in cirrhosis as compared to controls (741 vs. 244 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and correlated with serum levels of IgA-AAA and IgA-AGA. IgA-AAA positivity was associated with alcoholic liver disease, liver disease scores and decompensated clinical stage (all p < 0.001). Serological markers of BT were more often found in patients with elevated IgA-AAA compared to those without (72.3 vs. 13.5 % for IgA-EndoCab and 85.2 vs. 20.5% for IgA-anti-OMP, p < 0.001 for both). In patients with compensated disease stage (n = 131) the risk of decompensation was higher in patients with elevated IgA-AAA (HR [95%CI]: 1.85 [1.06–3.24]), as was the risk of liver-related mortality (HR: 2.66 [1.27–5.56]). Such associations were not observed for IgG-AAA and IgA/IgG-AGAs. In the overall cohort, IgA-AAA remained an independent predictor of liver-related death (HRadj: 1.96 [1.08–3.55]) when adjusting for important clinical variables (MELD score, etiology, clinical stage, see Table 1).

 Conclusion: Elevated serum concentrations of IgA antibodies against filamentous-actin indicate patients with an unfavourable outcome in cirrhosis, which may be related to intestinal damage beyond being related to bacterial translocation. IgA-AAA might be consider as a novel serologic marker of the disease progression.
Disclosure of Interest: G.L. Norman: Employee of INOVA
All other authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP103 SELF-CONFORMABLE COVERED VS SELF-CONFORMABLE UNCOVERED METALLIC STENTS IN THE PALLIATIVE TREATMENT OF MALIGNANT EXTRA-HEPATIC BILIARY STRICTURE: A MULTICENTRIC RANDOMIZED STUDY
B. Mangiavillano1, A. De Ceglie2, R. Filiberti3, A. Caruso4, L. De Luca5, S. Signorelli6, M. Marini7, P. Ravelli6, A. Parodi8, R. Conigliaro9, M. Conio2

1Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Unit, Humanitas - Mater Domini, Castellanza (VA)/Italy

2Gastroenterology And Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, Borea Hospital, Sanremo (IM)/Italy

3Clinical Epidemiology, IRCCS AOU San Martino, Genova/Italy

4Aou Modena, Gastroenterology and Digestive Endoscopy Unit, Modena/Italy

5Endoscopy Unit, Pesaro Hospital, Pesaro/Italy

6Ospedali Riuniti di Bergamo, Bergamo/Italy

7Gastroenterology, Santa Maria alle Scotte, Siena/Italy

8Ospedale Galliera, Genova/Italy

9Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, Baggiovara Hospital, Modena/Italy

Contact E-mail Address:
b_mangiavillano@hotmail.com

Introduction: Cancer of the pancreas, gallbladder and bile ducts is the most common cause of malignant biliary obstruction (MBO). In case of unresectable cancer the survival at 5 years is less than 2%. We present preliminary results of a prospective RCT (NCT 02930252) comparing covered (Niti-S Biliary ComVi) with uncovered (Niti-s D) self-conformable metal stent (SEMS) placed in patients with MBO conditioning jaundice. No RCTs are present in literature comparing these two types of stent.
Aims & Methods: Primary aim was to compare stent patency between the two groups. Secondary aims were to evaluate relationships between adverse events (AEs) rate and stent type (i.e. time to stent dysfunction and survival). 158 patients (76 M 82F, median age 78 ys) were randomized in two groups: 78 received a fully-covered SEMS (FCSEMS) and 78 an uncovered SEMS. Data from 148 (72 FCSEMS and 76 USEMS) out of 158 patients were analyzed. All patients received sphincterotomy before stent insertion.
Results: Placement was successful in 100% of patients with the uncovered and 98.7% patients with FCSEMS. Levels of conjugated bilirubin improved significantly (p < 0.001) in both groups during the first week, with a median variation of −70% for FCSEMS and −68% for SEMS. Normalization of bilirubin levels (≤1, 2 mg/dL) was observed in 42 patients (28.6%; 28.2% FCSEMS and 28.9% SEMS, p = 1.0). AEs occurred in 28 out of 147 patients [19.0%: 18 FCSEMS (25.4%) and 10 SEMS (13.1%), p = 0.092]. Stent occlusion occurred in 12 patients with FCSEMS and in 10 patients with SEMS. Cholangitis was observed in 6 patients for each group. In patients with SEMS, occlusion was due to in-growth and in 9 out of 10 patients, was reported as a late complication. In FCSEMS group, 6 out of 12 patients had stent occlusion within the first month. Cholecystitis was observed in a patient with FCSEMS. No stent migration occurred in SEMS group while it was observed in 5 (7%) of the FCSEMS group (p = 0.024). Median time of stent patency was lower for FCSEMS (9.5 months, 95%CI 7.2–11.8 months) vs 18.0 months (95% CI 10.7–25.4 months) for SEMS (p = 0.046). No differences were observed with regard of stent dysfunction in patient survival: 4.0 months (95%CI 2.5–5.5 months) for FCSEMS and 3.7 days (95%CI 2.3–5.0) for SEMS (p = 0.80). Median survival was 4.5 months (95%CI: 3.3–5.7 months) in FCSEMS group and 3.7 months (95%CI: 2.2–5.3 months) in the SEMS (p = 0.23).
Conclusion: No significant differences were observed in levels of bilirubin improvement, stent dysfunction-free and median survival between the two groups. AEs were higher, although not significantly, among FCSEMS group. FCSEMS had a significantly higher rate of migration. A significantly difference in patency was observed for SEMS group.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP104 CLINICAL EFFICACY OF ANTI-MIGRATION FEATURES IN FULLY-COVERED SELF-EXPANDABLE METALLIC STENTS FOR ANASTOMOTIC BILIARY STRICTURES AFTER LIVER TRANSPLANTATION: A RETROSPECTIVE COHORT COMPARISON OF STANDARD AND ANTI-MIGRATION STENTS
B. Bordacahar1, M. Barret2, M. Guillaumot2, O. Scatton3, F. Perdigao3, S. Leblanc4, S. Chaussade5, F. Prat6

1Endoscopy And Digestive Oncology Unit, Hopital Cochin, Paris/France

2Gastroenterology, Cochin Hospital, Paris/France

3Liver Transplant Unit, Pitié Salpétrière, paris/France

4CHU Cochin Dept. of Gastroenterology, Paris/France

5Service De Gastro-entérologie, CHU Cochin Dept. de Gastroenterologie, Paris/France

6Hôpital Cochin Dept. of Gastroenterology, Paris/France

Contact E-mail Address:
benoit.bordacahar@gmail.com

Introduction: Anastomotic biliary strictures (ABS) are one of the most frequent adverse effects occurring after orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT). Multiple plastic stents (MPS) have been validated in this indication. More recently, fully covered self-expandable metallic stents (FC-SEMS) have been used with positive outcomes but also a higher rate of migration which may limit success.
Aims & Methods: Our primary objective was to compare stent migration rates observed with commonly used FC-SEMS and so-called “anti-migration” FC-SEMS, newly designed with reversed proximal side flaps. Secondary objectives were to compare the rates of ABS recurrence, and sustained stricture resolution as well as procedure-related morbidity. We conducted a retrospective analysis of a subset of patients (FC-SEMS for post-OLT ABS) from 2 prospectively maintained databases of a) OLT patients, and b) ERCP and stenting. Between January 2008 and January 2016, consecutive patients presenting with ABS after OLT referred to Cochin Hospital (Paris, France) for ERCP and receiving an FC-SEMS were included. Exclusion criteria were any other cause of biliary stricture (i.e malignant stricture, ischemic origin), and biliary fistulae.
Results: One hundred and twenty-five FC-SEMS (57 anti-migration stents, 52 conventional stents type 1 and 16 conventional stents type 2) were used in 75 patients for ABS after OLT. The rate of FC-SEMS complete migration was 16% (20/125), respectively 1.7% (1/57) for anti-migration stents, 17.3% (9/52) for type 1 conventional stents and 62.5% (10/16) for type 2 conventional stents (p < 0.0001). An early endoscopic revision for cholestasis or acute cholangitis was necessary in 24.8% (31/125) of cases, 12.2% (7/57) for anti-migration stents, 26.9% (14/52) for type 1 conventional stents and 62.5% (10/16) for type 2 conventional stents (p < 0.0002). First ERCP follow-up after each FC-SEMS highlighted a stricture resolution in 80% (100/125) of cases, 93% (53/57) for anti-migration stents, 77% (40/52) for type 1 conventional stents and 37.5% (6/16) for type 2 conventional stents. There was no difference for patient characteristics (i.e previous endoscopic treatment, timing of ABS occurrence after OLT) or procedure-related morbidity between each type of FC-SEMS.
Conclusion: In patients with ABS after OLT, the use of anti-migration FC-SEMS significantly decreased the risk of stent migration and improved sustained stricture resolution. Endoscopic removal success and procedure-related morbidity were similar for both usual and anti-migration stents.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP105 UTILITY OF NEWLY DEVELOPED SHORT TYPE DOUBLE BALLOON ENDOSCOPY FOR ERCP IN POSTOPERATIVE PATIENTS WITH SURGICAL ANATOMIC VARIATIONS; A LARGE CASE SERIES
M. Shimatani1, M. Tokuhara1, M. Masuda1, S. Miyamoto1, M. Sakao1, H. Miyoshi1, T. Ikeura2, M. Takaoka1, K. Uchida1, K. Okazaki1

1The Third Department Of Internal Medicine, Kansai Medical University, Hirakata/Japan

2Kansai Medical University, Hirakata/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:

Introduction: The utility of conventional short-type DBE for pancreatobiliary disease in postoperative patients had been widely accepted 1–4. However, some technical problems yet remained, and the new short-type DBE that was specially designed for therapeutic endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) in postoperative patients solved these problems.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to evaluate the usefulness of new short DBE for ERCP in postoperative patients. From August 2015 to May 2017, ERCP using new short DBE (DB-ERCP) was performed in 222 postoperative patients (280 procedures). We retrospectively studied the success rate of reaching the blind end, the mean time to reach the blind end, the diagnostic success rate, the therapeutic success rate, the mean time to complete ERCP related interventions, the overall success rate, the mean time to complete DB-ERCP, and adverse events.
Results: The success rate of reaching the blind end was 98.6% (276/280). By type of reconstruction methods, the success rate of reaching the blind end was 95.6% (87/91) in Roux-en-Y (R-Y) hepaticojejunostomy, 100% (36/36) in R-Y partial gastrectomy, 100% (42/42) in R-Y total gastrectomy, 100% (19/19) in Billroth II gastrectomy (B-II), 100% (45/45) in pancreatoduoderectomy (PD), 100% (40/40) in pylorus preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (PpPD) and 100% (7/7) in others. The mean time to reach the blind end was 14.4 min. (1–105). By type of reconstruction methods, the mean time to reach the blind end was 20.9 min. (3–74) in R-Y hepaticojejunostomy, 16.9 min. (1–105) in R-Y partial gastrectomy, 13.4 min. (2–57) in R-Y total gastrectomy, 6.4 min. (1–22) in B-II, 8.4 min. (1–39) in PD, 20.9 min. (2–41) in PpPD and 11.0 min. (2–32) in others. The diagnostic success rate was 97.5% (269/276). By type of reconstruction methods, the diagnostic success rate was 100% (87/87) in R-Y hepaticojejunostomy, 100% (34/36) in R-Y partial gastrectomy, 95.2% (40/42) in R-Y total gastrectomy, 89.5% (17/19) in B-II, 100% (45/45) in PD, 97.5% (39/40) in PpPD and 100% (7/7) in others. Therapeutic intervention was achieved in all of the 269 procedures of successful deep cannulation (100%). The overall DB-ERCP success rate was 96.1% (269/280). By type of reconstruction methods, the overall DB-ERCP success rate was 95.6% (87/91) in R-Y hepaticojejunostomy, 94.4% (34/36) in R-Y partial gastrectomy, 95.2% (40/42) in R-Y total gastrectomy, 89.5%(17/19) in B-II, 100% (45/45) in PD, 97.7% (39/40) in PpPD and 100% (7/7) in others. The mean time to complete DB-ERCP was 61.0 min. (12–252). By type of reconstruction methods, the mean time required to complete DB-ERCP was 71.7 min. (18–228) in R-Y hepaticojejunostomy, 69.4 min. (21–170) in R-Y partial gastrectomy, 78.5 min. (16–252) in R-Y total gastrectomy, 51.9 min. (21–105) in B-II, 39.6 min. (12–107) in PD, 45.1 min. (15–144) in PpPD and 47.2 min. (17–86) in others. The occurrence of adverse events was 1.1% (3/280).
Conclusion: The newly developed short DBE for ERCP in postoperative patients is useful and safe. DB-ERCP is a promising therapeutic modality in such patients and should be selected as the first-line policy.

## OP106 AN INTERNATIONAL, MULTICENTER, COMPARATIVE TRIAL OF EUS-GUIDED GASTROGASTROSTOMY-ASSISTED ERCP VERSUS ENTEROSCOPY-ASSISTED ERCP IN PATIENTS WITH ROUX-EN-Y GASTRIC BYPASS ANATOMY
M. Bukhari1, A. A. Siddiqui2, J. Nieto3, R. Kunda4, N. K. Ahuja1, S.S. Irani5, A. Shah2, T. Kowalski2, D. Loren2, O.I. Brewer Gutierrez1, O. Sanaei1, L. Fayad1, Y. Chen1, S. Ngamruengphong1, V. Kumbhari1, Y. Haito-Chavez1, V. Singh1, H. Dakour Aridi1, M. A. Khashab1

1Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions, Baltimore/United States of America

2Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia/United States of America

3Borland-Groover Clinic, Jacksonville/United States of America/FL

4Department Of Surgical Gastroenterology, Arhus University Hospital, Aarhus/Denmark

5Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle/United States of America

Introduction: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is challenging in patients with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) anatomy. EUS-guided gastrogastrostomy (GG) creation is a promising novel technique by which to access the excluded stomach in order to facilitate conventional ERCP.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to compare procedural outcomes and adverse events (AEs) between EUS-guided gastrogastrostomy-assisted ERCP (EUS-GG-ERCP) and enteroscoy assisted ERCP (e-ERCP) in patients with RYGB. Patients with RYGB anatomy who underwent EUS-GG-ERCP or e-ERCP between 2014 and 2016 at 5 tertiary centers were included. The primary outcome was technical success of ERCP, defined as successful cannulation of the selected duct with successful intervention as intended. Secondary outcomes included: (1) total procedural time (in the EUS-GG group, total procedural time included EUS-GG creation plus ERCP procedure time); (2) length of hospital stay; and (3) rate/severity of AEs graded according to the ASGE lexicon.
Results: A total of 160 patients (mean age 58, 53.8% female) were included, of whom 53 (33.1%) underwent EUS-GG-ERCP and 107 (66.9%) underwent e-ERCP (DBE-ERCP 79, SBE-ERCP 25, other 3). The technical success rate was significantly higher in the EUS-GG-ERCP versus the e-ERCP group (88.7% vs. 60.8%, p < 0.001). Total procedure time was significantly shorter in patients who underwent EUS-GG-ERCP (50.1 min vs. 86.1 min, p < 0.001). Post-procedure median length of hospitalization was shorter in the EUS-GG group (2 vs. 7 days, p = 0.0001). Rate of AEs was similar in both groups (7.5% vs. 5.6%, p = 0.73).

 Conclusion: EUS-GG-ERCP is superior to e-ERCP in patients with RYGB anatomy in terms of technical success with a similar safety profile.

Introduction: Background: The role of the recently developed digital single-operator cholangioscopy (D-SOC) for the treatment of difficult biliary stones using electrohydraulic (EHL) and laser lithotripsy (LL) is not well known.
Aims & Methods: (1) To study the technical success (complete ductal clearance) and safety (rate/severity of adverse events (AE) per ASGE lexicon) of D-SOC with EHL/LL in the treatment of difficult biliary stones; (2) To compare the performance of EHL vs. LL. This is an international, multicenter, retrospective study at 22 tertiary centers between 02/2015 and 12/2016. Difficult bile duct stones were defined as large (≥15 mm), multiple (>3), impacted, intrahepatic/cystic duct location, associated with a stricture, difficult anatomic access, or Mirizzi’s syndrome. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with technical failure and more than one EHL/LL session
Results: A total of 407 patients (60% F, mean age 64 yr) underwent D-SOC for difficult bile duct stones and 74.5% had more than one indication which included: large stones (223), multiple (219), impacted stones (155), intrahepatic stones (72), cystic duct stones (50), stones above biliary stricture (80), difficult anatomic access (57) and Mirizzi’s syndrome (35). Of these, 85.8% had previous failed ERCP to clear the bile duct and 75.9% had a prior stent placed. Location of stones was CBD 59.7%, CHD 9.6%, intrahepatic ducts 15.2%, cystic duct 11.3%, hilar 1.5% and more than one location 2.6%. The mean stone size was 16.01 mm ± 7.14 mm. A total of 306 were treated with EHL and 101 with LL. Mean procedure time was 67 min±34.9 min. Complete ductal clearance using EHL/LL (technical success) was achieved in 396 (97.3%) patients, with a median number of lithotripsy sessions of 1 (range 1–4). Successful ductal clearance in a single session of EHL/LL was achieved in 328 (80.6%) cases. A total of 11 (2.7%) patients failed EHL/LL and were treated with surgery (n = 8), ESWL (n = 2) or both (n = 1). Fifteen (3.7%) AEs occurred, including 6 cholangitis, 5 abdominal pain, 1 pancreatitis, 1 transient bacteremia, 1 bleeding and 1 bile duct perforation (10 mild, 3 moderate, and 2 severe). Recurrent bile duct stones occurred in 17 (6.1%) patients during a median follow up of 83.5 days [IQR 33–155]. Technical success (96.7% vs 99%, p = 0.31), median number of lithotripsy sessions to achieve bile duct clearance (1 vs 1, p = 0.16), and rate of AEs (3.3% vs 5%, p = 0.44) were similar between EHL and LL groups, respectively. Mean procedure time (73.9 vs 49.9, p = <0.001) was significantly shorter in the LL group. Difficult anatomy/cannulation was significantly correlated with technical failure [aOR(95%CI):5.18(1.26–21.2), p = 0.02] while duration of procedure [aOR(95%CI):1.02(1.01–1.03), p = <0.001] was a significant predictor of the need for more than one session of D-SOC EHL/LL.

 Conclusion: D-SOC with EHL or LL is effective and safe in treating difficult bile duct stones. Few patients will require surgery or ESWL to achieve ductal clearance. Procedure time is significantly lower in the LL group as compared to EHL group.

## OP108 ERCP WITH PANCREATOSCOPY-GUIDED LASER LITHOTRIPSY FOR CHRONIC PANCREATITIS COMPLICATED BY PANCREATIC DUCT STONES: A FIVE YEAR SINGLE CENTER EXPERIENCE
A. Malachias, D. Kypraios, S. Stavrinidis, S.L. Hatzinicolaou, D. Dimitroulopoulos, G. Sofianidis, D. Xinopoulos

Department Of Gastroenterology, ST. Savvas Athens Cancer Hospital, Athens/Greece

Contact E-mail Address:
aposm@yahoo.gr

Introduction: Pancreatoscopy-guided laser lithotripsy is being increasingly used for pancreatic stone extraction, after unsuccessful conventional ERCP, with possible advantages over surgery, or extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy. We report our experience in the management of pancreatic duct stones over the past five years.
Aims & Methods: To evaluate the safety, feasibility and technical success of intracorporeal laser lithotripsy. In a five-year period a total of 19 patients (13 men, 6 women, aged 38 to 79 years) were referred with chronic pancreatitis, complicated with pancreatic duct stones. Treatment with conventional ERCP was unsuccessfully attempted for all patients. Laser lithotripsy was performed using a 10 Fr direct visualization system. For stone fragmentation a Holmium-YAG laser lithotripsy device was used. A 230μm or 365μm fiber with energy output settings at 800–1500 mJ and pulse rates of 8–10 Hz was used.
Results: Chronic calcific pancreatitis was the result of chronic ethanol abuse in 15 patients. Idiopathic pancreatitis was diagnosed in 4 patients. Presenting symptoms included chronic or recurrent pain, weight loss, use of opioids and multiple hospitalizations. Nine (9) patients had single stone located in the pancreatic head, while 10 had multiple stones (up to 4) in the head, neck and body of pancreas. The average stone size was 0.9 cm (0.4–1.2 cm). Successful treatment, defined as complete stone extraction, was achieved in 10 patients after a single laser lithotripsy procedure. In 8 patients a second lithotripsy session was performed to ensure total stone removal. In a single patient pancreatic duct cannulation with the pancreatoscope was not achieved. Dilation with a 3 cm long and 10 mm diameter balloon was necessary in 12 cases for associated main pancreatic duct strictures. Extraction of the fragments was performed using balloon catheter (up to 15 mm diameter) and in 7 patients a 10 mm diameter dormia basket was used. In all cases a 7 Fr pancreatic stent was placed. In 11 patients increased serum pancreatic enzyme levels were noted following laser lithotripsy. None of the patients showed clinical signs of acute pancreatitis. No other clinical adverse events were noted. Follow up was achieved by EUS, having the first appointment four months after lithotripsy. Fourteen patients have already been evaluated, with no stone recurrence. All patients report clinical improvement.
Conclusion: Pancreatoscopy-guided laser lithotripsy is a safe, effective and self-reliant treatment, compared to extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy, for patients with difficult pancreatic duct stones. It is technically challenging but is a promising and viable method in experienced centers. Further research and clinical studies are necessary to evaluate and standardize the technique.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP109 LONG-TERM USE OF ASPIRIN IS MORE EFFECTIVE TO REDUCE THE INCIDENCES OF GASTROINTESTINAL CANCERS THAN NON-GASTROINTESTINAL CANCERS: A 10-YEAR POPULATION-BASED STUDY IN HONG KONG
K. Kf Tsoi1, F.C. Chan1, H.W. Hirai1, J.J.Y. Sung2

1The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong/Hong Kong PRC

2Institute Of Digestive Disease And Department Of Medicine And Therapeutics, State Key Laboratory Of Digestive Disease, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong/Hong Kong PRC

Contact E-mail Address:
kelvintsoi@cuhk.edu.hk

Introduction: Aspirin has been shown to be a chemopreventive agent for colorectal cancer (CRC), and recent publications have also suggested chemopreventive effect of aspirin on other cancers.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study is to compare the benefits of long-term aspirin use to reduce the incidences of gastrointestinal (GI) cancers and non-gastrointestinal cancers. This is a matched-cohort study of a territory-wide database from all public hospitals in Hong Kong. Patients with aspirin prescribed for at least 6 months between 2000 and 2004 were extracted and matched with non-users in 1:2 ratios. Immortal time bias was further adjusted for the non-users who died in 6 months after matching. The incidences of GI cancers which referred to colorectum, liver, oesophageal, pancreas or stomach cancers, and the incidences of non-GI cancers which referred to breast, bladder, kidney, leukaemia, lung, multiple myeloma, or prostate cancers were the study outcomes. Patients' outcomes were documented for up to 14 years until 2013. Odds ratio (OR) with it associated 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were used to measure the association of long-term aspirin use and the cancer incidences.
Results: A total of 618,884 subjects were extracted and matched from the database, including 206,295 aspirin users and 412,589 non-aspirin users. The mean ages of patients in aspirin and non-aspirin group were 67.5 years and 67.6 years respectively. In the aspirin users, the average duration of aspirin prescribed was 7.7 years, and the median dose of aspirin prescribed was 80 mg with the inter-quartile range between 80 mg and 100 mg. Cancer incidences were found in 98, 533 (15.9%) out of 618, 884 subjects, and the lung cancer was the most common cancer. Long-term use of aspirin showed 24% to 47% significant reduction on major cancers in the GI tract including colorectal (OR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.73 to 0.78), liver (OR: 0.53, 95% CI: 0.51 to 0.56), oesophagus (OR: 0.53, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.59), pancreas (OR: 0.66, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.71) and stomach (OR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.58 to 0.65). For non-GI cancers, long-term use of aspirin only showed significant reduction on leukaemia, lung, and prostate cancers, but not breast, bladder, kidney and multiple myeloma cancers (Table 1). Table 1. Comparison between Aspirin Users and Non-users for Major Cancers Incidence.

 Conclusion: Long-term use of aspirin can reduce the major types of GI cancers, but the benefits are limited to some other non-GI cancers, such as breast and kidney.

## OP110 USE OF ASPIRIN AFTER CURATIVE SURGERY CAN REDUCE MORTALITY DUE TO COLORECTAL CANCER: A 10-YEAR POPULATION-BASED STUDY IN HONG KONG
J. Jy Sung1, F.C. Chan1, H.W. Hirai1, K. Kf Tsoi1

1Institute Of Digestive Disease, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong/Hong Kong PRC

Contact E-mail Address:
joesung@cuhk.edu.hk

Introduction: Aspirin was shown to be effective to reduce the risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) and mortality. However, the use of aspirin after curative colorectal surgery was uncertain.
Aims & Methods: This study aims to demonstrate if aspirin can also reduce colorectal cancer mortality after diagnosis and surgical resection. A cohort with long-term use of aspirin and a matched cohort of non-users were extracted from the electronic healthcare records in all public hospitals in Hong Kong. Patients with curative resection for CRC since 2000 were extracted according to the ICD-9 and procedure codes, such as resection of colon/rectum. Patients were categorized into two groups: (a) Patients with continuous use of aspirin after surgery were compared with those who stopped; (b) Patients with aspirin started after surgeries were compared with those who remained not taking aspirin. The primary outcome was CRC related mortality and the secondary outcome was overall mortality. Cox-proportional Hazard Models were fitted with the control of confounding factors including history of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular diseases. Sub-distribution Hazard Ratio (SHR) for competing risk mortality on CRC was fitted, and Hazard Ratio (HR) was used to measure all-cause mortality. Subgroup analyses on gender were performed.
Results: From the healthcare records between 2000 and 2013, a total of 13,552 subjects were included: 3,301 of them (24.4%) were aspirin users and 10,251 (75.6%) were non-users before CRC diagnosis. The median dose of aspirin used was 80 mg. Patients in group (a) with aspirin use before CRC diagnosis, 2,665 (80.7%) continued aspirin and 636 (19.3%) discontinued aspirin after curative surgery. Continuous use of aspirin significantly reduced 31% risk of CRC-caused mortality with SHR: 0.69 (95% CI: 0.59 – 0.81) and 42% risk of all-cause mortality with HR: 0.58 (95% CI: 0.49 – 0.68). Patients in group (b) who never use aspirin before CRC diagnosis, 1055 patients (10.3%) initiated aspirin after curative surgery and 9196 (89.7%) patients remained not to have aspirin. Initiating aspirin after surgery significantly reduced 12% risk of CRC-caused mortality with SHR: 0.88 (95% CI: 0.80 – 0.98) and 18% risk of all-cause mortality with HR: 0.82 (95% CI: 0.73 – 0.91). Subgroup analyses did not show significant different between male and female (Table 1). Table 1. The Sub-distribution Hazard Ratio (95% CI) and Hazard Ratio (95% CI) for Continuing and Initiating Aspirin after Curative Surgery

 1Presented by sub-distribution hazard ratio (SHR) for competing risk mortality on CRC 2 Presented by hazard ratio (HR) for all-cause mortality
Conclusion: Aspirin initiated after the curative surgery leads to significantly lower risks on both CRC-related and overall mortalities. Patients with regular use of aspirin even showed higher benefits.

Aims & Methods: We set up a multicenter nation-wide study in Spain with the following aims: 1) establishing the prevalence and cumulative incidence of colorectal cancer and other tumors in Lynch syndrome; 2) evaluating the effect of screening-surveillance on cancer incidence; and 3) assessing the cancer-specific survival. Herein we report the first preliminary analysis focused on the prevalence and the incidence of colorectal cancer. We designed a retrospective collection study of prospectively observed data in the setting of organized high-risk clinics. A centralized online database was used, including demographic, genetic, family and personal cancer history, and surveillance protocol and treatments. First prospectively colonoscopy planned as Lynch syndrome screening-surveillance was considered as date of inclusion. Cumulative incidence of the first colorectal cancer diagnosed under screening was calculated by mutated gene. For this analysis, colorectal cancers diagnosed prior or within 6-months of the beginning of follow-up (prevalent cancers) were excluded. Additionally, we calculated the cumulative incidence of subsequent colorectal cancers in patients with a prior colorectal cancer by mutated gene. Preliminary statistical analysis has been performed by Kaplan-Meier.
Introduction: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mutations in the mismatch DNA repair system (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM) and predisposes to colorectal, endometrial and other tumors. Estimates of cancer risk in Lynch syndrome have been frequently biased due to retrospective designed studies and small cohorts.
Results: One thousand one hundred eight patients with Lynch syndrome from 25 centers were included [MLH1, 449 (40.5%); MSH2, 371 (33.5%); MSH6, 197 (17.8%); PMS2, 68 (6.1%); EPCAM, 23 (2.1%)] and followed-up for a mean of 67.5 + 57.8 months. Mean age was 52.4 + 15.4, and 630 (56.9%) were female. Mean age at inclusion was 45.2 + 15. Colorectal cancer was present in 426 (38.4%) patients with Lynch syndrome and 114 where diagnosed of more than 1 colorectal cancer. The distribution per gene was: MLH1, 204 (48%); MSH2, 140 (33%); MSH6, 47 (11%); PMS2, 23 (5%); EPCAM, 12 (3%). First colorectal cancer under screening with colonoscopy was found in 49/713 (6.7%) patients with the following distibution per gene: MLH1, n = 23/268; MSH2, n = 18/249; MSH6, n = 4/154; PMS2, n = 2/47; EPCAM, n = 2/13. The cumulative incidences of the first colorectal cancer at 70 years by gene were 25.6% (95%CI = 13.2–38.2), 22.1% (95%CI = 11.3–35.1), 6.3% (95%CI = 0–12.8) and 25.9% (95%CI = 7–71) for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 mutation carriers, respectively. Tumor stages of first colorectal cancer under surveillence were: stage I (45.7%), stage II (28.6%), stage III (22.9%) and stage IV (2.9%). The 10-year cumulative incidences for subsequent colorectal cancers for patients with a prior colorectal cancer were 9.4% (95%CI = 5–17) for MLH1, 12.6% (95%CI = 5.6–27.6) for MSH2, and 17.2% (95%CI = 6.6–40) for MSH6, respectively. Two-hundred-sixteen (19.5%) patients with Lynch syndrome presented cancer in other locations: 119 endometrium (18.8% woman) [MLH1, 39 (32.8%); MSH2, 47 (39.5%); MSH6, 31 (26.1%); PMS2, 1 (0.8%); EPCAM, 1 (0.8%)], 26 ovarium (4.12% of woman), 12 stomach (1%), 17 urinary bladder (1.5%), 20 ureter (1.8%), 21 skin (1.9%), 19 breast (1.7%) and 9 prostate cancer (0.8%).
Conclusion: In this large multicenter study, a preliminary analysis shows that cumulative incidence of first colorectal cancer under screening colonoscopy is lower than in previous published series. This observation reinforces the importance of screening colonoscopy in patients with Lynch syndrome and may suggest differences in the penetrance of the syndrome in our environment. The results of this study will be key for the further improvement on the management of families with Lynch syndrome.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP112 CLINICAL AND MOLECULAR CHARACTERIZATION OF LYNCH-LIKE SYNDROME
M.D. Pico Sala1, R. Jover2, M. Giner-Calabuig2, M. Alustiza2, J.L. Soto3, A. Castillejo1, A.B. Sánchez1, A. Sánchez García4, F. Balaguer4, L. Moreira4, A. Castells4, M. Pellisé Urquiza4, T. Introduction: Lynch syndrome (LS) is the most common cause of inherited colorectal cancer (CRC). However, there is a group of patients that develop CRC or LS-related tumors in which the presence of microsatellite instability or loss of expression of the mismatch repair proteins is observed in the tumor, but no germinal pathogenic mutation is found in these genes. This group of patients is known as Lynch-like syndrome (LLS) and represents approximately 30% of all patients with unstable tumors (1). These cases and their relatives show high risk for CRC and there is no consensus about their management (2, 3).
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study is to know the clinical and molecular characteristics of these patients in a large nation-wide cohort and to analyze if there are clinical, pathology or molecular characteristics that could suggest a probably hereditary or sporadic origin. This is a multicenter nation-wide study, involving 25 Spanish hospitals. Patients with CRC were included when their tumors show immunochemical loss of MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 or loss of MLH1 with BRAF-wild type and/or no MLH1 methylation and absence of pathogenic mutation in these genes. Immunochemical study of the tumors was performed because of fulfilment of revised Bethesda Guidelines (4) or because of universal molecular screening for LS (5). These patients were included in a national registry (EPICOLON-III) and demographic, clinical and pathological variables, as well as family history of neoplasms were registered.
Results: Our study included 85 patients with LLS. Mean age at diagnosis of CRC was 55 years (SD 14). A total of 39 patients were female (46%). Loss of MLH1/PMS2 was found in 46% of CRC, loss of MSH2/MSH6 in 34%, isolated loss of MSH6 was found in 12% and isolated loss of PMS2 in a 6%. Revised Bethesda guidelines were fulfilled by 78% of cases, whereas Amsterdam I criteria were fulfilled by 10% and Amsterdam II in 13%. A total of 56 patients (66%) had CRC located in the right colon. Regarding TNM, 19% of tumors were in stage I, 32% in stage II, 28% in stage III and 8% in stage IV. None of the patients showed personal history of previous CRC. A total of 12 patients (14%) had personal history of non-colorectal cancer, and only 3 (3.5%) patients had previous history of LS-related cancer. Regarding family history, a total of 46 patients (54%) had at least one relative with CRC, and 38 patients (45%) showed familial history of LS-related cancer. Comparison of clinical and molecular characteristics of patients depending on age at diagnosis of CRC or family history can be seen in Table 1. *p < 0.05 for comparison

 Conclusion: In this cohort of LLS patients, the largest collected until now, there are no clinical, molecular or pathological characteristics that could be of help to distinguish between probably sporadic and hereditary patients. These results support the need of homogeneous follow-up for this group of patients.

## GLUTEN-RELATED DISORDERS - ROOM E2____________________

## OP113 THE PREVALENCE OF NON-CELIAC GLUTEN SENSITIVITY IN PATIENTS WITH ABDOMINAL PAIN AND BLOATING
M. Di Stefano1, G. Di Fede2, I. Benedetti3, M. Bresciani1, C. Pedroni2, A. Gabriele2, M. Bergonzi3, E.V. Pesatori3, G.F. Manfredi3, G.R. Corazza4

1IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo, Pavia/Italy

2istituto di medicina biologica, Milano/Italy

3First Department Of Internal Medicine, IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo, Pavia/Italy

4Cattedra Di Gastroenterologia - Dip. Di Med. Interna E Terapia Medica 1st Department of Medicine, University of Pavia, IRCCS, San Matteo? Hospital, Pavia, Italy, Pavia/Italy

Contact E-mail Address:
irene.benedetti89@gmail.com

Introduction: A new entity, called Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS), was recently proposed to categorize patients suffering from a wide range of both intestinal and extra-intestinal symptoms after gluten ingestion (Sapone A, et al, BMC Medicine 2012). A very high prevalence of this condition was reported (Sapone A, et al, BMC Medicine 2012), but in our experience such a high figure was not confirmed (Di Sabatino A, et al, CGH 2015). We have recently shown that the ingestion of gluten may hamper colonic fermentation (DLD) in healthy volunteers. Accordingly, it is possible that a high prevalence of NCGS could be present in patients with bloating.
Aims & Methods: Our aim was to detect the prevalence of non-celiac gluten sensitivity in functional patients with a long history of abdominal pain and bloating, claiming a relationship between gluten intake and symptom occurrence, and referred to an outpatient clinic for functional gastrointestinal disorders of a tertiary medical center. In accordance with the Salerno Criteria (Catassi C, et al, Nutrients 2015), we conducted a double-blind, placebo controlled trial with gluten vs placebo in thirty-two non-celiac patients with moderate to severe abdominal bloating and pain, enrolled in an outpatient clinic (M/F 3/29, mean age 31 ± 5). Symptoms were present for a mean period of 10 ± 3 years and were judged by patients as poorly responsive to all previous treatments. The presence of allergic, organic gastrointestinal and systemic disorders was ruled out in all patients. All subjects reported abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence, borborygmi, bowel habit alterations, dyspeptic symptoms on gluten-containing diet (GCD) and, considering gluten as the causal agent, had been spontaneously following a non-blinded gluten-free diet (GFD) for at least a 6-week period, reporting an improvement of symptoms. They then started a rigorous GFD and entered this trial. In a double-blind, crossover protocol, ten capsules, containing 475 mg of gluten or 475 mg of rice starch, were administered randomly, each day for a 1-week period, with a 1-week wash-out interval. The patients completed a diary of symptoms, every evening at the same time for the duration of the study. The two main symptoms recorded by all patients were bloating and abdominal pain: a mean value during gluten ingestion over 30% higher than the value during placebo was considered as indicative of gluten sensitivity (Catassi C, et al, Nutrients 2015).
Results: In seventeen out of 32 patients (53%), the severity of abdominal pain was significantly higher during the week of gluten capsule ingestion than during the week of placebo capsule ingestion: the severity of abdominal pain in the group of patients with NCGS was 2.8 ± 2.4 during gluten and 1.5 ± 2.0 during placebo (p = 0.00001), on the contrary, in the group of non-sensitive patients it was 0.7 ± 1.8 during gluten and 1.2 ± 1.9 during placebo (p = 0.013). In fifteen out of 32 patients (47%), the severity of bloating was significantly higher during gluten than during placebo: the severity of bloating in the group of patients with NCGS was 3.7 ± 2.5 during gluten and 2.2 ± 2.0 during placebo (p = 0.0001), while in the group of non-sensitive patients it was 2.1 ± 1.5 during gluten and 3.5 ± 2.3 during placebo (p = 0.00001). Considering the modification of at least one of the two main symptoms, the diagnosis of NCGS was possible in 22 out of 32 patients (68.7%).
Conclusion: Around half of the patients with a long history of abdominal pain and bloating, claiming a relationship with gluten ingestion, resistant to previous treatments and referred to a tertiary clinic, show a positive result at the double blind test for the diagnosis of NCGS.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP114 PROSPECTIVE EVALUATION OF TRANSGLUTAMINASE ANTIBODY CUT-OFF LIMITS TO PREDICT SCREEN-DETECTED COELIAC DISEASE
I.R. Korponay-Szabo1, J. Gyimesi1, G. Castillejo2, S. Vriezinga3, R. Auricchio4, A. Chmielewska5, K. Werkstetter6, P. Crespo7, C. Hartman8, E. Martinez9, P. Szillat10, H. Szajewska11, I. Polanco9, R. Shamir8, S. Koletzko6, C. Ribes Koninckx7, R. Troncone12, M.L. Mearin Manrique3

12Pediatrics, University Federico II Naples Dept. of Pediatrics, Naples/Italy
