## OP188 SPACING OF INFLIXIMAB THERAPY IN PATIENTS WITH INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASES IN CLINICAL REMISSION: PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A RETROSPECTIVE MULTICENTRE FRENCH NATIONAL COHORT
G. Dufour1, B. Pariente2, R. Altwegg1, L. Caillo3, J. Valats1, M. Bismuth1, J. Bourgaux3, L. Peyrin-Biroulet4, P. Desreumaux5, P. Pouderoux3, P. Blanc1, G. Pineton De Chambrun1

1Gastroenterology, Montpellier University Hospital, Montpellier/France

2Gastroenterology Unit, Hôpital Huriez, Lille University Hospital, Lille/France

3Gastroenterology, Nimes University Hospital, Nîmes/France

4Department Of Gastroenterology, Nancy University Hospital Inserm U954 Dept. of Hepato-Gastroenterology, Vandoeuvre les Nancy/France

5Gastroenterology department, CHRU Lille, Université Lille 2Lille/France

Contact E-mail Address:
g-dufour@chu-montpellier.fr

Introduction: Infliximab (IFX) is efficient to maintain clinical remission in patients with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) refractory to conventional therapies. To date, there is no clear guideline regarding the withdrawal of anti-TNF agents and the majority of IBD patients are treated with IFX for long term. An alternative to withdrawal of IFX may be the spacing of IFX infusion interval. This strategy was only evaluated in a large prospective controlled trial in rheumatoid arthritis patients with interesting results (Fautrel B, Ann Rheum Dis, 2016).
Aims & Methods: The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of a spacing of IFX infusion interval on the maintenance of clinical remission in IBD patients. Secondary aims of this study were to evaluate the occurrence of allergic reactions to IFX after spacing and the efficacy of IFX intensification after clinical relapse. This was a retrospective multicenter French national cohort including all IBD patients treated with infliximab who were in clinical remission according to the referring physician and had a spacing of their infusion interval over 9 weeks for at least two consecutive infusions. Clinical relapse after spacing according to referring physician and leading to IFX intensification was considered as primary endpoint. The clinical efficacy of IFX intensification after spacing and occurrence of drug reactions were also monitored.
Results: Eighty-nine patients were included in the study (61 patients with Crohn’s disease [CD] and 28 with an ulcerative colitis [UC]). Median delay between IFX introduction and spacing was 35.6 months (IQR: 17.6–64). Thirty-five (39%) patients were already treated with an immunosuppressive drug (thiopurine or methotrexate) at the time of IFX spacing. Maximum infusion interval spacing was of 13 weeks and 41 patients (46%) had infusion interval spacing ≥12 weeks. Cumulative probability of clinical relapse-free survival after spacing was 82.7% ± 4.1 and 72.6% ± 4.9 at one and two years, respectively. All IBD patients with a clinical relapse after spacing had an intensification of IFX therapy (n = 27) with a clinical response in 89% of patients. Only one patient had to withdrawal IFX therapy after clinical relapse due to IFX allergic reaction occurring three years after spacing. Regarding clinical relapse, the median delay between IFX introduction and spacing of infusion interval was significantly shorter in IBD patients with clinical relapse compared to patients without clinical relapse (22.9 months [IQR: 13.3–42] vs. 41.3 months [IQR: 22.5–67.1], respectively, p = 0.027). For CD patients, in univariate analysis, a delay >4 years between IFX introduction and spacing was significantly associated to the maintenance of clinical remission after spacing (RR = 0.26; CI 95%: 0.07–0.89, p = 0.032). For UC patients, radiologic inflammatory activity before spacing was associated to clinical relapse after spacing (RR = 13.9; CI 95%: 1.24–157.1, p = 0.033). In multivariate analysis, a delay >4 years between IFX introduction and spacing (RR 0.36, CI 95%: 0.19–0.68, p = 0.002), concomitant treatment with an immunosuppressant (RR = 0.31; CI 95%: 0.11–0.85, p = 0.022) and penetrating phenotype (RR = 0.57; CI 95%: 0.34–0.97, p = 0.039) were significantly associated to the maintenance of clinical remission after spacing in CD patients.
Conclusion: After spacing of IFX infusions over 9 weeks more than 70% of IBD patients remained in clinical remission over two years. Only one patient stopped IFX for allergic reaction after clinical relapse and IFX intensification. A short delay between IFX introduction and spacing seems to be a good predictive factor of clinical relapse after spacing, at least in CD. The collection and analysis of data from a larger national cohort is ongoing.

## OP189 HIGHER RATE OF CORTICORESISTANCE AND CORTICODEPENDENCE IN ELDERLY-ONSET UC PATIENTS DIAGNOSED <70 YEARS COMPARED TO ≥70 YEARS OF AGE: A POPULATION-BASED STUDY
D. Duricova1, H. Sarter1, M. Fumery2, A. Leroyer1, C. Charpentier3, B. Pariente4, L. Armengol-Debeir5, L. Peyrin-Biroulet6, C. Gower-Rousseau1, G. Savoye5

Introduction: Recent French population-based study reported that elderly-onset patients with Crohn's disease diagnosed over age of 70 years have different disease course regarding localization, disease progression and exposure to medication than patients aged 60–69 years (1).
Aims & Methods: The aims of this study was to assess whether the disease phenotype and long-term outcome also differs in elderly-onset (ulcerative colitis) UC diagnosed before and after the age of 70 years. Elderly-onset UC patients (≥60 years at diagnosis) from a French prospective population-based Registry (EPIMAD) were included. Demographic and clinical data at diagnosis and at maximal follow-up were collected using predefined questionnaire.
Results: 468 elderly-onset UC patients were included (median follow-up 6.2 years) of whom 277 (59%) were <70 years and 191 (41%) ≥70 years at diagnosis. Male gender was more frequent in patients <70 years than in older individuals (54% vs. 65%; p = 0.01) while patients ≥70 years had higher rate of left-sided colitis than younger ones (63% vs. 49%; p = 0.02). The 1 and 5-year cumulative probabilities of medication exposure were similar between the two age groups (5-aminosalicylic acid: 60% vs. 70% and 77% vs. 77%, p = 0.75; corticosteroids: 19% vs. 23% and 30% vs. 34%, p = 0.54; immunosuppressants: 3% vs. 2% and 10% vs. 9%, p = 0.78). However, patients <70 years compared to older individuals experienced significantly more corticoresistance (12% vs. 3%, p = 0.03) and tended to be more corticodependent (24% vs. 16%, p = 0.08). Only 4 patients received anti-TNFa therapy, 3 of them diagnosed <70 years. The rate of surgery was not influenced by age at diagnosis (1 and 5 year risk: 6% vs. 4% and 10% vs. 6%, p = 0.39).
Conclusion: Elderly-onset UC is heterogeneous group of patients with respect to disease phenotype and prognosis. Patients ≥70 years at diagnosis had higher frequency of left-sided colitis than younger ones. Importantly, patients diagnosed <70 years had more severe disease course in terms of higher rate of corticoresistance and corticodependence than those ≥70years.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP190 INCIDENCE OF MALIGNANT PROGRESSION IN PERSISTENT NONDYSPLASTIC BARRETT'S ESOPHAGUS - A DUTCH NATIONWIDE COHORT STUDY
Y. Peters1, J. Honing1, W. Kievit2, C. Kestens3, W. Pestman4, I.D. Nagtegaal5, P.D. Siersema6

1Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Radboud UMC, Nijmegen/Netherlands

2Radboud Institute For Health Science, Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen/Netherlands

3University Medical Center Utrecht Gastroenterology, Utrecht/Netherlands

4Department For Health Evidence, Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen/Netherlands

5Radboud University Nijmegen Medical Center, Radboud University Nijmegen Medical Center Dept. of Pathology, Nijmegen/Netherlands

6Gastroenterology & Hepatology, University Merdical Center Gastroenterology & Hepatology - Gastroenterology & Hepatology, University, Nijmegen/Netherlands

Introduction: The risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) in patients with non-dysplastic Barrett’s esophagus (NDBE) may have been overestimated in some studies. Lower progression rates could lead to changes in the current surveillance strategy, thereby reducing its associated risks and costs.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to evaluate whether persistence of NDBE during consecutive surveillance endoscopies identifies patients at a very low risk for malignant progression. In this population-based retrospective study, patients with a first diagnosis of NDBE between 2003 and 2012 were selected using the Dutch nationwide registry of histopathology (PALGA). Patients were followed until the development of EAC or high-grade dysplasia (HGD), or until the last endoscopy contact with biopsy sampling (through May 2016). Incidence rates and rate ratios for EAC and HGD/EAC combined were calculated to evaluate whether persistence of NDBE during consecutive endoscopies and progression-free time reduce the risk of malignant progression.
Results: In this study, 12,729 patients with NDBE were included, with a total follow-up of 64,563 (median 4.4 (IQR 3.0 – 6.8)) years. Malignant progression was seen in 437 patients (3.4%) after a median follow-up of 5.1 years (IQR 3.2 – 7.3). This resulted in an overall progression rate to EAC of 0.47 (95% CI: 0.42 – 0.53) per 100 person-years and a progression rate to HGD/EAC combined of 0.68 (95% CI: 0.62 – 0.74) per 100 person-years. At first follow-up endoscopy after a median of 2.3 years (IQR 1.8 – 3.2), 11,782 patients (93%) were found to have persistent NDBE, whereas 727 (5.7%) and 220 (1.7%) patients showed progression to low-grade dysplasia and HGD/EAC, respectively. In patients with two consecutive endoscopies showing NDBE after a median of 2.8 years (IQR 1.8 – 4.0), the malignant progression rate was 0.52 (95% CI: 0.40 – 0.67) per 100 person-years (RR 0.61 (95% CI: 0.45 – 0.81)) versus 0.86 in patients after one endoscopy. Patients with five consecutive non-progressive endoscopies had a 60% rate reduction (RR 0.40 (95% CI: 0.13 – 0.97)) for development of EAC (progression rate: 0.34 (95% CI: 0.11- 0.41) per 100 person-years). The incidence of EAC decreased with 30% (adjusted HR 0.71, 95%: CI: 0.67 – 0.75 for each year of FU without progression (progression-free time).
Conclusion: Persistent NDBE at two consecutive surveillance endoscopies reduces the risk of malignant progression towards HGD/EAC by approximately twofold. As progression risk reduces even further after more consecutive negative follow-up endoscopies, this study contributes to the growing evidence that surveillance intervals in subgroups of patients with persistent BE might be lengthened and/or that surveillance may be discontinued at an earlier endpoint than currently recommended.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

Introduction: Neoplastic Barrett esophagus (BE) is currently treated by a combined endoscopic resection and ablation therapy of the entire BE. For the ablation part, argon plasma coagulation (APC) had recently been introduced in a combination with prior submucosal injection (Hybrid-APC, H-APC) and reached results in a range comparable to radiofrequency ablation (RFA) in a small pilot study.
Aims & Methods: Multicenter study in 9 European centers on patients with biopsy proven neoplastic BE. Therapy consisted of combination of endoresection (EMR/ESD) plus maximum of 5 H-APC sessions for visible lesions and/or cancer diagnosis, or of exclusive ablation for neoplastic BE (LGIN/HGIN) without visible lesions at the discretion of the endoscopists. Immediate therapeutic success was defined as one follow-up endoscopy showing normal endoscopic neo-Z-line with negative biopsies.
Results: 106 of 164 included patients (92 male, 14 female, mean age 63, 8 years) completed therapy and had 3-month follow-up. Final diagnoses were mucosal cancer (n = 66), high-grade (HGIN, n = 17), low-grade dysplasia (LGIN n = 21) and normal BE (n = 1). Therapy consisted of combined resection and ablation (n = 94) or exclusive ablation (n = 12) with a mean number of H-APC sessions of 2.5 (range 1–5). Short-term treatment outcome: Endoscopic treatment success (normal Z line) was seen in 80 cases, but in 4 cases histopathology showed intestinal metaplasia (minor residual BE disease) or (n = 1) residual cancer. 20 further cases had unclear endoscopy (minor residual BE possible) but negative biopsies. Failure was seen in 6 cases, 4 of whom had minor residual BE and 2 had macroscopic and histologic diagnosis of complete ablation failure. Based on histopathologic proof, short-term eradication rates were 91, 5% (97/106). Treatment for minor residual BE is currently ongoing in some patients of the entire cohort (n = 164): Immediate complications: bleeding n = 2, post-procedure fever n = 9 and 1 perforation treated conservatively by clipping. Strictures requiring dilatation: n = 5.
Conclusion: H-APC appears to be feasible and safe and has a short-term efficacy of 92% in this interim analysis; final results of this large prospective study have to be awaited. The comparative value of H-APC to alternative methods such as RFA is then to be assessed in a prospective randomized trial.

## OP192 SAFETY OF THE SIX-SHOOTER MULTIBAND MUCOSECTOMY DEVICE FOR ENDOSCOPIC RESECTION IN BARRETT’S ESOPHAGUS IN 4327 RESECTIONS: A RETROSPECTIVE INTERNATIONAL MULTICENTER STUDY
K. Belghazi1, M. A. Everson2, R. Haidry2, P. Kandel3, L.K. Mejia3, M.J. Bourke4, F. Bahin4, B.L. a.m. Weusten5, G.G. Ginsberg6, G. Ma6, A.D. Koch7, R.V. Milano1, S. Seewald8, K. Ragunath9, R. Bisschops10, J.J. G. h.m. Bergman1, R. E. Pouw1

1Gastroenterology, Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam/Netherlands

k.belghazi@amc.uva.nl

Introduction: Endoscopic resection (ER) is an important treatment modality for patients with Barrett’s esophagus (BE) containing high-grade dysplasia (HGD) or early cancer. The most widely used device for ER is the six-shooter multi-band mucosectomy (MBM) device. This six-shooter consists of a modified variceal band ligator and requires no submucosal lifting or prelooping of a snare in the cap. A randomized study demonstrated that MBM with the six-shooter was equally effective and safe as ER with the classic cap-technique, but significantly faster and cheaper. However, large studies enabling accurate assessment of the associated complication risk are lacking.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this investigator-initiated non-sponsored study was to assess safety of ER with MBM using the six-shooter in BE in a large patient cohort. We retrospectively analyzed all patients treated with MBM using the six-shooter for ER in BE in 9 international tertiary referral centers for Barrett’s neoplasia. Primary outcome: perforation rate. Secondary outcomes: significant bleeding rate (defined as bleeding requiring an intervention), stricture rate, macroscopically radical resection rate (defined as complete resection of the target area, including all delineation markings).
Results: Between 2001 and 2017 a total of 1510 MBM procedures with the six-shooter were performed in 1100 patients (921 men, median 68 yrs, median BE C2M4) for the following indications: focal lesion suspicious for neoplasia (n = 961), diffuse HGD (n = 190), part of radical ER protocol (n = 213), escape treatment after endoscopic ablation (n = 29). A median of 3 (IQR 2–4) resections were performed per procedure, with a total of 4327 resections in this study. The median diameter of the ER specimens was maximum of 13 mm (IQR 10–16) and a minimum of 9 mm (IQR 6–12). Worst pathology was cancer in 511, HGD in 499, low-grade dysplasia in 209, and no-dysplasia in 267 procedures. In 9/1510 (0.6%, 95% CI 0.32% – 1.1%) MBM procedures a perforation occurred, treated with clips (n = 6), a stent (n = 2) or conservative treatment (n = 1). No surgery was required. Significant bleeding was seen in 7.1% (95% CI 5.9% – 8.5%) of MBM procedures and 8.3% (95% CI 6.8% – 10%) of the patients developed a stricture, requiring a median of 2 dilatations. Macroscopically radical resection of the target lesion was achieved in 92%.
Conclusion: This is the largest study on MBM using the six-shooter for ER in BE. This study therefore provides the most accurate assessment of the risk of serious complications associated with this procedure. Our results show that MBM using the six-shooter is a safe and effective procedure with a low rate of perforation of 0.6% (95% CI 0.32% – 1.1%), all of which could be managed endoscopically.

## OP193 ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION FOR BARRETT’S EARLY NEOPLASIA: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
D. Yang1, F. Zou1, S. Xiong2, J. J. Forde3, P.V. Draganov1

1Gastroenterology, University of Florida, Gainesville/United States of America/FL

2Biostatistics, University of Florida, Gainesville/United States of America/FL

3Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville/United States of America/FL

Contact E-mail Address:
dennis.yang@medicine.ufl.edu

Introduction: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is an endoscopic technique that permits en-bloc resection of lesions, irrespective of size. Recent studies suggest that ESD is superior to endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) in terms of en-bloc resection, curative resection rates, and local recurrence for tumors of the gastrointestinal tract, including esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC). The role of ESD for the management of dysplastic Barrett’s esophagus (BE) and early EAC has not been fully evaluated.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ESD for visible dysplastic BE and EAC lesions. Methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published up to March 2017 that reported on clinical outcomes of ESD on BE early neoplasia. Three online databases (Medline, Ovid, Embase) were searched. Pooled means and proportions were computed. The Cochran’s Q test and I2 were used to test for heterogeneity. If yes, then a fixed meta-analysis approach (FE Model) was applied; otherwise, random meta-analysis (RE Model) was used. For the main outcomes, evaluation for potential sources of heterogeneity were evaluated via meta-regression analysis.
Results: A total of 11 studies involving 501 patients (83% male; mean age 64.4) were included. The mean visible lesion size was 27 mm (95% confidence interval [CI] 20.9–33.1). Mean total procedure time was 107.5 minutes (95% CI 86.4–128.5). The pooled estimate for en-bloc resection was 92.9% (95% CI: 90.3 to 95.2%). The pooled R0 (negative lateral and deep margins for dysplastic BE and EAC) and curative resection rates were 74.5% (95% CI: 66.3 to 81.9%) and 64.9% (95% CI: 55.7 to 73.6%) respectively. There was significant heterogeneity found in both R0 (Cochran Q test P < 0.001, I2 = 70.5) and curative (Cochran Q test P < 0.001, I2 = 72.3) resection rates. However, there was no statistically significant association between R0 or curative resection rates and study location (Asia vs. Europe/United States), length of BE, lesion characteristics, procedural time or length of follow-up. The pooled estimate for adverse events such as perforation and bleeding were 1.5% (95% CI 0.4–3.0%) and 1.7% (95% CI 0.6–3.4%) respectively. The incidence of esophageal stricture formation was 11.6% (95% CI: 0.9–29.6%). All of these were managed successfully with endoscopic dilation. In aggregate, the estimated recurrence rate for dysplastic BE and EAC following curative resection was 0.17% (95% CI 0–0.3%) at a mean follow-up 22.9 months (95% CI: 17.5 to 28.3).
Conclusion: ESD is a safe endoscopic treatment option for BE early neoplasia associated with high-en bloc resection and R0 (complete) resection rates. The recurrence rate of dysplastic BE and EAC is low in patients with curative resection after ESD. Overall, ESD can be considered for the evaluation and management of visible neoplastic BE; especially for large lesions not amenable for en-bloc resection with standard EMR techniques.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP194 NEUTROPHIL LYMPHOCYTE RATIO AS PREDICTIVE MARKER OF SURVIVAL IN ESOPHAGEAL CANCER: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
G. Pirozzolo1, S.S. Gisbertz2, C. Castoro1, M.I. Van Berge Henegouwen2, M. Scarpa1

1Esophageal And Digestive Tract Surgical Unit, Regional Centre For Esophageal Disease, Veneto Institute of Oncology (IOV-IRCCS), Padova/Italy

2Surgical Department, Academic Medical Centre, Amsterdam/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
giovanni.pirozzolo@gmail.com

Introduction: Several studies showed that a high preoperative Neutrophil-Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR) is a predictor of worse survival in many solid tumors, including esophageal cancer. Neutrophils are a consistent part of the peritumoral inflammatory cell infiltrate, called tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs). This infiltrate seems to be a direct result of cancer cells activity, suggesting that TANs are related to tumor growth. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to collect all the data about this marker in order to quantify its strength in esophageal cancer prognostication.
Aims & Methods: The meta-analysis was performed using the Preferred reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We used inclusion criteria adapted from the REporting recommendations for tumor MARKer prognostic studies criteria. We conducted a comprehensive search of all prospective or observational studies reporting NLR prognostic data in esophageal cancer patients. The primary outcome measure was Overall Survival (OS) while Disease Free Survival (DFS) and Progression Free Survival (PFS) were secondary outcome measures. All included studies had a directly or indirectly available HR. We analyzed data using fixed effect model or random effect model depending on heterogeneity.
Results: We included in the quantitative synthesis 17 studies published between 2011 and 2017, comprising 5672 patients. The NLR cut-off value ranged from 2 to 5. Our analysis about OS of all included studies showed that a high preoperative NLR is an effective predictor of a worse survival (HR 1.72, p < 0.00001). Similar results were obtained about DFS (HR 1.94, p < 0.00001) and PFS (HR 1.66, p < 0.00001). We conducted sub-analysis both for cut-off ranges subgroups and treatment modality subgroups obtaining the same prognostic relevance.
Conclusion: Retrospective design of included study is the major bias. There is heterogeneity about treatment modalities, patients characteristics, duration of follow-up and cut-off threshold. Moreover, NLR has been proposed in several studies as a prognostic marker for non-oncological diseases, mostly heart disease. However, our meta-analysis confirmed that preoperative high NLR is associated with a worse outcome in esophageal cancer. Some issues about its clinical use are still unclear; first of all the most effective cut-off in survival prognostication, and its role in predicting postoperative complications.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP195 THE OPTIMAL TIME INTERVAL BETWEEN NEOADJUVANT CHEMORADIOTHERAPY AND ESOPHAGECTOMY: A NATIONWIDE STUDY
L. R. Van Der Werf1, J. Dikken2, E. Van Der Willik3, M.I. Van Berge Henegouwen4, V. E.p.p. Lemmens5, G. A.p. Nieuwenhuijzen6, B.P.l. Wijnhoven7 On Behalf Of The Dutch Upper Gi Cancer Audit Group8

1Oncological Surgery, Erasmus Medical Center, Rotterdam/Netherlands

2Surgery, LUMC, Leiden/Netherlands

3Methodology, Dutch Institute of Clinical Auditing, Leiden/Netherlands

4Surgical Department, Academic Medical Centre, Amsterdam/Netherlands

5Epidemiology, Erasmus Medical Centre, Rotterdam/Netherlands

6Oncological Surgery, Catharina ziekenhuis, Eindhoven/Netherlands

7Surgery, Erasmus MC Rotterdam Dept. of Surgery, Rotterdam/Netherlands

8Dutch Institute for Clinical Auditing, Leiden/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
L.vanderwerf@dica.nl

Introduction: The most optimal timing of oesophagectomy after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) is unknown. Theoretically, an extended interval between nCRT and surgery might increase the chance of the best pathological respons: pathological complete respons (pCR) because of a prolonged effect of the nCRT and this might possibly improve disease-free and overall survival. Conversely, it is thought that an extended interval might lead to residual tumor outgrowth, a more difficult surgical resection, with a higher complication rate, and possibly a worse survival. The aim of this study was to assess the time interval between nCT and surgery in the Netherlands and to correlate this with pathological response of the tumor and surgical morbidity and mortality.
Aims & Methods: Patients with esophageal cancer treated with nCRT and surgery between 2011 and 2016 were selected from a national database of the Dutch Upper gastrointestinal Cancer Audit.(1) Differences in patient and treatment characteristics, tumor stage and morbidity/mortality after surgery were compared across six subgroups discriminated by the length between end of nCRT and surgery. To evaluate the association between the interval and pathological complete respons (pCR), intraoperative, postoperative complications and mortality, multivariable logistic regression analysis was used.
Results: In total 3102 patients were included. The median [interquartile range] time interval between the end of nCT and surgery was 8 [7–10] weeks. The interval between end of nCRT and surgery was divided into six (A-F) groups: 0–5 weeks (A; n = 157), 6–7 weeks (B; n = 878), 8–9 weeks (C; n = 972), 10–12 weeks (D; n = 720), 13–14 weeks (E; n = 195) and 15 or more weeks (F; n = 180). In intervals E and F, there were significantly more patients with ASA III+ and with proximal to mid-esophageal tumors. The pCR rate in group A to F was 31%, 28%, 26%, 31%, 40%, and 37%, respectively. In multivariable analysis, a longer interval (groups D-F for adenocarcinoma and groups E and F for squamous cell carcinoma) was associated with a higher probability of a pCR. These groups had the same probability for intraoperative and severe postoperative complications. The extended interval groups were associated with higher total postoperative complications (E and F) and mortality (D and F).
Conclusion: An extended interval (≥10 weeks for adenocarcinoma and ≥12 weeks for squamous cell carcinoma) between nCRT and esophagectomy is associated with a higher probability of a pCR and does not lead to a higher occurrence of intraoperative and severe complications. We suggest that the higher total postoperative complications and mortality is due to selection bias.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.
Reference
Busweiler LA, Wijnhoven BP, van Berge Henegouwen MI, et al. Early outcomes from the Dutch Upper Gastrointestinal Cancer Audit. Br J Surg. 2016;103(13):1855–1863.

## OP196 HELICOBACTER PYLORI ERADICATION AND THE RISK OF GASTRIC CANCER: A POPULATION-BASED COHORT STUDY
E. Doorakkers1, J. Lagergren2, L. Engstrand3, N. Brusselaers4

1Department Of Molecular Medicine And Surgery, Upper Gastrointestinal Surgery, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm/Sweden

2Department Of Molecular Medicine And Surgery, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm/Sweden

3Dept. Of Of Microbiology, Tumor & Cell Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm/Sweden

4Centre For Translational Microbiome Research, Department Of Microbiology, Tumor And Cell Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm/Sweden

Contact E-mail Address:
eva.doorakkers@ki.se

Introduction:
Helicobacter pylori is a stomach bacterium associated with an increased risk for gastric cancer. We aimed to assess if the risk of gastric cancer remains increased after H. pylori eradication.
Aims & Methods: This was a population-based, nationwide cohort study in Sweden conducted between 1 July 2005 and 31 December 2012. Data on H. pylori eradication were retrieved from the Swedish Prescribed Drug Registry and eradication consisted of triple therapy with a proton pump inhibitor and 2 antibiotics (clarithromycin and amoxicillin or metronidazole). The cancer incidence in the cohort was compared to that of the corresponding background population using standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Results: In total, 92, 852 individuals (46.3% men) received eradication therapy during the study period. The total follow-up time after eradication was 331, 694 person-years (mean 3.6 years). Of the eradicated participants, 76 (0.08%) developed gastric cancer, corresponding with an incidence of 22.9/100, 000 person years. The SIR of gastric cancer after eradication was increased (SIR 1.46, 95% CI 1.15–1.83). The SIR for men was 1.30 (95% CI 0.94–1.77) and for women the SIR was 1.70 (95% CI 1.18–2.36). The SIRs were higher in the age groups <40 years (SIR 3.18, 95% CI 0.04–17.69), 40–49 years (SIR 3.78, 95% CI 1.38–8.22), 50–59 years (SIR 2.36, 95% CI 1.22–4.11), and not consistently increased in the age groups 60–69 years (SIR 0.97, 95% CI 0.50–1.69) and ≥70 years (SIR 1.38, 95% CI 1.00–1.84).
Conclusion: The overall risk for gastric cancer after eradication for H. pylori remained increased compared to the general population.

Introduction: Due to the diversity of strains, resistances and geographical particularities, the best approach for Helicobacter pylori management remains unclear.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to assess the management of H. pylori infection by gastroenterologists in Europe and to evaluate the efficacy of first-line treatments. A systematic prospective registry of the clinical practice of European gastroenterologists regarding H. pylori infection and treatment (30 countries and 250 recruiting investigators). A local coordinator was selected from each country with more than 10 H. pylori references on PubMed. Each coordinator selected a representative group of recruiting investigators from its country. An electronic clinical research file was created on AEG-REDCap to systematically register all adult patients infected with H. pylori. Variables included: Patients’ demographics, previous eradication attempts, prescribed eradication treatment, adverse events, and outcomes (cure rates, compliance, follow up, etc.).
Results: Up to now, 20,175 patients (60% women) have finished follow up. Mean age was 49 years. Of all patients, 4.2% had drug allergies (81% to penicillin), 56% of had dyspepsia, 18% had gastroduodenal ulcer. Two-thirds (66%) were diagnosed using endoscopy-based methods. The treatments were: first-line in 78% of the patients, second-line in 16%, third-line in 4.4%, fourth-line in 1.2%, and fifth-line in 0.4%. Within the first-line prescriptions, 56% of first-line prescriptions were triple regimens (PPI + 2 antibiotics), 21% non-bismuth quadruple concomitant, 9% sequential, and 7% bismuth quadruple. Overall, first-line modified intention-to-treat (mITT) eradication rate was 78%. First-line efficacy per antibiotic combination is shown in the table.

 Conclusion:
H. pylori management by gastroenterologists in Europe is extremely diverse and the overall eradication rate is suboptimal, mainly due to the frequent use of triple therapies where they are ineffective (most European regions). In order to achieve ≥90% eradication, physicians are encouraged to use quadruple therapies.

## OP198 HELICOBACTER PYLORI ERADICATION THERAPY WITH VONOPRAZAN WAS MORE EFFECTIVE COMPARED TO PROTON PUMP INHIBITORS, AND THE EFFECT WAS NOT DISTURBED IN THE PATIENTS WITH LIFE STYLE-RELATED DISEASES
H. Endo1, Y. Takara1, T. Matsunaga1, H. Hidaka1, S. Shirai2, R. Shimoda2, R. Iwakiri3, K. Fujimoto3

1Department Of Internal Medicine, Saiseikai Kratsu Hospital, Karatsu/Japan

2Internal Medicine And Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, Saga Medical School, Saga/Japan

3Internal Medicine, Saga Medical School, Saga/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
hiro714@vc1.people-i.ne.jp

Introduction: Vonoprazan (VPZ) combined with two anti-biotics therapy has been applied for Helicobacter pylori (HP) eradication in Japan, and there is still little information of the detailed eradication results. The aim of the present study was to retrospectively compare the HP eradication outcomes between proton pump inhibitors (PPI) and VPZ with 1,774 subjects of our hospital in 2012–2016. In addition, we evaluated whether the eradication effect with VPZ was affected by lifestyle-related diseases including obesity, hypertension (HT) and diabetes mellitus (DM).
Aims & Methods: In total, 1774 subjects (primary eradication: 1485, secondary: 289) received HP eradication therapy in our hospital in 2012 – 2016. The eradication judgment was performed by 13C-urea breath test (UBT), and the eradication rate (%, per-protocol analysis) was calculated. Eradication therapy was performed with PPI (lansoprazole (LPZ) 30 mg or rabeprazole (RPZ) 10 mg or esomeprazole (EPZ) 20 mg) or VPZ 20 mg + clarithromycin (CAM) 200 mg + amoxicillin (AMPC) 750 mg twice/day for 7 days as primary eradication. Failure of the primary eradication was follows by the secondary eradication with PPI or VPZ 20 mg + metronidazole (MNZ) 250 mg + AMPC 750 mg twice/day for 7 days.
Results: The primary eradication rates were VPZ 90.5% (371/410), LPZ 73.7% (246/334), RPZ 75.9% (366/482), and EPZ 83.0% (215/259). The eradication rate of VPZ was significantly high compared to that of all the other three PPI 77.0% (828/1076) (P < 0.001) and each PPI. The secondary eradication rate was VPZ 93.1% (54/58), LPZ 87.7% (50/57), RPZ 90.5% (67/74), EPZ 91.0% (91/100). Secondary eradication rate tended to be high in VPZ (93.1%) but not significant compared to that in all the other PPI (90.0%) (208/231) (P = 0.47). Next, we analyzed the influence of the lifestyle-related diseases on eradication. The primary HP eradication rate did not depend on the body weight: obese subjects (BMI > 25, n = 262: VPZ 97.0% vs PPI 72.4%) and no obese subjects (n = 771: VPZ 90.5% vs PPI 77.7%). As indicated, VPZ worked better in the obese subjects compared to the non-obese subjects (BMI > 25: 97.0% vs BMI < 25: 90.5%: P = 0.089), suggesting the effect of VPZ was not influenced by the body weight. Regarding HT, primary eradication rate was better in VPZ compared to PPI (VPZ 87.3%, PPI 76.8%). The primary eradication rate of the 118 patients with DM (VPZ 89.3%, PPI 68.9%) was not different from 1368 non-DM subjects (VPZ 90.6%, PPI 77.7%). There was not the serious adverse event with VPZ and PPI during the investigation period.
Conclusion: HP eradication therapy using VPZ was effective compared to that of PPI, and life-style related diseases including obesity, hypertension, DM, had no influence on the HP eradication with VPZ.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP199 OPTIMIZED 14-DAY SEQUENTIAL VERSUS 10-DAY BISMUTH QUADRUPLE THERAPY CONTAINING HIGH DOSE ESOMEPRAZOLE IN THE FIRST-LINE TREATMENT OF HELICOBACTER PYLORI –A MULTICENTER RANDOMIZED TRIAL
J. Liou1, Y. Fang2, C. Chen1, M. Bair3, J. Lin4, M. Wu1

1Dept. Of Internal Medicine, National Taiwan University Hospital Dept. of Internal Medicine Taiwan Helicobacter Consortium, Taipei/Taiwan

2National Taiwan University Hospital, Yun-Lin Branch, Yun-Lin/Taiwan

3Mackay Memorial Hospital, Taitung Branch, Taitung/Taiwan

4College Of Medicine, Fu-Jen Catholic University, New Taipei City/Taiwan

Contact E-mail Address:
dtmed046@pchome.com.tw

Introduction: Our previous trial and meta-analysis showed that 14-day sequential therapy was superior to 14-day triple therapy in the first line treatment of H. pylori infection. However, whether the optimized 14-day sequential therapy is superior to 10-day bismuth quadruple therapy has not been reported. We aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of 14-day sequential therapy and 10-day bismuth quadruple therapy containing high dose esomeprazole in the first-line treatment of H. pylori.
Aims & Methods: For this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial, we recruited adult patients (≥20 years of age) with H. pylori infection naïve to treatment from 9 centers in Taiwan. Eligible patients were randomized to receive either sequential therapy (esomeprazole 40 mg and amoxicillin 1 g for the first 7 days, followed by esomeprazole 40 mg, clarithromycin 500 mg, and metronidazole 500 mg for another 7 days; with all drugs given twice daily) for 14 days or bismuth quadruple therapy (bismuth tripotassium dicitrate 300 mg four times a day, esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily, tetracycline 500 mg four times a day, and metronidazole 500 mg three times a day) for 10 days. Our primary outcome was the eradication rate in the first-line therapy by intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. The minimum inhibitory concentrations were determined by agar dilution test.
Results: A total of 620 patients have been recruited. The prevalence of clarithromycin resistance was about 14.3% in the study population. The eradication rates of the optimized 14-day sequential therapy and 10-day bismuth quadruple therapy were 95.0% (245/258) and 94.7% (249/263) in the ITT analysis (p = 0.884), respectively and were 96.1% (245/255) and 95.8% (249/260) in the PP analysis (p = 0.859). The frequencies of any adverse effects were 37.3% (109/292) and 72.8% (219/301) in patients treated with 14-day sequential therapy and 10-day bismuth quadruple therapy, respectively (p < 0.001). The eradication rates of 14-day sequential therapy for clarithromycin resistant and susceptible strains were 75% (12/16) and 100% (114/114), respectively (p < 0.001), whereas that of 10-day bismuth quadruple therapy was not affected by clarithromycin resistance.
Conclusion: Both bismuth quadruple therapy and 14-day sequential therapy containing high dose esomeprazole are highly effective in regions with low to intermediate clarithromycin resistance rate. Sequential therapy is better tolerated but is less effective in the presence of clarithromycin resistance.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP200 THE ABUNDANCE OF ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE GENES IN HUMAN GUTS AFTER H. PYLORI ERADICATION THERAPY
S. Y. Malanin1, D. D. Safina1, D. R. Khusnutdinova1, I. Y. Vasilyev1, T.V. Grigoryeva1, M. N. Siniagina1, M.I. Markelova1, E. A. Boulygina1, S.R. Abdulkhakov2, R. A. Abdulkhakov3, V. M. Chernov1

1Kazan Federal University, Kazan/Russian Federation

2Department Of Normal Human Anathomy, Kazan State Medical University, Kazan/Russian Federation

3Kazan State Medical University, Kazan/Russian Federation

Contact E-mail Address:
tatabio@inbox.ru

Introduction: It is well known that one of the adverse effects of antibiotic therapy is the enrichment of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria. Resistance may be due to the presence of the resistance genes that can be acquired through mutations or horizontal transfer and spread not only among pathogenic bacteria, but also among the members of the normal microflora. Thus the intestinal microflora may serve as a potential reservoir of resistance genes and contribute to the spread of antibiotic resistance genes. H. pylori eradication therapy consisting of treatment by several antimicrobial drugs is a good model for studying the effect of antibiotics on the abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in the gut.
Aims & Methods: The aim of the study was to explore the gut resistome before and after antibiotic therapy by shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Seventy stool samples were used for analysis: 35 samples from H. pylori-positive patients before eradication therapy, 35 - from the same patients after the completion of eradication therapy consisted of treatment by amoxicillin (1000 mg), clarithromycin (500 mg), proton pump inhibitor in a standard dose, bismuth subsalicylate (240 mg) bid for 14 days, lactulose was added as a prebiotic. Total DNA was isolated from the stool samples using beat beating method and sequenced on Solid 5500xl-W platform. Reads were aligned to the Comprehensive Antibiotic Database (CARD, version 1.1.7) using bowtie 1.2.0. Significant changes of antibiotic resistance genes abundances in the microbiomes of patients before and after eradication were assessed using Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p-value <0.05 was considered significant).
Results: Eradication therapy of H. pylori infection leads to increasing of abundance of different antibiotic resistance genes. Significant changes of abundance were shown for genes conferring resistance to 12 from 27 groups of antibiotics (CARD). The largest significant fold changes were found for beta-lactams (for some patients quantity of TEM beta-lactamases increased up to 125-fold), for macrolides (mrx and mphA genes up to 288 and 360-fold increase, respectively), for aminoglycoside (aph, aadA, increase up to 297, 352-fold), fluoroquinolones (oqxB up to 133-fold increase). Moreover significant expansion of genes coding several multidrug efflux pumps was also detected. Notably, a large number of antibiotic resistance genes were found to appear in the microbiome after therapy. Most of these genes confer resistance to beta-lactams (TEM beta-lactamases and shv genes), aminoglycoside (aac, aad), vancomycin (vanXYC), fluoroquinolones (qnr genes). Thus eradication therapy leads to the accumulation of genes promoting the resistance to antibiotics, that were not part of the treatment.
Conclusion: The antibiotic therapy of H.pylori infection favours the accumulation of the wide range of antibiotic resistance genes, implying higher risks for resistance acquisition by pathogenic bacteria. Further research should be aimed to studying mechanisms of gene spreading, as well as determining the duration of these changes in intestinal resistome.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.
Reference
This work was financially supported by the Ministry of Education and Science of Russian Federation (agreement #14.575.21.0076, ID RFMEFI575I4X0076).

## OP202 CALCITONIN GENE-RELATED PEPTIDE INNERVATING ENTERIC PLEXUSES IS DOWNREGULATED IN DIVERTICULAR DISEASE: IMPLICATIONS FOR PATHOGENESIS
J.I. Lukosiene1, A. G. Pauza2, K. Rysevaite-Kyguoliene2, J. Kupcinskas3, Z. Saladzinskas4, A. Tamelis4, N. Pauziene2

1Department Of Gastroenterology, Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, Kaunas/Lithuania

2Institute Of Anatomy, Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, Kaunas/Lithuania

3Lithuanian University Of Helath Sciences, Kaunas, Kaunas/Lithuania

4Department Of Surgery, Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, Kaunas/Lithuania

Contact E-mail Address:
jaune.lukosiene@gmail.com

Introduction: Diverticular disease (DD) of the colon is a frequent gastrointestinal disorder and an important cause of hospital admissions in Western and industrialized nations [1]. Several aetiological cofactors have been implicated in the pathogenesis of the disease, that involve both structural remodelling and functional alterations [1]. It is hypothesized that abnormal colonic motility, likely resulting from changes to enteric nervous system [2], and increased intraluminal pressure are both important predisposing factors in the development of colonic diverticula. CGRP (calcitonin gene related peptide) is a potent smooth muscle relaxant involved in a variety of physiological processes throughout the digestive system. Within the alimentary tract, CGRP is capable to induce peristaltic reflexes [3], relax smooth muscle cells [4], induce phasic contractile activity [5] and excite myenteric neurons [6].
Aims & Methods: The aim of the study was to investigate CGRP signalling pathway in symptomatic (SDD) and asymptomatic diverticular disease (ADD) patients. Full-thickness sigmoid specimens were obtained from patients undergoing surgery for non-obstructing colorectal carcinoma, that served as control (n = 10, age: 50–75 years) and as ADD (n = 10, age: 57–76 years) if colonic diverticula were present and patient had no previous anamnesis of DD associated symptoms. Tissue specimens for SDD (n = 10, age: 39–80 years) were obtained from patients who underwent sigmoid resection or left hemicolectomy after recurrent attacks of diverticulitis. Full-thickness colon sections were processed for CGRP and its receptors CRLR (calcitonin receptor-like receptor) and RAMP1 (receptor activity-modifying protein 1) immunohistochemistry and analysed by means of quantitative fluorescence microscopy. Protein expression was determined by measuring densitometric fluorescence within the ganglia of myenteric (MP), outer (oSP) and inner (iSP) submucosal plexuses.
Results: We found that in SDD patients CGRP expression is decreased by 40 % within all divisions of enteric nervous system (MP – p < 0.001, oSP – p < 0.01, iSP – p < 0.001), with ADD patients having the intermediate values. CGRP receptor – CRLR – was found to be upregulated in an opposite manner in DD patients, with SDD being 25 % greater than control patients (MP – p < 0.01, oSP – p < 0.01, iSP – n.s.). Second protein necessary for CGRP signalling – RAMP1 – expression was found to be unaltered.
Conclusion: We can conclude that CGRP signalling pathway is subjected to alteration in DD. Gradual decrease of CGRP may be suspected since ADD had the intermediate values for both CGRP and CRLR. Knowing that CGRP is involved both in smooth muscle contractility and intestinal motility it is reasonable to hypothesize that upregulation CRLR may have develop as a compensatory mechanism for declining levels of CGRP.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP203 IMMUNE ACTIVATION AND NERVE SPROUTING IN THE COLONIC MUCOSA OF PATIENTS WITH DIVERTICULAR DISEASE
M.R. Barbaro1, C. Cremon1, D. Fuschi1, E. Scaioli1, G. Marasco1, M. Carapelle2, E. Benatti1, E. Capelli1, A. Colecchia1, D. Festi1, V. Stanghellini1, G. Barbara1

1Dept. Medical And Surgical Sciences, University of Bologna Dept. of Medical and Surgical Sciences, Bologna/Italy

2University of Bologna, Bologna/Italy

Contact E-mail Address:
maria.barbaro2@unibo.it

Introduction: Colonic diverticulosis is a common clinical condition in industrialized countries, with the highest rates in the United States and Europe. Symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease (SUDD) is a syndrome characterized by abdominal symptoms similar to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) attributed to diverticula. A role for low-grade inflammation, sensory-motor dysfunction, and dysbiosis may be suggested in a clinical picture that mimics IBS. We hypothesized that mucosal immune activation, nerve fiber density and sprouting may play a role in symptom generation in patients with SUDD.
Aims & Methods: The aim of the present study was to characterize immune cells, nerve density and sprouting in patients with SUDD, diverticulosis and healthy controls (HC). 14 HC, 16 patients with diverticulosis and 10 with SUDD were enrolled in the study. In patients with diverticula, mucosal biopsies were obtained close to diverticula and at least 20 cm from the last observed diverticula (normal mucosa). In HC, biopsies were performed at sigmoid and at descending colon. Quantitative immunohistochemistry was used to assess the expression of tryptase (mast cell marker), CD3 (T cell marker), CD68 (macrophage marker), neuronal specific enolase (NSE) [nerve marker], and growth-associated protein 43 (GAP-43) [neuronal outgrowth marker]. IBS-like symptoms severity and frequency were graded using a 5 point Likert scale. Correlation analyses were performed between immune cell counts and nerve fiber ones.
Results: Mast cells were significantly increased in the peridiverticular mucosa of patients fulfilling the Roma III criteria for the diagnosis of IBS in comparison with HC (5.9 ± 0.7% vs 3.6 ± 0.5%; P < 0.05), but not in patients with SUDD as compared to diverticulosis or HC. No differences were detected in the T-cell counts among the three groups. Macrophages were significantly increased in patients with SUDD and diverticulosis as compared to HC, both in the peridiverticular (5.8 ± 0.4%, 6.9 ± 0.6%, 4.9 ± 0.4%, respectively; P < 0.05) and in normal mucosa (7.1 ± 0.7%, 6.6 ± 0.4%, 4.0 ± 0.3%, respectively; P < 0.001). The percentage of NSE + fibers over lamina propria area was significantly enhanced in patients with SUDD and diverticulosis in comparison with HC (5.1 ± 0.7%, 5.5 ± 0.8% vs 3.4 ± 0.4%, respectively; P < 0.05) in the peridiverticular region. Interestingly, GAP-43 immunoreactivity was significantly increased only in patients with SUDD as compared to HC (5 ± 0.6% vs 2.4 ± 0.7%, respectively; P < 0.05) in the peridiverticular region, while no differences were found in the normal mucosa. Significant correlations were found between GAP43+ fibers and immune cells in the peridiverticular region but not in the normal mucosa.
Conclusion: Patients with SUDD and diverticulosis are characterized by increased macrophage counts, while nerve fiber sprouting is increased only in patients with SUDD and is specific of the peridiverticular region. The significant correlation between immune cell counts and nerve sprouting suggests an interesting cross-talk potentially involved in symptom generation in SUDD.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP204 PROLONGED RECURRENT ABDOMINAL PAIN IS ASSOCIATED WITH ON-GOING UNDERLYING MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION IN PATIENTS WHO HAD AN EPISODE OF ACUTE COMPLICATED DIVERTICULITS
A. Lahat1, D. Necula2, M. Yavzori2, O. Picard2, R. Eliakim2, S. Ben-Horin2

1Gastroenterology, Chaim Sheba Medical Center, Ramat Gan/Israel

2Chaim Sheba Medical Center, Ramat Gan/Israel

Contact E-mail Address:
zokadi@gmail.com

Introduction: Recent data suggest continuous chronic inflammation in patients post complicated acute diverticulitis (AD).
Aims & Methods: We aimed to compare clinical parameters, inflammatory cytokine expression and immune-cell infiltrates between patients post complicated versus uncomplicated AD. Sixteen patients post AD were included, of them 8 had a complicated disease. Demographic data, disease characteristics and inflammatory markers were collected. Tissue samples from diverticular and healthy tissue were obtained during colonoscopy. Mucosal inflammation was assessed histologically and by measuring inflammatory cytokines messenger -RNA expression using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT- PCR).
Results: Clinically, continued non-specific abdominal symptoms were significantly more prevalent among patients post-complicated AD compared to patients after non-complicated AD (p = 0.0002). Patients after complicated AD also had significantly higher CRP levels (9.85 ± 7.5 vs 3 ± 2.1 mg/dl p = 0.027) and tendency for higher calprotectin levels (115.7 ± 85 vs 35 ± 8.7 mg/gr, p = 0.08).  Conclusion: In our current study we showed that following an attack of complicated AD, patients suffer from prolonged inflammatory process, manifesting clinically by recurrent abdominal pain and high inflammatory markers in the blood and stool, and structurally with high expression of inflammatory cytokines and inflammatory infiltrates in the affected tissue. In contrary, patients post uncomplicated AD did not suffer from continued inflammation. If corroborated by further research, our results can contribute to patient's risk stratification and guide therapeutic decisions.

## OP205 INCIDENCE OF COMPLICATED DIVERTICULAR DISEASE (ABSCESS AND PERFORATION): A POPULATION BASED COHORT STUDY FROM ENGLAND
H.E. Otete1, C.J. Crooks2, J. West3, D. J. Humes4

1Division Of Pharmacology, The University Of Nottingham, Nottingham/United Kingdom

2Nottingham City Hospital, University of Nottingham, Nottingham/United Kingdom

3Division Of Epidemiology And Public Health, Univesity of Nottingham, Nottingham/United Kingdom

4NDDC NIHR BRC, University of Nottingham, Nottingham/United Kingdom

Contact E-mail Address:
david.humes@nottingham.ac.uk

Introduction: Diverticular perforation and abscess are the two most significant complications of diverticular disease with a substantial associated morbidity and mortality. Prior population-based studies have suggested the incidence of perforated disease is increasing; however, these studies are no longer contemporary and were unable to describe the change in incidence by age over time [1–3].
Aims & Methods: This study aimed to provide contemporary population-based estimates of the incidence of complicated diverticular disease and assess variation by age, calendar time and sex. We used linked primary and secondary care data from 2000–2014 from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and Hospital Episode Statistics to identify cases of complicated diverticular disease in England who were older than 18 years. Incidence rates were calculated and modelled using Poisson regression.
Results: We identified 3717 cases of complicated diverticular disease with an overall incidence of 9.23 per 100, 000 person years (pyrs) (interquartile range (IQR) 9.94–9.53 per 100, 000 pyrs). The incidence was higher in women 10.81 per 100, 000 pyrs than in men representing a 1.2 fold increase in risk (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) 1.21, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.13–1.29). The incidence increased from 7.51 per 100, 000 pyrs (95% CI 6.38–8.79 per 100, 000 pyrs) in 2000 to 10.88 per 100, 000 pyrs in 2013 (95% CI, 9.65–12.23 per 100, 000 pyrs) representing a 1.4 fold increase (IRR 1.42, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.17–1.72). Incidence increased with increasing age with the highest absolute rate in those over the age of 85 years (45.23 per 100, 000 pyrs) which represented a 5.5 fold increase in incidence compared to those aged 45–54 years (IRR 5.45, 95% CI 4.78–6.22). The increase in incidence of complicated diverticular disease from 2000 to 2013 predominantly occurred in those less than 65 years of age with rates in those over the age of 65 years remaining similar across the time period (Table 1). Table 1. Incidence of complicated diverticular disease by age group and calendar year.

 Conclusion: The incidence of complicated diverticular disease has increased by 1.4 fold from 2000 to 2013 and this increase in incidence appears to be in those under the age of 65 years. This could be due to the increase in known risk factors for complicated diverticular disease such as obesity and physical inactivity or the increased use of prescription medications such as steroids or opiate analgesics which are associated with an increased risk of perforation. It is also possible part of this increase may be due to increased ascertainment of cases due to increased use of diagnostic imaging and endoscopy.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

2. Makela J. Prevalence of perforated sigmoid diverticulitis is increasing. Dis Colon Rectum. 2002;45(7):955–61.
3. Morris C. Incidence of perforated diverticulitis and risk factors for death in a UK population. Br J Surg. 2008;95:876–81.

## OP206 COLONIC DIVERTICULA ARE NOT ASSOCIATED WITH MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION OR CHRONIC GASTROINTESTINAL SYMPTOMS
A. Peery, T. Keku, C. Addamo, A. Mccoy, C. Martin, J. Galanko, R. Sandler

Department Of Medicine, Division Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill/United States of America

Contact E-mail Address:
anne_peery@med.unc.edu

Introduction: Colonic diverticula are prevalent in Western countries.1, 2 While diverticula are classically complicated by acute diverticulitis, there is some thought that diverticula may be associated with low-grade mucosal inflammation.3 This low-grade diverticular inflammation is believed to drive chronic gastrointestinal symptoms.3 Chronic gastrointestinal symptoms from colonic diverticula (in the absence of overt inflammation) has been termed symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease.3 Despite the literature associating colonic diverticulosis with low-grade mucosal inflammation and symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease, there is little evidence for these associations.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to determine whether colonic diverticula are associated with markers of colonic mucosal inflammation in a prospective study of patients undergoing a complete screening colonoscopy. We also assessed whether colonic diverticula are associated with chronic gastrointestinal symptoms and explored whether markers of mucosal inflammation were increased among participants with chronic gastrointestinal symptoms. We analyzed data from a prospective study of 619 patients who had a first-time screening colonoscopy. We included those with a satisfactory preparation for colonoscopy and complete exam to the cecum. We excluded those wtih a prior colonoscopy, colon resection, history of diverticulitis or overt diverticular inflammation. Colonic mucosal biopsies were taken and analyzed for cytokine gene expression of interleukin (IL)-6, IL-10 and tumor necrosis factor-α by quantitative reverse-transcriptase PCR and immune cells (CD4, CD8, CD57 and mast cell tryptase) by immunohistochemistry. Gastrointestinal symptoms were assessed by Rome III criteria. Proportional odds models were used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Results: Our primary analysis included 619 participants; 255 (41%) had one or more colonic diverticula. Participants with diverticula were more likely to be older, male, and overweight or obese than those without diverticula. Compared to those without diverticula, there was no association between participants with diverticulosis and gene expression levels of tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α) (OR 0.85; 95% CI 0.63–1.16) and no association with CD4 (OR 1.18; 95% CI 0.87–1.60), CD8 (OR 0.97; 95% CI 0.71–1.32), or CD57 (OR 0.80; 95% CI 0.59–1.09) after adjusting for age, sex and body mass index. There was no association with mast cell tryptase (OR 1.02; 95% CI 0.75–1.39). There was a reduced likelihood of mucosal concentrations of IL-6 (OR 0.58; 95% CI 0.41–0.83) and IL-10 (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.49–0.91). Our analysis of gastrointestinal symptoms included 448 participants; 12% met diagnostic criteria for Rome III irritable bowel syndrome and 14% reported chronic abdominal pain. Compared to those without diverticula, there was no association between diverticulosis and irritable bowel syndrome (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.26–1.05) or chronic abdominal pain (OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.38–1.23). There was no evidence for chronic mucosal inflammation among symptomatic participants comparing those with and without diverticulosis.
Conclusion: In this large colonoscopy-based study, we found no evidence that colonic diverticulosis is associated with mucosal inflammation, chronic abdominal pain or the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome. Among those with symptoms and diverticula, we found no mucosal inflammation. Our work challenges the theory that colonic diverticula are associated with mucosal inflammation or chronic gastrointestinal symptoms.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP207 UTILITY TO ENDOSCOPIC SUBMUCOSAL DISSECTION IN THE COLORECTAL TUMORS NEAR OR WITHIN DIVERTICULUM: CASE SERIES
V.A. Jimenez-Garcia1, M. Yamada1, H. Ikematsu2, S. Abe1, T. Sakamoto1, T. Nakajima1, T. Matsuda1, Y. Saito1

1Endoscopy Division, National Cancer Center Hospital, Tokyo, Tokyo/Japan

2Endoscopy Division, National Cancer Center Hospital East, Chiba/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
drajimenezg@hotmail.com

Introduction: Surgery is standard treatment for colon tumors coexistence with diverticulum. However, it is currently controversial whether colon tumors near or within diverticulum can be treated by endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD).
Aims & Methods: The aim of this retrospective case series was to clarify feasibility of ESD for superficial colorectal tumors near or within diverticulum. Consecutive patients with colorectal tumors near or within diverticulum removed by ESD in two referral centers were involved. Clinicopathological characteristics and clinical outcomes were analyzed.
Results: There were 11 patients including 6 cases of the near-type and 5 cases of within-type diverticulum. The tumor showed type 2 in NBI International Colorectal Endoscopic (NICE) Classification in 10 cases [1, 2]. Pit pattern diagnosis in Kudo’s classification was type IIIL for one case, type IV with serration features for one case, type IV without serration features in 2 cases and type VI in 7 cases [3]. In 4 of them the diverticulum could not be recognized in the tumor before the ESD. En-bloc R0 resection was achieved in 7 patients (64%). Median tumor size and procedure time were 23 mm (15–80) and 120 min (50–210), respectively. The ESD could not be continued in four cases due to the intra-diverticulum tumor extension and required strip biopsy, band ligation, polypectomy and/or argon plasma coagulation. Traction device using the “clip-and-line method” [4] was used in one case having two diverticulum within the tumor and had kept good traction during ESD. One pin-hole perforation was occurred at the diverticulum and was endoscopically managed by immediate closure by endoclips. Emergency surgery was not required in any cases. During median 12 month follow-up period, only two cases detected residual tumors. One case was successfully ablated and other case required additional surgery.

 Conclusion: The present study demonstrated that ESD was effective and safe for the treatment of colorectal tumors near or within diverticulum. The use of traction device may be helpful to see the cutting site at the diverticulum and to achieve en-bloc R0 resection.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP208 ENHANCED EXPRESSION OF K-RAS PROTEIN IN PANCREAS PROMOTES DEVELOPMENT OF CIGARETTE SMOKE INDUCED CHRONIC PANCREATITIS IN MICE
J. Daniluk1, U. Daniluk2, J. Reszec3, A. Dabrowski1

1Department Of Gastroenterology And Internal Medicine, Medical University of Bialystok, Bialystok/Poland

2Department Of Pediatrics, Gastroenterology And Allergology, Medical University of Bialystok, Bialystok/Poland

3Department Of Medical Pathomorphology, Medical University of Bialystok, Bialystok/Poland

Contact E-mail Address:
danilukj@poczta.onet.pl

Introduction: Epidemiological studies have demonstrated a strong association between smoking and the increased risk for developing chronic pancreatitis (CP) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). The exact mechanism underlying the effects of cigarette smoke (CS) on pancreatic injury remains unknown. We have previously showed that increased Ras activity is a key element in development of pancreatic inflammation and its progression to PDAC. However, it is not clear if similar phenomenon is involved in CS-induced CP.
Aims & Methods: Therefore, the aim of our study was to determine if CS will promote development of CP in mice exposed to repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis (AP). Our secondary aim was to evaluate the involvement of K-Ras protein in this process. Mice were exposed to CS or a sham treatment (no smoke exposure) using a cigarette smoking inhalation system for 12 weeks. After two weeks of experiment, half of the animals from the CS and sham exposure groups were additionally subjected to a repeated caerulein treatment (7-hourly i.p. injections 50μg/kg/dose, once a week, for 10 consecutive weeks) to mimic recurrent episodes of AP. At the end of experiment the extension of pancreatic damage was determined by H&E and Trichrome staining. The expression of K-Ras protein was evaluated by immunohistochemistry (K-Ras-2B Antibody (C-19): sc-521).
Results: C57BL6/cmdb mice exposed to CS or caerulein injections alone did not develop any pancreatic damage determined by histopathology examination. However, concomitant treatment with both of these agents caused focal acinar atrophy, with slight intralobular and perivascular areas of fibrosis, resembling mild CP. Moreover, immunohistochemistry examinations revealed increased pancreatic expression of K-Ras only in mice treated both with CS and caerulein.
Conclusion: CS promotes development of CP in mice exposed to repeated episodes of AP. This process may be, at least partially, related to increased expression of K-Ras protein. Further studies are needed to determine the exact role of K-Ras and downstream signaling pathways in CS-induced CP.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP209 EXPRESSION OF TN ANTIGEN CAUSES CHRONIC PANCREATITIS IN A TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODEL
B. Mercanoglu, K. Karstens, C. Güngör, J.R. Izbicki, M. Bockhorn, G. Wolters-Eisfeld

Department Of General, Visceral And Thoracic Surgery, University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Hamburg/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
b.mercanoglu@uke.de

Introduction: Dysfunctionalities of Cosmc result in the expression of Tn antigen (Tn) and thereby in formation of truncated O-GalNAc glycans with pathophysiological implications.1 Tn expression also arises in up to 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC) and is associated with poor prognosis.2 This is of particular relevance, since PDAC is one of the most aggressive human tumors with a dismal overall prognosis.3 Additionally, ppGalNAcT 2 (GalNT2) overexpression is observed in numerous tumor entities, further supporting the appearance of Tn.4
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to mimicry the circumstances in PDAC and thus to investigate the effect of tumor-associated O-glycosylation on physiological functions of the pancreas in vivo. For this purpose, we generated a transgenic mouse model with a conditional Cosmc knockout and simultaneous GalNT2 overexpression mediated by the pancreas specific transcription factor 1a (Ptf1a)-cre mouse strain. Immunohistochemical, molecular biological, biochemical and immunological investigations of wildtype and transgenic murine pankreata were performed. Furthermore, Tn-modified proteins were identified to explore their pathophysiological implications using the Tn antigen-binding plant lectin Vicia villosa agglutinin (VVA) for purification and subsequent mass spectrometric proteome analysis.
Results: Deletion of Cosmc with simultaneous overexpression of GalNT2 induces Tn expression in murine pancreas. Histopathological staining reveals a chronic pancreatitis phenotype with interlobulär fibrosis and focal necroses already at 4 weeks of age. Furthermore, flow cytometric and immunohistochemical analysis display immune cell infiltration. In the course, loss of parenchyma results in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and malnutrition, compared to wildtype littermates.
Conclusion: Altogether, in our transgenic mouse model presented here, causality between Tn expression and the etiopathogenesis of chronic pancreatitis is shown, which highlights the pathophysiological relevance of truncated O-glycan formation. Moreover, it is conceivable that the inflammatory microenvironment, caused by Tn expression, influences on the tumor progression in PDAC.

## OP210 LIPOXIN A4 INHIBITS PANCREATIC STELLATE CELL DIFFERENTIATION INTO PANCREATIC TUMOR STROMAL MYOFIBROBLASTS AND PANCREATIC TUMOR GROWTH IN VIVO
M. Heinrich, J. Schnittert, J. Prakash

Biomaterials Science And Technology/Targeted Therapeutics, University of Twente, Enschede/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
j.schnittert@utwente.nl

Introduction: The pancreatic tumor stroma has shown to strongly support tumor growth and metastasis. Human pancreatic stellate cells (hPSCs), as precursors of cancer-associated fibroblast like myofibroblasts (CAF), are a main component of the tumor stroma of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Upon activation, human hPSCs differentiate into CAF and promote tumor growth, invasion and metastasis in PDAC [1]. LipoxinA4 (LXA4), a natural bioactive lipid, has shown to inhibit fibroblast activation [2]. This makes LXA4 a potential therapeutic to diminish the pro-tumorigenic effects of the pancreatic tumor stroma, by inhibiting hPSC activation into CAF.
Aims & Methods: The aim of the present study was to investigated whether LXA4 can inhibit the differentiation of human pancreatic stellate cells (hPSCs) into CAF and thereby inhibit hPSC-induced tumor growth in 3D co-culture heterospheroids in vitro and in a co-injection tumor model in vivo. TGF-β was used to activate hPSCs into CAF. The expression of the LXA4-specific surface receptor FRP2/ALX on hPSCs and hPSCs activated with TGF-β was investigated using qPCR. Actin staining, migration assay, QPCR and Western Blot analysis was used to analyze the inhibitory effect of LXA4 on hPSC activation. Western Blot and immunostaining were performed to analyze the ability of LXA4 to control Smad2/3 phosphorylation. LXA4 effect on paracrine signaling between hPSCs and Panc-1 endothelial tumor cell growth were investigated in conditioned medium experiments by monitoring cell growth and migration. 3D heterospheroids composed of hPSCs and Panc-1 as well as stroma rich hPSC/Panc-1 tumors in mice were used to investigate the effect of LXA4 on pancreatic tumor growth.
Results: The LXA4-specific surface receptor FPR2/ALX was found to be upregulated in TGFβ activated hPSCs. LXA4 treatment, significantly inhibited TGF-b induced activation markers (e.g. αSMA, collagen, PDGFRβ), migration and morphological changes in hPSCs. These inhibition of hPSC differentiation were caused by inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation by LXA4. Conditioned medium obtained from TGF-b-activated hPSCs induced the migration and proliferation of Panc-1. These inductions could be inhibited by conditioned medium of LXA4-treated hPSCs. Additionally, LXA4 inhibited the activation of hPSCs with conditioned medium of Panc-1. These results demonstrated that LXA4 could inhibit pro-tumoral paracrine signaling between hPSC and Panc-1 cells. We investigated the effect of LXA4 on hPSC/Panc-1 heterospheroids, which we used as an in vitro tumor model. LXA4 significantly decreased the size & growth rate of the heterospheroids, supported by a decreased expression of ECM proteins and cell number. Furthermore an increased loss of E-Cadherin in control spheroids indicated that LXA4 is able to inhibit the endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition of Panc-1 cells within the spheroid. Finally, injection of LXA4 reduced the growth of subcutaneous tumors in mice.
Conclusion: LXA4 is capable to inhibit the hPSC differentiation into CAF and hPSC induced tumor promoting effects and the growth of stroma containing subcutaneous tumors in mice making it a potential therapeutic agent to modulate the tumor promoting effects of the pancreatic tumor stroma and ultimately treatment of pancreatic cancer.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP211 PROTEIN FACTORS PRESENTED IN SERUM OF PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENTS ENHANCES THE MOTILITY OF CANCER CELLS - A NOVEL VIEW OF PANCREATIC CANCER CELL METASTASIS
A. Poniewierska-Baran1, K. Dąbkowski2, T. Starzynska2, M.Z. Ratajczak3

1Department Of Physiology, Pomeranian Medical University in Szczecin, Szczecin/Poland

2Department Of Gastroenterology, Pomeranian Medical University in Szczecin, Szczecin/Poland

3Regenerative Medicine, Warsaw Medical University, Warsaw/Poland

Contact E-mail Address:
agata.poniewierska@gmail.com

Introduction: Pancreatic cancer remains a serious clinical problem and a challenge for doctors and scientists. Despite the new possibilities in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, 5-year survival rate applies to less than 5% of patients. Although many studies pathogenesis of pancreatic cancer, as well as other cancers remains unknown and needs further investigation. The process of metastasis is a cascade of events involving proteolysis, cell motility and migration, proliferation and neoangiogenesis. Cells released from the primary tumor must penetrate into the lymphatic vessels and/or blood vessels, which occurs by spreading. Circulating cells can then migrate through the walls of blood into surrounding tissues, where they settle, proliferate and form a new outbreak of disease. Understanding cellular processes responsible for the spread of cancer can be useful to improve the diagnosis and prognosis of the disease in patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.
Aims & Methods: The aim of study was to supplement the knowledge about the metastasis process of pancreatic cancer and to understand the role of protein factors presented in serum of pancreatic cancer patients that enhances the motility of cancer cells. The effect of pancreatic cancer patients serum were compared to the serum of control group and were added to pancreatic cancer cell line BxPC-3 (adenocarcinoma, ATCC® cell bank CRL-1687 ™). We evaluated cell migration, proliferation, adhesion response, activation of MAPK44/42 kinase and Akt kinase, and we measured the concentrations of pro-metastatic factors (including HGF, VEGF and SDF-1) in the blood of patients, by ELISA test.
Results: We report that 1) serum from patients group and control group, and factors such as SDF-1, HGF and VEGF can activate migration, adhesion and proliferation of pancreatic cancer cell line CRL1687; 2) we discovered higher metastatic potential of serum from patients with pancreatic cancer compared to control serum; 3) we report higher concentration of SDF-1, HGF/SF, VEGF in the serum of patients with pancreatic cancer. We report for the first time that diluted (1%) serum and plasma induces migration of malignant pancreatic cancer cell line much more strongly than any others knowns potent pro-metastatic factors. We found that this remarkable pro-migratory activity of diluted plasma is associated with a ∼50–100-kD protein that interacts with GαI protein-coupled receptors and activates p42/44 MAPK and AKT signaling in target cells. We report for the firs time that this pro-migratory factor, chaperoned by fibrinogen, is vitronectin and that this effect can be inhibited by fibrinogen.
Conclusion: The results prove a strong metastatic activity of blood serum and a significant role of HGF/SF, VEGF and SDF-1 factors in pancreatic cancer cell metastasis. Our results provide a novel mechanism for the metastasis of pancreatic cancer cells to lymphatics and body cavities, in which the concentration of fibrinogen is low, and thus suggests that free vitronectin stimulates migration of tumor cells.

## OP212 ATM-DEFICIENCY GENERATES GENOMIC INSTABILITY IN PANCREATIC DUCTAL ADENOCARCINOMA AND SENSITIZES TOWARD THERAPEUTIC DNA-DAMAGE
L. Perkhofer1, A. Schmitt2, E. Hessmann3, D. A. Ruess4, M. Lesina4, A. Neese3, B. Sipos5, T. Seufferlein1, H.C. Reinhardt2, P. Frappart1, A. Kleger1

1Internal Medicine 1Universitätsklinik Ulm, Ulm/Germany

2Department of Internal Medicine, Division I, Cologne/Germany

3University Medical Center Göttingen Gastroenterology and Gastrointestinal Oncology, Göttingen/Germany

4II. Med. Klinik, TU Munich, Klinikum rechts der Isar, Munich/Germany

5Department of Pathology and Neuropathology, Tübingen/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
alexander.kleger@uni-ulm.de

Introduction: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC) are characterized by an accumulation of oncogenic mutations. Recent genome sequencing studies identified recurrent protein-damaging ataxia telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) mutations in human PDAC. We previously showed in a mouse model of PDAC, and also in human cancer that loss of Atm accelerates pancreatic cancer formation and epithelial–mesenchymal transition. ATM, a serine/threonine kinase, is a master regulator of the DNA damage response (DDR), impacting on cell cycle checkpoint control and apoptosis. ATM thus has a barrier function to prevent outgrowth of genomically instable incipient tumor cells.
Aims & Methods: Genomic instability, chromosomal aberrations and aneuploidy are characteristic features of most human cancers. To study whether and how Atm-deficiency affects genome integrity, we used a conditional deletion of Atm in a mouse model of PDAC and performed in depth functional and molecular analyses.
Results: First, an independent cohort of resected human PDAC was analyzed via immunostaining with an antibody previously described in a trial setting for tailored therapies in ATM low expressing human metastatic gastric cancer. Interestingly, we frequently observed areas of clonal ATM loss along with a weak staining pattern leading to a correlation between ATM protein expression and survival in a cohort of 49 resected human PDAC. Next, we made use of our previously described ATM-deficient mouse model and subsequently isolated cell lines to characterise the DNA damage response upon ATM deletion. Interestingly, we found increased mitotic defects, recurrent genomic rearrangements and deregulated DNA integrity checkpoints in ATM-deficient murine PDAC reminiscent of human counterparts. Array CGH and SKY analysis show that ATM deficiency leads to chromosomal instability with recurrent and dramatic structural aberrations including chromotripsis. We hypothesized that altered genome integrity might allow synthetic lethality-based options for targeted therapeutic intervention. Indeed, DDR defects sensitize ATM-deficient PDAC toward additional genotoxic stress as shown for gamma-irradiation. In addition and in line with our hypothesis, we found synthetic lethality between Atm deletion and PARP-inhibition in PDAC tumor cells in vitro and in vivo upon orthotopic transplantation by a genotype-selective increase in apoptosis.
Conclusion: Thus, our data establish a novel route for the treatment of ATM-mutant PDAC patients.
