## OP213 COMBINED INHIBITION OF HISTONE DEACETYLASES AND SIRTUIN 1 LEADS TO PARTIAL REDIFFERENTIATION OF DUCTAL NEOPLASIA TOWARDS A MORE ACINAR PHENOTYPE IN MOUSE PANCREATIC TUMOR ORGANOIDS
S. Zhang, X. Zou

Department Of Gastroenterology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Nanjing/China

Contact E-mail Address:
13770771661@163.com

Introduction: Recent studies in genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs) suggest that ductal neoplasia predominantly initiates from acinar cells after transdifferentiation to a ductal phenotype. We hypothesized that it might be possible to redifferentiate pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) to a more acinar phenotype by blocking selected cell signaling pathways.
Aims & Methods: We treated Mist1CreERT2/+;LSL-KrasG12D; R26mTmG(“KCiMist1G”) mouse PanIN 3D organoids and Pdx1-Cre;Kras+/LSL−G12D;Trp53+/LSL−R172H (“KPC”) mouse PDAC 3D organoids with selected compounds in vitro, including histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor SAHA, DNA methyltransferase inhibitor (5-Aza), and sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) inhibitor EX527. We analyzed the differentiation status of the organoids by detecting the expression of typical acinar and ductal markers using immunoblot, reverse transcription PCR, and immunofluorescence (IF) analyses.
Results: Although single use of SAHA, 5-Aza, and EX527 all failed to upregulate the mRNA expression of the acinar markers, combined use of SAHA and EX527 was able to increase the mRNA expression of the acinar markers Amylase, Elastase, and CPA1 in “KCiMist1G” PanIN organoids by a factor of two- to four-fold, associated with a simultaneous decrease in ductal markers, including SOX9, HNF1B, and Muc5ac. We then performed a kinetic analysis in “KPC” PDAC organoids at day 3, day 6, and day 9. We found that combined use of SAHA and EX527 significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of the acinar markers including Amylase and CPA1 by a factor of more than 10-fold, and downregulated the mRNA expression of the ductal markers including SOX9 (p < 0.05), HNF1B (p < 0.05), and Muc5ac (p < 0.01) at day 9, indicating partial conversion to a more acinar phenotype. We then treated the same PDAC organoid with SAHA and EX527 for 9 days, and observed an obvious increase in the protein expression of the acinar marker Mist1. Besides, IF staining showed that combined use of SAHA and EX527 induced remarkable expression of the acinar marker Amylase in the same “KPC” PDAC organoid.
Conclusion: Blocking selected cell signaling pathways could lead to partial redifferentiation of murine Kras-mutant pancreatic ductal neoplasia to a more acinar phenotype, of which combined inhibition of HDACs and SIRT1 had the greatest efficacy. HDACs and SIRT1 might therefore be potential therapeutic targets for PDAC. The underlying mechanisms of the redifferentiating effect need to be further investigated.

## OP214 VERIFICATION OF IMMUNOGLOBULIN A REGULATION OF MICROFLORA AND PROTECTION OF INTESTINAL MUCOSA
N. Tsugawa1, T. Nagaishi1, T. Watabe1, N. Jose1, A. Hosoya1, Y. Kojima1, T. Adachi2, R.S. Blumberg3, M. Watanabe1

1Gastroenterology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Graduate School of Medical Science, Tokyo/Japan

2Immunology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Medical Research Institute, Tokyo/Japan

3Brigham and Womens Hospital, Boston/United States of America

Contact E-mail Address:
ntsgast@tmd.ac.jp

Introduction: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A is believed to be involved in maintaining mucosal homeostasis in the gut. In fact, IgA deficiency has been associated with gastrointestinal diseases such as celiac disease and inflammatory bowel diseases. In addition, it has been reported that the lack of Ig class-switching in B cells due to deficiency of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) in mice results in aberrant microflora composition in the gut. However, it is still unclear whether this is directly caused by the lack of secreted IgA since AID deficiency also results in the suppressed expression of other classes of Ig.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to verify the importance of IgA secretion in the regulation of intestinal microflora. To this end, we have recently generated an animal model of IgA deficiency (IgA−/−) by using the CRISPR/Cas9 system, and then analyzed their intestinal flora as well as histopathological changes of the gastrointestinal tissues.
Results: The guide RNAs specific for IgE and IgA cytoplasmic domains and Cas9 mRNA were injected into C57BL/6 zygotes. Sequencing of the regions between IgE and IgA tails from the offsprings revealed that one of these had a deletion of the entire IgA region and thus identified as IgA−/−. We confirmed that the expressions of other Ig classes except IgA were not altered in these animals. To assess the alterations of microflora in these mice, we first analyzed the intestinal mucosa. Scanning electron microscopy revealed significantly increased segmented filamentous bacteria on the intestinal epithelia in IgA−/− compared to that of littermate control. Next, microbial 16S rRNAs were isolated from the luminal contents of jejunum, ileum or colon, and then applied for metagenomic analysis. We observed significantly altered diversity in microflora especially in the ileum. Given these observation, we sought to assess the effects of altered intestinal flora on mucosal homeostasis in IgA−/−. Histopathologcal analysis revealed inflamed ileal mucosa and no significant changes in other tissues including stomach, duodenum, jejunum and colon. Flow cytometry showed increased CD4+ T cells in the ileal lamina propria associated with increased IFN-g and IL-17 and decreased IL-4 production in the IgA−/−. Given these data, we intercrossed IgA−/− with CD19 Cre and YC3.60 transgenic mice to observe Ca2+ influx specifically in the B cells. We had originally expected suppressed B cell function due to decrease of Th2 cytokine production in the IgA−/− ileum. However, interestingly, intra-vital imaging revealed activated B cells in Peyer’s patches at the IgA−/− ileum.
Conclusion: Our current study is the first to provide evidence to verify that the lack of IgA induce altered microflora as previously observed in AID−/− mice. In addition, our observation also implied that such alteration may result in mucosal inflammation specifically in the ileum caused by disregulated homeostasis in the gut. Additional experiments are currently ongoing.

## OP215 MONOCYTE-DERIVED MACROPHAGES RESTORE GUT MOTILITY IN POSTOPERATIVE ILEUS BY LIMITING ENTERIC NEURONAL DAMAGE
M. Stakenborg1, G. Farro1, G. Goverse1, V. De Simone1, P. J. Gomez-Pinilla1, Z. Lisowski2, D. Laoui3, J. Van Ginderachter3, D. A. Hume2, G. E. Boeckxstaens1, G. Matteoli1

1Translational Research Center For Gastrointestinal Disorders, KU Leuven, Leuven/Belgium

2The Roslin Institute And Royal School Of Veterinary Studies, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh/United Kingdom

3Lab Of Cellular And Molecular Immunology, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Brussel/Belgium

Contact E-mail Address:
gianluca.matteoli@kuleuven.be

Introduction: Patients undergoing open abdominal surgery often suffer from a transient episode of intestinal dysmotility referred to as postoperative ileus (POI). The current view is that ileus depends upon a local inflammatory response in the intestinal muscularis externa (ME) and current therapies mainly focus on reducing influx of leucocytes to the ME. However, recent studies have shown that recruitment of leukocytes, and in particular monocytes, is crucial to the timely resolution of inflammation and to prevent excessive tissue damage.
Aims & Methods: In the current study, we used a murine model of intestinal manipulation (IM)-induced POI to clarify whether monocytes mediate tissue damage and intestinal dysfunction or they are rather involved in the recovery of intestinal motility. IM was performed in mice with defective monocyte migration to tissues (C-C motif chemokine receptor 2, Ccr2−/− mice) and wild-type (WT) mice to study the role of monocytes and monocyte-derived MΦs during the resolution of ME inflammation. The severity of POI was evaluated by assessing GI transit, neuronal damage (IHC) and ME inflammation via flow cytometric analysis of recruited immune cells.
Results: IM in Ccr2−/− mice resulted at day 1 in the same GI transit delay as in WT mice (geometric center WT: 3.72 ± 0.29; Ccr2−/−: 3.55 ± 0.22), proving that monocyte infiltration to the ME is not responsible for the development of intestinal stasis after abdominal surgery, as previously hypothesized. However, GI transit recovery after IM was significantly delayed in Ccr2−/− mice compared to WT mice, associated with increased neutrophil-mediated immunopathology and impaired neuromuscular function (see table). To assess whether the lack of monocytes could induce neuronal alteration at the morphological level, we used confocal microscopy to dissect the sub-cellular localization of HuC/D in enteric neurons in the ME of WT and Ccr2−/− mice 5 days after IM. Although our data showed that HuC/D+ neurons are comparable in volume (WT: 671.1 ± 9.44; K Ccr2−/−: 692.1 ± 9.77 µm3), we detected significantly higher nuclear localization of HuC/D+ in enteric neurons of Ccr2−/− mice (% HuC/D nucleus/cell in WT: 51.32 ± 0.54%; Ccr2−/−: 55.51 ± 0;54%), suggestive of neuronal dysfunction. Given that the MΦ growth factor colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) promotes tissue repair via monocyte recruitment and maturation, we administered CSF1-Fc in WT and Ccr2−/− mice during the recovery phase after IM. CSF1-Fc treatment resulted in reduced neutrophil infiltration and restored circulating monocytes and accumulation of MΦs in the ME of Ccr2−/− mice 3 days after IM. Moreover, with regard to intestinal motility, CSF1-Fc-treated Ccr2−/−mice recovered GI transit 3 days after IM.

 Conclusion: Our study reveals a critical role for monocyte-derived MΦs in supporting neuromuscular function and restoring intestinal homeostasis after surgical trauma. From a therapeutic point of view, our data indicate that inappropriate targeting of monocytes may increase neutrophil-mediated immunopathology and prolong the clinical outcome of POI, while future therapies should be aimed at enhancing MΦ repair functions.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP216 VONOPRAZAN, A NOVEL ACTIVE POTASSIUM-COMPETITIVE ACID BLOCKER, AND RABEPRAZOLE INDUCE SMALL INTESTINAL DYSBIOSIS AND EXACERBATE THE NON-STEROIDAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY DRUG-INDUCED SMALL INTESTINAL ENTEROPATHY
Y. Nadatani1, T. Watanabe1, N. Sugimura1, K. Otani1, K. Taira1, S. Hosomi1, Y. Nagami1, F. Tanaka1, N. Kamata1, H. Yamagami1, T. Tanigawa1, M. Shiba1, Y. Fujiwara2

1Dept. Of Gastroenterology, Osaka City University Graduate School of Medicine Dept. of Gastroenterology, Osaka/Japan

2Dept. Of Gastroenterology, Osaka City University, Osaka/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
dada@med.osaka-cu.ac.jp

Introduction: Vonoprazan fumarate, a novel active potassium-competitive acid blocker, was launched in Japan before it entered the world market. Vonoprazan has a stronger inhibitory effect on gastric acid secretion than proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as rabeprazole and esomeprazole. Recent studies show that PPIs alter the composition of the intestinal microbiome, and the resulting dysbiosis exacerbates the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)-induced small intestinal enteropathy.
Aims & Methods: Aim of this study is to investigate the effect of vonoprazan on the microbiota in the small intestine and NSAID-induced small intestinal enteropathy in mice. C57BL/6J mice received intraperitoneal administration of vonoprazan, rabeprazole, or vehicle for 7 days, and were administered indomethacin by gavage to induce damage to the small intestine. Some mice administered either of the 2 drugs were killed without administration of indomethacin. We analyzed the microbiota in their small intestine by using operational taxonomic units (OTU) sequenced on MiSeq using the V1–V2 region of the 16S rRNA. The mice administered with the antibiotic cocktail in drinking water for 28 days were transplanted with contents from the small intestine of the mice treated with either vonoprazan or rabeprazole; thereafter the donor mice were administered with indomethacin.
Results: Administration of vonoprazan and rabeprazole altered the diversity and composition of the microbiota of the small intestine. Vonoprazan and rabeprazole significantly increased the OTU number by 1.39- and 1.87-fold, respectively. ANOSIM of weighted Unifrac distances showed significant differences between the vehicle- and rabeprazole-treated groups (p < 0.01). Compared to the vehicle-treated group, the vonoprazan- and rabeprazole-treated groups showed 2.8-fold and 1.7-fold increases in indomethacin-induced damage to the small intestine, respectively. This high sensitivity to indomethacin-induced damage was caused by the intestinal microbiota obtained from the mice treated with vonoprazan or rabeprazole.
Conclusion: Vonoprazan and rabeprazole induced small intestinal dysbiosis, which exacerbated the NSAID-induced small intestinal enteropathy.

## OP217 COMPOSITION OF MUCOSA-ASSOCIATED MICROBIOME ALONG THE ENTIRE GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT IN HUMANS
F.E. r. Vuik1, G. M. Fuhler1, S. R. Konstantinov1, J. Dicksved2, L. Engstrand3, A. Van De Winkel1, M.C. w. Spaander1, E.J. Kuipers1, M. P. Peppelenbosch1

1Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam/Netherlands

2Animal Nutrition And Management, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, Uppsala/Sweden

3Dept. Of Of Microbiology, Tumor & Cell Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm/Sweden

Contact E-mail Address:
f.vuik@erasmusmc.nl

Introduction: The importance of the gastrointestinal (GI) microbiome in human health and disease is unambiguous. However, while the colonic microbiome is well studied due to easy accessibility of faecal material, the microbiome composition along the full GI-tract remains underexplored. Furthermore, luminal bacterial content is not a direct reflection of the microbiome at the mucosal interface, the latter being arguably more important due to its closer interaction with host cells.
Aims & Methods: We therefore aimed to analyse the mucosal microbiome along the entire gastrointestinal tract within the same individuals. Patients with unexplained complaints, such as weight loss, abdominal pain, diarrhea and iron deficiency anaemia were scheduled for anterograde and subsequent retrograde double-balloon enteroscopy (DBE). Mucosal samples were taken from 9 different sites: oesophagus, antrum, proximal duodenum, distal jejunum, proximal ileum, distal ileum, colon ascendens, colon descendens and rectum. The microbiome was analysed using Illumina Miseq sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene.
Results: Fourteen patients were included with a median age of 51 (IQR 42–60) years. No significant clinical abnormalities were seen at DBE, except for one patient with a cecum tumour and ulcerative lesions in the distal ileum. Microbiome profiles in this patient were characterised by a high abundance of enterobacteriaceae along the entire digestive tract, and were excluded for further analysis. Diversity of the microbiome at genus level increased from upper gastric locations to the lower intestine. Although differences in community structure were seen between individuals, the major difference was between the upper and lower GI-tract. In the upper digestive tract firmicutes (relative abundance of 37, 5%), proteobacteria (relative abundance of 39, 8%) and actinobacteria (relative abundance of 8, 3%) dominate, whereas bacteroides (relative abundance of 28, 0%) and firmicutes (relative abundance of 62, 2%) are the major phyla in the lower digestive tract.
Conclusion: To the best of our knowledge we are the first to describe the microbiome along the entire GI-tract within in the same individuals. Diversity of the microbiome increases in the lower digestive tract and a clear difference is seen between the upper and lower GI-tract microbiome composition.

## OP218 HYPOXIA DISRUPTS INTESTINAL BARRIER VIA REGULATING NHE8-TIGHT JUNCTION IN SEVERE ACUTE PANCREATITIS RAT MODELS
X. Li1, C. Geng1, X. Lei1, C. Wang1

1Department Of Gastroenterology, West China Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu/China

Contact E-mail Address:
lixiao5166@hotmail.com

Introduction: Intestine barrier dysfunction is attributed to various diseases, including inflammation, hypoxia, ischemia, intoxication, and considered as an important pathogenic factor for many diseases. In severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), it is well established that intestinal barrier dysfunction is a major element to promote SAP development and hypoxia plays a crucial role in infectious complications. Thus, deeply comprehending the mechanisms of intestine barrier dysfunction is indeed required for SAP treatment. Extensive evidences has indicated that intestine hypoxia triggered by SAP disrupting tight junction (TJ) is responsible for barrier dysfunction. Recently, the protective role of sodium/hydrogen exchanger 8 (NHE8) in intestine in various conditions has been well documented. We have previously demonstrated that inflammation reduced intestinal NHE8 expression. However, the role of NHE8 in SAP induced intestine barrier dysfunction has not been reported.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study is to explore the intestinal expression of NHE8 in SAP rat model, and further explore the effects of hypoxia on NHE8 expression and potential mechanisms in Caco-2 cells hypoxia model. To induce SAP, SD rats were retrograde injected with 3% sodium taurocholate into the pancreatic duct, and ileum mucosal tissues were collected 24 hours later. For mechanism study, Caco-2 cells were incubated with 200μM cobalt chloride (Cocl2) for 6 hours to induce acute hypoxia model. Hypoxia-inducible factor-1alpha (HIF-1α) specific inhibitor 2-Methoxyestradiol (2-MeOE2) was incubated with Caco-2 cells for 6 hours under hypoxia. To further investigate the relationship between NHE8 and TJ proteins, NHE8-shRNA plasmid (shNHE8) were constructed.
Results: In SAP group, NHE8 protein expression was significantly decreased compared with the control group (0.5 ± 0.04 vs. 1.2 ± 0.04, n = 12, P < 0.05). For Cocl2 intervened Caco-2 cells, HIF-1α protein expression were significantly stimulated compared with the control (4.53 ± 0.25 vs. 1.21 ± 0.15, n = 3, P < 0.05), whereas NHE8 proteins expression were significantly reduced compared with the control (0.58 ± 0.06 vs. 1.02 ± 0.09, n = 3, P < 0.05). Additionally, Cocl2 treatment significantly reduced Claudin-1 and ZO-1 proteins expression when compared with the control (1.05 ± 0.02 vs. 2.38 ± 0.15; 1.33 ± 0.06 vs. 1.53 ± 0.06, n = 3, P < 0.05). 2-MeOE2 treatment obviously blocked Cocl2 induced HIF-1α protein expression (3.59 ± 0.29 vs. 4.53 ± 0.25, n = 3, P < 0.05). Furthermore, 2-MeOE2 treatment dramatically increased the expression of NHE8 (0.91 ± 0.07 vs. 0.58 ± 0.06, n = 3, P < 0.05), Claudin-1 (1.6 ± 0.16 vs. 1.05 ± 0.02, n = 3, P < 0.05) and ZO-1 (1.56 ± 0.08 vs. 1.33 ± 0.06, n = 3, P < 0.05) compared with Cocl2 pretreated cells (P < 0.05). Interestingly, compared with the mock shRNA transfected cells, the expressions of Claudin-1 and ZO-1 proteins in the cells transferred with shNHE8 were significantly decreased (1.87 ± 0.15 vs. 2.38 ± 0.12; 1.06 ± 0.06 vs. 1.44 ± 0.06, n = 3, P < 0.05).
Conclusion: In SAP, the decrease of intestinal NHE8 expression is responsible for intestine barrier dysfunction. Moreover, intestinal hypoxia caused by SAP might alter intestinal function through HIF-1α-NHE8-TJs signal pathway.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP219 MODULATION OF THE ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM BY FATTY ACID AMIDE HYDROLASE, MONO- AND DIACYLGLYCEROL LIPASE INHIBITORS AS AN ATTRACTIVE TARGET FOR SECRETORY DIARRHEA THERAPY
A. Wasilewski1, A. Misicka2, M. Sacharczuk3, J. Fichna1

1Department Of Biochemistry, Medical University of Lodz, Łódź/Poland

2Department Of Neuropeptides, Mossakowski Medical Research Centre, Polish Academy of Sciences, Warsaw/Poland

3Laboratory Of Neurogenomics, Institute of Genetics and Animal Breeding, Polish Academy of Sciences, Magdalenka/Poland

Contact E-mail Address:
jakub.fichna@umed.lodz.pl

Introduction: Secretory diarrhea remains a major global public health problem and is the second leading cause of death, particularly in children and the elderly. Thus, it is clear that there is an urgent need for developing effective anti-diarrheal strategies. Many disorders can disrupt intestinal fluid and electrolyte absorption, including Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, and diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome. The aim of our study was to characterize the effect of inhibition of selected enzymes involved in the synthesis and degradation of endocannabinoids on electrolyte equilibrium in the mouse colonic tissue.
Aims & Methods: Male Swiss-Webster mice were used in this study. The effects of PF-3845, JZL-184 and RHC-80267 (inhibitors for fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), mono- (MAGL) and diacylglycerol lipase (DAGL), respectively) on epithelial ion transport were characterized in isolated mouse colon stimulated by forskolin (FSK), veratridine (VER) and bethanechol (BET). Next, colonic tissue was co-incubated with selected inhibitors and cannabinoid receptor antagonists: AM 251 and AM 630 (CB1 and CB2 antagonists, respectively). To assess changes in the active ion transport in response to addition of tested drugs, the measurements of short-circuit current (Isc) in mouse colon and ileum in vitro were performed.
Results: We observed that basolateral addition of PF-3845 induced antisecretory effect in FSK-stimulated colonic tissue (p < 0.01), which was significantly reversed by AM 251 (p < 0.001) and AM 630 (p < 0.01). JZL-184 significantly reduced epithelial ion transport (p < 0.05) under FSK-stimulated conditions. Furthermore, co-incubation with AM 630 reversed this effect leading to an increase in ion transport when compared to JZL-184 alone (p < 0.05). After addition of JZL-184 and tissue stimulation by VER, we did not observe any significant effect on colonic Isc. However, application of AM 630 to colonic tissue treated subsequently with JZL-184 led to a pronounced increase in Isc compared with JZL-184 alone (p < 0.01). In turn, basolateral addition of PF-3845, JZL-184 or RHC-80267 was without any statistically significant effect on BET-evoked ion transport when compared to control.
Conclusion: For the first time, we report that the modulation of the endocannabinoid system may play a crucial role in providing a novel effective secretory diarrhea treatment, devoid of side effects on the central nervous system caused by direct administration of cannabinoid receptor agonists.

## OP220 ENRICHMENT OF CIRCULATING DOUBLE POSITIVE INTERLEUKIN-17 PRODUCING FOXP3+ CD4+ T CELL SUBSETS ARE ASSOCIATED WITH A HIGHER RISK OF FURTHER RELAPSE IN CROHN’S DISEASE IN REMISSION: AN OBSERVATIONAL, PROSPECTIVE MULTICENTER STUDY
G. Boschetti1, B. Flourie1, X. Roblin2, S. Paul3, J. Bienvenu4, G. Bommelaer5, A. Buisson6, E. Del Tedesco2, C. Josson7, S. Legastelois7, S. Nancey1

1Gastroenterology, Lyon-Sud University Hospital, Pierre Benite/France

2Gastroenterology, CHU Saint-Etienne, Saint-Etienne/France

3Laboratory Of Immunology And Immunomonitoring, CHU Saint-Etienne, Saint-Etienne/France

4Laboratory Of Immunology, Lyon-Sud University Hospital, Pierre Benite/France

5Chu Estaing, Clermont-Ferrand/France

6Dept. Of Gastroenterology, CHU Estaing Clermont-Ferrand, Clermont-ferrand/France

7Indicia, Lyon/France

Contact E-mail Address:
gilles.boschetti@chu-lyon.fr

Introduction: The balance between Foxp3+ regulatory T-cells (Tregs) and effector T cells, including Th1 and Th17 CD4+ T cell subsets are critical for protecting the host from infection while maintaining gut homeostasis. All these T-cell subsets contribute to the pathogenesis of Crohn’s disease (CD). The dynamics of most of the peripheral effector and regulator T-cell subsets during the course of CD in remission and their relationships with the risk of relapse remain unknown. We aimed to systematically analyse the evolution of frequencies of circulating Th1, Th17 and Tregs with respect to disease remission - relapse in CD.
Aims & Methods: A cohort of 113 CD patients in clinical remission were regularly followed up on a 3-month basis. Blood samples were collected at each visit for routine monitoring inflammatory markers, including ultrasensitive CRP and for measurements of various serum cytokines, including IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-13, IL-17A, IL-23, TNFa, IFNg, TGFb, by an ultrasensitive Erenna method. The frequencies of circulating single positive Th1, Th17 and Tregs CD4+ T cell subsets, as well as double positive CD4+ T cell subsets co-expressing IFNg-IL17, Foxp3-IFNg and Foxp3-IL-17 were analysed by multicolour flow cytometry.
Results: Among the whole cohort, 34 (30%) out of 113 patients relapsed within the follow-up period. The prevalence of circulating IFNg-secreting CD4+ T cells (Th1), IL-17-secreting CD4+ T cells (Th17) and Foxp3-expressing CD4+ T cells (Treg) as well as the concentrations of a wide broad of cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, 17A, TGFb, TNFa, IFNg, IL-13, IL-23) measured in the serum were not significantly different all over the time between patients who relapsed and those who stay in clinical remission. Various circulating double positive CD4+ T-cell subsets co-expressing Foxp3 and IL-17, Foxp3 and IFNg and triple positive Foxp3+ IL-17+ and IFNg+ were detectable in CD patients in remission. The subset of CD4+ T cells co-expressing IL-17 and Foxp3 was found significantly enriched (≈2-fold increase) in the circulating compartment in the cohort of patients in remission who further experienced a clinical relapse 3 months later compared with that of CD patients who stayed in remission all over the follow-up period. In a multivariate analysis, elevated serum usCRP, low serum IL-10 and high number of double positive IL-17 and Foxp3 CD4+ T cells were 3 independent factors significantly associated with the risk of further clinical relapse in CD patients in remission.
Conclusion: Detectable circulating crossover immune CD4+ T-cell subsets co-expressing Foxp3, IL-17 and IFNg in CD patients in remission argues in favour of the recent concept of T cell plasticity. A significant enrichment of a unique CD4+ T-cell subset co-expressing Foxp3 and IL-17 that preceding the occurrence of a flare suggests the potential contribution of this double positive T-cell subset in the pathogenesis of CD.

## OP221 INFLIXIMAB TROUGH LEVELS ABOVE 7 MG/ML IN INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE TREATED WITH INFLIXIMAB: BETTER CONTROL OF INFLAMMATION WITHOUT INCREASED RISK OF INFECTION
D. Drobne1, T. Kurent1, S. Golob1, P. Svegl1, P. Rajar1, S. Terzic2, M. Kozelj1, G. Novak1, N. Smrekar1, S. Plut1, A. Smid1, N. Sever1, L. Strnisa1, J. Brecelj1, D. Urlep1, J. Osredkar3, M. Homan1, R. Orel1, B. Stabuc1, I. Ferkolj1

1Department Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, University Medical Centre Ljubljana Slovenia, Ljubljana/Slovenia

2Department Of Infectious Diseases, University Medical Centre Ljubljana Slovenia, Ljubljana/Slovenia

3Clinical Institute Of Clinical Chemistry And Biochemistry, University Medical Centre Ljubljana Slovenia, Ljubljana/Slovenia

Contact E-mail Address:
david.drobne@gmail.com

Introduction: Target infliximab trough level for optimal control of inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is not clear. A prospective trial suggested target infliximab trough level of 3 – 7 µg/ml [1], but data on additional therapeutic benefit of higher trough levels are conflicting. It is also not clear if higher infliximab trough levels increase the risk of infection.
Aims & Methods: Our aim was to explore whether infliximab trough levels above 7 µg/ml are more effective and still safe regarding the risk of infection compared to levels below this threshold. In this single-centre cohort study we included 183 IBD patients (109 Crohn's disease, 74 ulcerative colitis including IBD - unclassified) who received infliximab maintenance treatment between 2010 and 2015 at tertiary referral university IBD Centre (162 adults, 21 children) with available infliximab trough level data. Effectiveness and safety of high trough levels (≥7 µg/ml) was compared to trough levels below 7 µg/ml. Effectiveness was assessed by correlating fecal calprotectin (114 matched samples), CRP (379 matched samples) and endoscopy (69 colonoscopies) data to infliximab trough levels (426 samples, ELISA assay). Safety was assessed by comparing rates of infections in semesters (defined by 3-month periods) with high trough levels (≥7 µg/ml) compared to semesters with infliximab trough levels below this threshold. Data on trough levels were available in 473/1681 (28%) semesters. Continuous variables were described using the median and interquartile range (IQR) and analyzed with the Mann–Whitney U test. Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical variables.
Results: Median fecal calprotectin and median C-reactive protein (CRP) were lower in patients with high infliximab trough levels (fecal calprotectin median 66 mg/kg [IQR: 30–257]; CRP median 3 mg/L [IQR: 3–3]) compared to infliximab trough levels below 7 µg/ml (fecal calprotectin median 155 mg/kg [IQR: 72–474]; CRP median 3 mg/L [IQR: 3–14.5]) (fecal calprotectin p < 0.001; CRP p < 0.001). Similarly, the proportion of patients with fecal calprotectin below 100 mg/kg and with normal CRP was higher in patients with high trough levels (Table 1). Superior effectiveness of high trough levels compared to trough levels below 7 µg/ml was maintained also after excluding samples with low trough levels (<3 µg/ml) from the analysis. Furthermore, in 14/17 (82%) patients who had available paired trough level samples and had increased fecal calprotectin/CRP at trough level between 3–7 µg/ml, fecal calprotectin/CRP decreased (to normal in 62%) when trough levels increased to >7 µg/ml after infliximab dose optimization. In Crohn’s disease, patients with mucosal healing had higher trough levels (4.62 [IQR: 2.21–7.31]) compared to patients with ulcers (2.29 [IQR: 0.3–4.45]) (p = 0.034). Eleven out of 14 (79%) patients with TL ≥ 7 µg/ml and available endoscopy data had mucosal healing. During the total follow-up time of 420 patient-years 160 infections which necessitated postponing infusion of infliximab (101 viral, 59 bacterial) occurred. None of the infections were fatal. No differences in rates of infections were observed in semesters with high trough levels (16 semesters out of 129 (12.4%)) compared to semesters with trough level <7 µg/ml (32 semesters out of 344 (9.3%)) (p = 0.32). In addition, there was no difference in median infliximab trough levels in semesters with infections (4.25 [1.04 to 8.34] µg/ml) compared to semesters without infections (4.09 [1.58 to 7.2]) (p = 0.867). Eighteen out of 48 (37.5%) of infections occurred in semesters on combination therapy (systemic steroids in 5 patients; systemic steroids and thipurines in 13 patients).

 Conclusion: Infliximab trough levels above 7 µg/ml provide better control of inflammation in IBD without increasing the risk of infection compared to infliximab trough levels below 7 µg/ml. Our data suggest that patients who have active disease despite infliximab trough levels between 3–7 µg/ml should have their dose of infliximab optimized to achieve higher trough levels as this is clinically effective and safe.

1. Vande Casteele et al. Gastroenterology 2015

## OP222 AN UPDATED ANALYSIS OF IN VITRO CYTOKINE INHIBITION PROFILES OF A NUMBER OF JANUS KINASE INHIBITORS AT CLINICALLY MEANINGFUL CONCENTRATIONS
M. E. Dowty1, T. H. Lin2, L. Wang1, J. M. Jussif1, L. Li1, E. Moy1, J. Telliez1

1Pfizer Worldwide R&D, Cambridge/United States of America/MA

2Pfizer Inflammation & Immunology Research Unit, Cambridge/United States of America/MA

Contact E-mail Address:
Martin.Dowty@pfizer.com

Introduction: Tofacitinib is an oral, small molecule Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor that is being investigated for ulcerative colitis (UC). A number of JAK inhibitors are being investigated for the treatment of inflammatory diseases such as UC and rheumatoid arthritis, including tofacitinib, baricitinib and filgotinib (GLPG0634). However, it is unclear how these drugs may differentiate from each other in clinic, based on their profiles of JAK-dependent cytokine inhibition.
Aims & Methods: We aimed to provide an integrated modelling approach – using knowledge of both in vitro whole cell JAK inhibition potencies and plasma pharmacokinetics – to better understand profiles of cytokine inhibition for clinical JAK inhibitors in the context of clinically meaningful doses. IC50 values for interferon (IFN)α, IFNγ, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-15, IL-21, IL-10, IL-27, IL-12, IL-23 and erythropoietin (EPO) signalling of tofacitinib, baricitinib and filgotinib and its metabolite were measured in total lymphocytes, CD34+ cells (EPO) and CD3+ cells (IL-6) in human whole blood by a flow cytometry-based assay, quantifying the phosphorylation state of various signal transducer and activator of transcription proteins. Human daily average plasma concentrations (Cav) were used as reported for tofacitinib (5 mg BID; 68 nM), baricitinib (4 mg QD; 27 nM) and filgotinib (200 mg QD; 474 nM) and its metabolite (7438 nM) and converted to unbound values with measured plasma fraction unbound (fu) values of 0.61, 0.59, 0.49 and 0.42, respectively. Whole blood IC50 values were converted to unbound values with measured blood/plasma ratios of 1.2, 1.3, 1.2 and 1.1, respectively, and fu values. Percentage levels of cytokine inhibition (ICxx = 100*Cav/(IC50 + Cav)) were then determined at clinically meaningful doses.
Results: Compared between JAK inhibitors, tofacitinib and baricitinib were overall more potent inhibitors than filgotinib and its metabolite (data not shown). Combining potency with clinical pharmacokinetics showed a similar profile of cytokine inhibition (Table), with some exceptions. A greater level of IL-6 inhibition was noted with filgotinib and its metabolite. However, this did not translate into greater levels of published C-reactive protein reductions compared with tofacitinib1 and baricitinib.2 Likewise, the minor difference noted in IL-15 inhibition between tofacitinib1 and baricitinib3 did not translate into a clinically meaningful difference in natural killer cell populations.

 Conclusion: These analyses illustrate the importance of studying a broad range of JAK pairing potencies and clinical concentrations when comparing JAK inhibitor compounds. Calculated profiles of cytokine inhibition for a number of JAK inhibitors were generally similar when efficacious doses are considered, with only minor differences in percentage cytokine inhibition, suggesting limited differentiation of these JAK inhibitors based on JAK pharmacology. Ultimately, only robust clinical testing will determine whether there are clinical differences between JAK inhibitors.

## OP223 IDENTIFICATION OF GENETIC SIGNATURES AND IMMUNE MECHANISMS THAT DEFINE THERAPEUTIC RESPONSE AND FAILURE TO ANTI-INTEGRIN THERAPY WITH VEDOLIZUMAB IN IBD PATIENTS
T. Rath1, U. Billmeier1, F. Ferrazzii2, M. Vieth3, A. Ekici2, M.F. Neurath1, R. Atreya1

1Department Of Medicine I, Division Of Gastroenterology, Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Erlangen/Germany

2Department Of Human Genetics, Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Erlangen/Germany

3Abt. Pathologie, Klinikum Bayreuth, Bayreuth/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
Timo.Rath@uk-erlangen.de

Introduction: In 2014 Vedolizumab (VDZ), a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting the α4β7 integrin, was approved for the treatment of Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Despite proven clinical efficacy for inducing and maintaining remission, subgroups of patients have no clinical benefit from anti-adhesion therapy with VDZ.
Aims & Methods: Within this study, we aimed to identify genetic, cellular and immunological mechanisms that define and predict response and failure of VDZ therapy. For this purpose, intestinal RNA Sequencing was performed in UC and CD patients (remitters and non-remitters) before and at week 14 of VDZ therapy. α4β7 expression on peripheral and mucosal immune cells was assessed by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry. Cellular modes of VDZ mediated action were analysed ex vivo and in VDZ treated IBD patients.
Results: Transcriptome analysis showed an impairment of signaling cascades associated with adhesion, diapedesis and migration of granulocytes and agranulocytes upon VDZ therapy. In non-remitters to VDZ therapy, a tissue-destructive and leucocyte-mediated inflammatory activity with activation of TNF dependent pathways was present, all of which were inhibited in remitters to VDZ. Clinical remission was associated with a significant reduction of α4β7 expression on Th2 and Th17 polarized mucosal CD4+ T cells at week 14 of VDZ therapy and with significantly higher numbers of α4β7 expressing mucosal cells prior to the initiation of VDZ therapy compared to non-remitters.
Conclusion: Intestinal α4β7 expression prior to VDZ therapy might represent a biomarker that predicts therapeutic response to subsequent VDZ treatment. Due to high activation of TNF signaling in VDZ non-remitters, anti-TNF treatment might represent a promising therapeutic strategy in VDZ refractory patients.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP224 EXPANSION OF IL-23 RECEPTOR BEARING TNFR2+ T CELLS DRIVES RESISTANCE TO ANTI-TNF THERAPY IN CROHN'S DISEASE
H. Schmitt1, U. Billmeier1, W. Dieterich1, T. Rath1, S. Hirschmann1, C. Neufert1, K. Hildner1, M. J. Waldner1, J. Mudter2, T. Münster3, M.F. Neurath1, R. Atreya1

1Medicine 1University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Erlangen/Germany

2Sana Kliniken Ostholstein, Eutin/Germany

3Anesthesiology, University Erlangen-Nuremberg, Erlangen/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
Heike.Schmitt@uk-erlangen.de

Introduction: Anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) antibodies are successfully used for the treatment of Crohn’s disease. Nevertheless, approximately 40% of patients display failure to anti-TNF therapy. Here, we characterized molecular mechanisms that drive resistance to anti-TNF therapy. Although various studies have addressed potential mechanisms of action of anti-TNF antibodies in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the molecular pathways that drive anti-TNF resistance are still poorly understood. The mechanistic reasons responsible for anti-TNF refractory disease in Crohn’s disease are still unknown, but it has been shown that inhibition of IL-23 was particularly effective in patients with non-response to previous anti-TNF therapy.
Aims & Methods: Although the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-23 has been linked to IBD pathogenesis, the context-dependent functions of IL-23 mediated signaling in anti-TNF refractory mucosal inflammation have not been resolved yet. The aim of the current study was therefore to characterize the functional role of IL-23 in this context. Lamina propria mononuclear cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were isolated from Crohn’s disease patients before and after anti-TNF therapy. Cytokine profiles and expression of cell surface markers and signaling proteins were assessed by immunohistology, qPCR, ELISA and FACS, respectively. Cell apoptosis was determined in cultured mononuclear cells and gut sections.
Results: Crohn’s disease patients responding to anti-TNF therapy displayed a significantly higher expression of TNF receptor 2 (TNFR2) but not IL23R on mucosal T cells than non-responders prior to the initiation of therapy. During anti-TNF therapy, there was a significant up-regulation of mucosal IL-23 p19, IL23R and IL-17A levels in anti-TNF non-responders as compared to responders. Apoptosis-resistant TNFR2+IL23R+ T cells were significantly expanded in anti-TNF non-responders compared to responders and exhibited increased expression of IFN-γ, T-bet, IL-17A and RORγt compared to TNFR2+IL23R− cells, indicating a mixed Th1/Th17-like phenotype. Intestinal TNFR2+IL23R+ T cells were activated by IL-23 derived from CD14+ macrophages, whose presence was significantly elevated in non-responders prior to the start of anti-TNF therapy. Functional studies demonstrated that anti-TNF induced apoptosis in lamina propria T cells from Crohn’s disease patients is abrogated by IL-23. TNFR2+IL23R+ mucosal T cells express the activated anti-apoptotic protein pSTAT3 and produce marked amounts of both Th1 and Th17 cytokines. They accumulate in the mucosa of anti-TNF refractory Crohn's disease patients where they may perpetuate chronic intestinal inflammation through IL-23 stimulation.
Conclusion: Expansion of apoptosis-resistant TNFR2+IL23R+ T cells in the mucosa drives resistance to anti-TNF therapy in Crohn’s disease patients. These findings identify IL-23 as suitable molecular target in IBD patients refractory to anti-TNF therapy.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

Aims & Methods: Adult pts naïve to immunosuppressive and biologic therapy included in CALM had: 1) baseline (BL) CDAI > 150 and ≤450 (for receiving prednisone >20 mg or equivalent) or ≥220 and ≤450 (for receiving no or ≤20 mg prednisone or equivalent); 2) active endoscopic CD, defined as total CD endoscopic index of severity (CDEIS) > 6 and sum of CDEIS subscores > 6 in ≥1 segment with ulcers; 3) CRP ≥ 5 mg/L and/or FC ≥ 250 μg/g. Pts were randomized 1:1 to T2T or CM groups, following up to an 8 week (wk) of 40 mg/day prednisone burst and taper. Pts were eligible for early randomization between BL (wk 0) and wk 8 if CDAI > 220 and were either on corticosteroids for 4 wks, or had intolerance/contraindication for prednisone therapy or per investigator assessment. Pts received the following treatment options (TO) 1–4 administered in a stepwise manner: TO1 = no treatment; TO2 = 160/80 mg adalimumab (ADA) wks 0/2, 40 mg every other wk; TO3 = ADA 40 mg wkly; TO4 = ADA 40 mg wkly + azathioprine [AZA] 2.5 mg/kg/day. Early randomized pts were assigned to TO2. Treatment at randomization and 3 following visits was based on failure to fulfil success criteria: CDAI < 150, CRP < 5 mg/L, FC < 250μg/g, and no prednisone for the T2T group and CDAI decrease ≥70 or 100 (at randomization or post-randomization, respectively) or CDAI < 200 and no prednisone for the CM group. The primary endpoint was CDEIS < 4 and absence of deep ulcers at wk 48. Secondary endpoints at wk 48 included deep remission (CDAI < 150, discontinuation of steroids ≥8 wks, absence of draining fistula, CDEIS < 4, and no deep ulcers), biologic remission (FC < 250μg/g, CRP < 5 mg/L, and CDEIS < 4), CDEIS < 4, and CDEIS < 4 in each segment, and CDEIS = 0. Missing data were imputed using non-responder imputation.
Introduction: The concept of “treat to target” (T2T) implies that close serial monitoring of patients (pts) with Crohn’s disease (CD) using biomarkers of inflammation, serum C-reactive protein (CRP) and fecal calprotectin (FC), assists in timely treatment escalation in order to improve outcome. CALM, a prospective, open-label, multicenter, active-controlled, Phase 3 study, assessed the benefit of T2T versus standard clinical management (CM) of CD.
Results: A total of 244 pts were randomized. At BL, the mean ± SD age was 31.6 ± 11.7 years, mean ± SD CD duration was 0.95 ± 1.98 years and 57.8% were female. BL characteristics between T2T and CM groups were similar. Results are shown in the Table. No new safety signals with ADA were observed. The overall rate of adverse events was similar between T2T and CM groups.
Table. Summary of primary and select secondary endpoints of CALM study

 Conclusion: This is the first study showing that the treat-to-target approach leads to superior endoscopic and deep remission outcomes in CD compared with symptom-driven care.

## OP226 EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF A BRIDGING STRATEGY WITH CALCINEURIN INHIBITORS TO VEDOLIZUMAB IN PATIENTS WITH SEVERE ULCERATIVE COLITIS
G. Pellet1, C. Stefanescu2, F. Carbonnel3, L. Peyrin-Biroulet4, X. Roblin5, C. Allimant6, M. Nachury7, S. Nancey8, J. Filippi9, R. Altwegg10, H. Brixi11, G. Fotsing Makougang12, S. Shili1, D. Laharie1

1CHU de Bordeaux Hopital Haut-Leveque Dept. de Gastroenterologie, Pessac cedex/France

2Service De Gastroenterologie Et Assistance Nutritive, Beaujon Hospital, Clichy, Clichy/France

3Dept. De Hepato-gastroenterologie, CHU Bicetre - Dept. de Hepato-Gastroenterologie, CHU Bicetre; Le Kremlin Bicetre/FR, Le Kremlin Bicetre/France

4Department Of Gastroenterology, Nancy University Hospital Inserm U954 Dept. of Hepato-Gastroenterology, Vandoeuvre les Nancy/France

5University of St. Etienne Dept. de Gastroenterologie, Saint Etienne/France

6Dept. Of Gastroenterology, CHU Estaing Clermont-Ferrand, Clermont-ferrand/France

7Gastroenterology department, CHRU Lille, Université Lille 2Lille/France

8Gastroenterologie, CH Lyon Sud Gastro secteur Jules Courmont, Pierre Benite Cedex/France

9Dept. De Gastroenterologie, Hopital de lAchet Dept. de Gastroenterlogie Dept. de Nutrition Oncologie, Nice Cedex/France

10Hopital Saint Eloi Hepatologie Gastro enterologie, Montpellier cedex/France

11Hépato-gastroenterologiee, Hôpital Robert Debré, Reims Cedex/France

12Service D'hépato-gastro-entérologie, CHU de Poitiers, Poitiers/France

Contact E-mail Address:
david.laharie@chu-bordeaux.fr

Introduction: Vedolizumab showed efficacy as induction and maintenance therapy in patients with ulcerative colitis (UC). Patients with an acute severe UC (ASUC) were excluded from pivotal trials. The aim of this study was to assess efficacy and safety of the bridging strategy with a calcineurin inhibitor to vedolizumab in patients with steroid-refractory ASUC or non-severe UC.
Aims & Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted in 12 referential centers, including all consecutive patients who have been treated for an active steroid-refractory UC (ASUC or non-severe UC) by a calcineurin inhibitor (ciclosporin or tacrolimus) as induction therapy and vedolizumab as maintenance therapy. Inclusion was defined by the day of the first vedolizumab infusion. Outcomes were survival without colectomy and safety.
Results: Thirty-eight patients (22W, mean age 34 years) were recruited and received a calcineurin inhibitor - ciclosporin in 36 and tacrolimus in 2 - and vedolizumab with a median interval of 9.5 days, for treating a steroid-refractory ASUC in 31 or for a steroid-refractory non-severe UC in 4 cases. Regarding previous medications, 34 (89%) patients had failed to respond to conventional immunosuppressants (thiopurines and/or methotrexate) and they were contra-indicated in 4 (11%); 35 (92%) patients had failed to at least one anti-TNF agent, while these drugs were contra-indicated in 3 (8%). At inclusion, 29 (76%) patients had pancolitis, 23 (61%) had already presented an ASUC; median CRP was 12.9 mg/L; median Lichtiger score and Total Mayo Score were 9 and 10, respectively. The median duration of calcineurin inhibitor treatment was 2.7 months. After a median follow-up duration of 6.9 months, 12 (31.6%) patients underwent colectomy (5 ASUC, 7 refractory UC) after a median interval of 4.2 months. Rates of survival without colectomy at 1, 3 and 6 months were 89.5% [IC95%: 80.2–99.8], 86.8% [IC95%: 76.7–98.3], and 70.7% [IC95%: 56.7–88], respectively. During follow-up, 22 (58%) patients were optimized for vedolizumab and 5 (13%) stopped the drug due to lack of efficacy; among the 22 patients receiving steroids at inclusion, 13 (59%) were weaned. Concerning safety, 3 patients developed mild and transient renal failure, leading to ciclosporin withdrawal in one case, and one had Campylobacter jejuni colitis. No death was observed.
Conclusion: In steroid-refractory UC, a bridging strategy combining a calcineurin inhibitor with vedolizumab seems effective for avoiding emergent colectomy with an acceptable safety profile. About one-third of patients underwent colectomy. This therapeutic strategy might be considered in patients with ASUC and non-severe UC refractory to conventional therapies, including anti-TNF. The safety profile of this approach will require further investigation.

## OP227 A TREAT-TO-TARGET APPROACH DECREASES THE RATE OF CD-RELATED ADVERSE OUTCOMES VERSUS A CLINICAL APPROACH IN PATIENTS WITH MODERATE TO SEVERELY ACTIVE CROHN'S DISEASE: DATA FROM CALM
J. Colombel1, R. Panaccione2, P. Bossuyt3, F. Baert4, T. Vanásek5, A. Danalıoğlu6, G. Novacek7, A. Armuzzi8, X. Hebuterne9, S. Travis10, S. Danese11, W. Reinisch7, W. J. Sandborn12, P. Introduction: The primary results of the Phase 3 CALM study demonstrated that a treat-to-target (T2T) approach using tight control of inflammation by the biomarkers (i.e., C-reactive protein [CRP] and fecal calprotectin [FC]), led to superior endoscopic and deep remission (combined clinical plus endoscopic remission) outcomes in moderate to severely active Crohn’s disease (CD) compared to standard clinical management (CM). This analysis assessed major adverse outcomes, such as hospitalizations, surgical procedures, including major surgeries, and serious disease-related complications in patients enrolled in CALM.
Aims & Methods: Immunosuppressive and biologic-naïve adult patients with CD treated with or without corticosteroids (CS), and with baseline (BL; week 0) CDAI>150–450 (for high-dose CS) or 200–450 (low-dose CS) or 220–450 (for no CS), active endoscopic CD (overall CD Endoscopic Index of Severity [CDEIS]>6 and sum of CDEIS subscores >6 in ≥1 segment with ulcers), and CRP ≥ 5 mg/L and/or FC ≥ 250 μg/g were treated with prednisone burst and taper for up to 8 weeks and then randomized to the T2Tor CM arms at week 9. Some patients with CDAI > 220 and CS for >4 weeks or intolerance/contraindication for CS or per investigator assessment were able to be randomized early. Patients received up to four treatment options (TO) administered in a stepwise manner based on pre-defined success criteria: TO1 = no treatment; TO2 = 160/80 mg adalimumab (HumiraÒ; ADA) weeks 0/2, 40 mg every other week; TO3 = ADA 40 mg weekly; TO4 = ADA 40 mg weekly + azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day. CD-related hospitalizations, CD-related surgical procedures (major CD-related surgeries [bowel resection, ostomy, by-pass, strictureplasty, and surgical drainage of abdominal/pelvic abscess] and non-major CD-related surgeries [debridment, abscess drainage, seton placement, fistulotomy, placement of a TPN access line]) after randomization and a composite endpoint of CD-related hospitalization or serious complication (presence of abscess, fistula or stricture, skin and ocular extra-intestinal manifestation, and serious adverse drug reaction) from randomization to up to week 48 or last dose date, whichever was later, were summarized as incidences or rates (events [E]/100 Patient Years [PY]). Differences between treatment groups in rates of CD-related hospitalizations and surgical procedures or in incidences of the composite endpoint were analyzed using a Chi-square test. Hazard ratio (95% CI) of the composite endpoint was determined using Cox proportional hazard model. Any hospitalization on or after randomization and up to 70 days after last dosing were summarized in all randomized patients.
Results: A total of 244 patients were randomized 1:1 to the T2T and CM arms. Mean age ± SD at BL was 31.6 ± 11.7 and 57.8% were female. The rate of CD-related hospitalizations after randomization was significantly lower in the T2T compared to CM arm: 14 events (13.2 E/100 PY) vs 29 events (28.0 E/100 PY), P = 0.021. The rates of CD-related surgical procedures between treatment arms were not significantly different: 7 events (6.6 E/100 PY) in T2T and 9 events (8.7 E/100 PY) in CM, P = 0.582. The proportion of patients with CD-related hospitalization or serious complication was numerically lower in T2T compared with CM: 18 patients (14.8%) vs 25 patients (20.5%), P = 0.240. T2T was associated with numerically lower risk of CD-related hospitalization or serious complication than CM: hazard ratio = 0.7, 95% CI 0.4–1.3, P = 0.249.
Conclusion: The T2T approach using tight control of inflammation by biomarkers lead to a reduction of major adverse outcomes indicative for a detrimental course of disease, including CD-related hospitalizations. A longer study would be needed to confirm these findings.

## OP228 PROFILE TRIAL: PREDICTING OUTCOMES FOR CROHN’S DISEASE USING A MOLECULAR BIOMARKER
J. C. Lee1, D. Biasci1, N. M. Noor1, E. F. Mckinney1, T. Ahmad2, N. R. Lewis3, A. Hart4, P. A. Lyons1, M. Parkes1, K. G. Smith1

1Department Of Medicine, University of Cambridge School of Clinical Medicine, CBQQ/United Kingdom

2Exeter IBD And Pharmacogenetics Research Group, University of Exeter, EXDW/United Kingdom

3Department Of Gastroenterology, Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, NGHA/United Kingdom

4Gastroenterology, St Mark’s Hospital and Academic Institue, London/United Kingdom

Contact E-mail Address:
nn281@cam.ac.uk

Introduction: The course of Crohn’s disease (CD) varies substantially between affected individuals, but reliable prognostic markers are not available in clinical practice. This hinders disease management because patients with aggressive disease will be undertreated by conventional “step-up” therapy, while those with indolent disease would be exposed to the risks of unnecessary immunosuppression of a “top-down” approach. Previously, we have described a transcriptional signature that is detectable within peripheral blood CD8 T cells at diagnosis and which correlates with subsequent disease course. To translate this work to the bedside and overcome the technical challenges of separating cell populations, we sought to develop a whole blood qPCR-based biomarker that can re-capitulate the CD8 subgroups without the need for cell separation. Here we describe the development and validation of this biomarker and the upcoming biomarker-stratified trial that will test whether it can deliver personalised medicine in CD.
Aims & Methods: From a training cohort of 69 newly diagnosed IBD patients, we simultaneously obtained a whole blood PAXgene RNA tube and peripheral blood CD8 T-cell sample. Gene expression in both samples was measured by microarray. After confirming that the CD8 transcriptional signature was detectable and correlated with prognosis, we used machine learning to identify a transcriptional classifier in whole blood gene expression data that would re-capitulate the CD8 transcriptional subgroups. Model selection was performed using Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and the genes identified were subsequently tested by qPCR and optimised to produce an 18 gene qPCR assay.
Results: Independent validation of this biomarker was established using a second, independent cohort of 85 newly diagnosed patients with CD from 4 sites around the United Kingdom. This validated the biomarker and confirmed that the subgroups it identified had significantly different disease courses (analogous to those observed with the CD8 T-cell subgroups). The hazard ratio for time to treatment escalation in this validation cohort was 3.52 (1.84–6.76, 95% confidence intervals, P = 0.0002). We now propose to conduct the first ever biomarker-stratified trial in any inflammatory disease to determine whether this biomarker can deliver personalised medicine in CD.
Conclusion: We have developed, optimised and validated a whole blood qPCR classifier that is able to predict disease course from diagnosis in IBD patients. This represents a major step towards personalised therapy in IBD, and we will soon investigate whether this could make personalised medicine a reality in CD.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP229 LYMPHATIC INVASION MAY BE MOST RELEVANT TO NODAL METASTASES IN EARLY-STAGE GASTRIC CANCERS: A RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS IN 65 CASES
T. Akimoto1, O. Goto1, N. Ueki2, H. Kawakubo3, H. Noda2, G. Ikeda2, K. Higuchi2, Y. Mitsunaga1, H. Yamawaki2, Y. Kodaka2, A. Nakayama1, M. Kato1, A. Fujimoto1, Y. Ochiai1, T. Maehata1, K. Suda3, T. Uraoka1, T. Kawagoe2, S. Futagami2, I. Fujita4, M. Kaise2, Y. Kitagawa3, K. Iwakiri2, N. Yahagi1

1Division Of Research And Development For Minimally Invasive Treatment, Cancer Center, Keio University, School of Medicine, Tokyo/Japan

2Department Of Gastroenterology, Nippon Medical School, Tokyo/Japan

3Department Of Surgery, Keio University School of Medicine, Tokyo/Japan

4Department Of Surgery, Nippon Medical School, Tokyo/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
t-akimoto@nms.ac.jp

Introduction: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) for early-stage gastric cancer (EGC)s is gaining an acceptance as one of curative treatment options. With regard to the possibility of lymph node metastasis (LNM) or residual cancer in the stomach after ESD, ESD specimens having non-curative pathological factors (positive lymphovascular invasion, undifferentiated cancer invading submucosal layer, undifferentiated mucosal cancer sized more than 2 cm, differentiated cancer sized more than 3 cm invading submucosal layer or having ulceration, and R1 resection), which were based on the Japanese gastric cancer treatment guidelines from Japanese Gastric Cancer Association (JGCA), are thought to require additional treatments after endoscopic resection. However, additional gastrectomy and lymph node dissection frequently reveal neither LNM nor residual cancer in the extracted stomach. Regarding the guidelines from JGCA, non-curative pathological factors of endoscopic resection were defined according to the LNM rates of past surgical cases for EGCs. On the other hands, the LNM rate detected according to endoscopically resected specimens, which is more detailedly assessed pathologically than operatively extracted specimens, has not been fully investigated.
Aims & Methods: To compare the potential risk of LNM and residual cancer between these pathological characteristics of specimen resected endoscopically, we retrospectively assessed the surgical cases following non-curative endoscopic resection. We identified 1137 patients who underwent ESD from August 2006 to December 2016. Of these, pathological diagnosis was non-curative resection in 142 lesions in 142 patients excluding the cases of only having positive horizontal margin without any other non-curative factors. Out of the patients, 66 patients received additional gastrectomy and lymph node dissection. Excluding 1 lesion, which could not be endoscopically resected with en bloc specimen, we investigated 65 lesions in 65 patients. The rates of LNM and residual cancer after surgery were analyzed with pathological factors of ESD specimens: tumor size, histological type (differentiated type/undifferentiated type), invasion depth (M/SM), ulceration (negative/positive), lymphatic invasion (negative/positive), vascular invasion (negative/positive), and curability (R0 resection/R1 resection).
Results: The mean age was 66.6 years old. The tumor locations were U/M/L/R: 16/16/31/2. The mean size of lesions was 31.3 ± 20.1 mm. R0 resection rate of ESD was 52.3% (34/65). The rate of nodal metastasis in dissected lymph nodes and the rate of residual cancer in extracted stomach were 16.9% (11/65) and 16.9% (11/65), respectively. Univariate analyses indicated the LNM rates of each pathological factor: differentiated type/undifferentiated type was 15.6% (7/45)/20.0% (4/20) (p = 0.4547); M/SM was 0% (0/14)/16.9% (11/51) (p = 0.0532); ulceration negative/positive was 11.9% (5/42)/26.1% (6/23) (p = 0.1337), lymphatic invasion negative/positive was 3.1% (1/32)/30.3% (10/33) (p = 0.0035); vascular invasion negative/positive was 16.3% (8/49)/18.8% (3/16) (p = 0.5451). The tumor sizes of LNM negative/positive were 30 ± 25 mm/38 ± 19 mm (p = 0.0871); the tumor sizes of residual cancer negative/positive were 29 ± 18 mm/41 ± 27 mm (p = 0.0467). Residual cancer rates of R0 resection/R1 resection and was 0% (0/34)/35.5% (11/31) (p < 0.0001). There was no difference between residual cancer rates of any other pathological factors. Multivariate analyses indicated that lymphatic invasion was an only significant independent factor of lymph node metastasis (p = 0.0445) and that the tumor size and R1 resection were significant independent factors of residual cancer (p = 0.0211 and p < 0.0001).
Conclusion: The probability of LNM and residual cancer may contribute more to lymphatic invasion and tumor size and R1 resection, respectively, compared to any other pathological factors of ESD specimens. Therefore, additional treatments after ESD should be positively considered in cases of having them. On the other hand, the data implied that further treatment could be avoided after ESD in some non-curative cases of R0 resection without lymphatic invasion.

## OP230 CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS AND MANAGEMENT OF PATIENTS WITH GASTRIC PRECANCEROUS LESIONS IN FRANCE: A LARGE 15-YEAR SINGLE CENTER RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
M. Péron1, N. Chapelle2, A. Bourget1, J. Mosnier3, S. Bruley Des Varannes4, Y. Touchefeu4, E. Coron2, E. Cauchin5, T. Matysiak Budnik2

1Loire Atlantique, Institut des Maladies de l'Appareil Digestif, Hopital Hotel Dieu, Nantes, France, Nantes/France

2Université de Nantes, Nantes/France

3Loire Atlantique, Service d’anatomie et cytologie pathologiques, Hopital Hotel Dieu, Nantes/France

4Institut Des Maladies De L'appareil Digestif, CHU de Nantes IMAD, Nantes/France

5U1235, INSERM, Nantes/France

Contact E-mail Address:
matthieu.peron13@gmail.com

Introduction: Early detection and adequate surveillance of gastric precancerous lesions (GPL) may prevent the development of gastric adenocarcinoma (GADK) and reduce GADK-related mortality. The epidemiological and clinical data on GPL lesions in France are missing.
Aims & Methods: Our aim was to analyse, in a large retrospective study, the frequency, clinical characteristics, evolution, and modalities of surveillance of GPL in France. All the patients having undergone endoscopy with gastric biopsies between 2000 and 2015 in one academic center, and in whom GPL [atrophic gastritis (AG), or intestinal metaplasia (IM), or dysplasia (D)] was diagnosed by histology, were identified in the hospital pathology database. The clinical, endoscopic, histological and follow-up data were collected from the electronic files and analysed using SAS software.
Results: During a 15-year period, out of 16,764 patients having undergone upper endoscopy with gastric biopsies, 485 patients (60% of men, median age 68 years, min 11 - max 97) with GPL, were identified (detection rate 2.9%). The most frequent indications for endoscopy were anaemia (38%), digestive bleeding (22%), abdominal pain (17%), surveillance (15%), alteration of general status (11%), and dyspepsia (6%). At initial endoscopy, 11 patients (2.2%) had AG, 362 (75%) IM, 80 (16%) low grade dysplasia (LGD), 10 (2%) high grade dysplasia (HGD), and 22 (4.5%) had GADK with concomitant GPL (IM or D). H. pylori infection was found by histology in 204 patients (42%). Endoscopic aspect was considered normal in 17.5% of patients with IM, in 6% of patients with LGD, and in 20% of patients with HGD. The median number of biopsies obtained during initial endoscopy was 4 (min 0 - max 30, Q1-Q3: 2–6). Patients with HGD, were significantly older than those with IM and LGD (median age 75 vs 68 years, p = 0.006). From 485 patients, 326 (67%) had at least one follow-up endoscopy (median: 1, min 0 - max 24, Q1-Q3: 0–3), after the median time period of 2.9 months (min 0 - max 124, Q1-Q3: 1–14) since the initial diagnosis of GPL. During a median follow-up of 40 months (min 0.3 - max 137 months), out of 362 patients with IM, 18 (5%) showed progression to LGD, 2 (0.6%) to HGD, and 5 (1.4%) to GADK. Among 485 patients, 8 developed GADK during follow-up (annual incidence rate 0.11%). Altogether, with the 22 patients in whom GADK was found already at the time of the diagnosis of GPL, 30 GADK were identified in the studied population (6.2%).
Conclusion: This study showed that in France: 1) Most of GPL were diagnosed in patients referred for endoscopy for anaemia or digestive bleeding, 2) Patients with HGD were older than those with LGD and IM, 3) The progression from IM to more severe lesions (LGD, HGD, GADK) was observed in 7% of patients during a median follow-up of 3.3 years, and the annual incidence of GADK in this population was 0.11%, 4) Modalities of surveillance of GPL were heterogeneous, 5) New endoscopic techniques may improve the endoscopic diagnosis of GPL in the future.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP232 COLONIC POST-POLYPECTOMY BLEEDING IN PATIENTS ON NEW ORAL ANTI-COAGULANT – A CASE CONTROL STUDY
L.Y.K. Lam, T.Y.T. Lam, J.Y.L. Ching, S.H. Wong, S.C. C. Ng, F.K.L. Chan

Medicine And Therapeutics, Institute of Digestive Disease, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong/Hong Kong PRC

Contact E-mail Address:
yanlam2@hotmail.com

Introduction: Anticoagulants are commonly used to treat patients with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases. Recently developed new oral anticoagulants (NOAC) that are direct thrombin inhibitor and direct factor Xa inhibitor overcome some limitations of vitamin K antagonist, including drug drug interaction and regular dose adjustments on the basis of laboratory monitoring(1–3). The risk of post-polypectomy bleeding (PPB) in patients on anti-platelet therapy and vitamin K antagonist has been well studied(4, 5). However, data on the risk of post polypectomy bleeding in patients on NOAC are scanty.
Aims & Methods: This aim of this study aim was to determine the risk of colonic post-polypectomy bleeding in patients on NOAC. Data of consecutive inpatients with age between 18 – 89 in five-year period (from 2012 to 2016), who underwent colonic polypectomy with NOAC therapy (dabigatran, rivaroxaban and apixaban), were collected in 16 Hong Kong Public Hospitals by Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System (CDARS). NOAC were stopped 1–2 days before colonoscopy and resumed after procedure according to the local hospital practice. The control cohort who underwent colonic polypectomy without anti-platelet, anti-coagulation and NOAC were collected from the same system, matched with centre of procedure, age and sex during the same study period with a ratio 1:3. Post polypectomy bleeding was defined as fresh PR bleed after procedure with at least 2 g/dL drop in haemoglobin, requiring blood transfusion, repeat endoscopy for haemostasis or surgical intervention within 30 days of index colonoscopy. The relative risk and characteristics of PPB were analysed.
Results: Among 272 patients on NOAC underwent colonoscopy, 106 patients underwent colonic polypectomy. 7/106 (6.6%) patients had PPB. Among 51980 patients with colonic polypectomy without anti-platelet, anticoagulants and NOAC, 318 controls were selected with centre, age and sex matched. In the control group, 6/318 (1.9%) patients had PPB. The relative risk of PPB in patients on NOAC was 3.5 (p = 0.022). The onset of PPB in patients on NOAC ranged from day 1 to day 25 (median day 4). 4 patients underwent repeat colonoscopy and 3 patients were treated with supportive transfusion. No patients required surgery for haemostasis.

 Conclusion: The risk of colonic post-polypectomy bleeding in patients with NOAC is high and often delayed in presentation. Resuming NOAC 4 days after colonoscopy may reduce the bleeding risk by half. However, this strategy should be study in prospective trial to address the bleeding and thrombotic risk.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP233 MRI IMPROVEMENT AFTER ANTI-TNF THERAPY IS PREDICTIVE OF SUSTAINED CLINICAL REMISSION AND IS A POTENTIAL THERAPEUTIC TARGET IN CROHN’S DISEASE
A. Buisson1, L. Messadeg2, G. Bouguen3, F. Goutorbe4, J. Reimund5, M. Goutte1, C. Sautel6, A. Boucher6, I. Ticlete6, C. Duron7, J. Scanzi1, M. Reymond1, C. Allimant1, M. Dapoigny1, G. Bommelaer1, B. Pereira8, C. Hordonneau2

1Dept. Of Gastroenterology, CHU Estaing Clermont-Ferrand, Clermont-ferrand/France

2Dept. Of Radiology, CHU Estaing Clermont-Ferrand, Clermont-ferrand/France

3CHU Rennes, Rennes/France

4CH Bayonne, Bayonne/France

5Hépato-gastroentérologie Et Assistance Nutritive, Hôpitaux Universitaires De Strasbourg, Chu De Hautepierre, Strasbourg Cedex/France

6CH Issoire, Issoire/France

7Dept. Of Gastroenterology, CH Montluçon, Montluçon/France

8Dept. Of Statistics, CHU Clermont-Ferrand, Clermont-ferrand/France

Contact E-mail Address:
a_buisson@hotmail.fr

Introduction: MRI has been suggested as a potential alternative to endoscopy to evaluate therapeutic efficacy in ileocolonic Crohn’s disease (CD).
Aims & Methods: We aimed to determine if MRI endpoints at week 12 (W12) are able to predict corticosteroids-free deep remission (CFREM) and MRI remission at W52 in patients treated with anti-TNF. CD adult patients needing anti-TNF therapy with CDAI > 150 and at least one diseased-bowel segment on MRI were consecutively included in this multicenter prospective study. All the patients underwent MREC including diffusion-weighted sequences with no bowel cleansing and no rectal enema, before starting therapy, at W12 and W52. The MRI were interpreted independently by two radiologists blinded from clinical data. Clermont score [1] and magnetic resonance index of activity (MaRIA) [2] were calculated according to previous publications. CFREM was defined as CDAI < 150 and CRP < 5 g/L and faecal calprotectin <250 with no switch of anti-TNF agents and no bowel resection. MRI remission was defined as no segmental MaRIA > 11 or no segmental Clermont score > 12.5 and deep MRI remission as no segmental MaRIA > 7 or no segmental Clermont score >8.4.
Results: Overall, 64 CD patients were enrolled in the study. Nine patients were primary non-reponders and left the study before the second MRI. Among the included patients, 41.4% were active smokers and 22.0% previously underwent intestinal resection. CD location was ileal, colonic and ileocolonic in 48.3%, 8.6% and 43.1%, respectively. Overall, 65.5% received concomitant immunosuppressive therapies. In addition, 46.6% and 53.4% of the patients were treated with infliximab and adalimumab, respectively. We assessed the variation of MRI parameters between baseline and W12 in patients achieving CFREM at W52 compared to those who did not among 55 CD patients. In univariate analysis, five factors evaluated at W12 were predictors of CFREM at W52: disappearances of ulcerations (OR = 6.4, p = 0.05), of oedema (OR = 3.3, p = 0.05), of enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (OR = 5.9, 0.041), or of sclerolipomatosis (OR = 12, p = 0.03), and 10%-increase of ADC (OR = 4.3, p = 0.02). Using several multivariate models, we defined transmural response at W12 as at least one factor among the three following factors: disappearance of ulcerations, increase of ADC (ΔADC > 10 %), and disappearance of at least one extra-enteric sign (sclerolipomatosis OR enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes). Transmural response predicted CFREM at W52 in 18%, 53%, 67% and 100% of the patients when respectively none, one, two or three criteria were achieved at W12. Using ROC curves, we identified that 25%-decrease of Clermont score or MaRIA index at W12 were the best variations of these scores to predict CFREM at W52. All the MRI endpoints (Table 1) evaluated at W12 were highly predictive of CFREM at W52. In addition, transmural reponse (AUC = 0.66, Se = 71.4%, Spe = 60.0%, NPV = 75.0%, PPV = 55.6%) and MRI response according to Clermont score (AUC = 0.77, Se = 64.3%, Spe = 90.0%, NPV = 78.3%, PPV = 81.3%) or MaRIA (AUC = 0.84, Se = 78.6%, Spe = 90.0%, NPV = 85.7%, PPV = 85.7%) evaluated at W12 were highly predictive of deep MRI remission at W52.

 Conclusion: MRI is a reliable tool to monitor therapeutic response in ileocolonic CD. Our short-term MRI endpoints are highly predictive of CFREM or transmural healing at W52, supporting their use in daily practice and clinical trials.

Demographic data were collected and a harmonized monitoring strategy was applied. Clinical remission, response and biochemical response was evaluated at week 14, 30 and 54. None of the patients had received infliximab within 12 months prior to initiation of the biosimilar infliximab. Safety data was registered.
Results: 353 consecutive IBD (209 CD and 144 UC) patients were included of which 229 patients reached the week 54 endpoint. The age at disease onset was 24/28 years (median, IQR: 19–34 and 22–39) in CD and UC patients, respectively. 31/41% of CD patients had colonic/ileocolonic disease location, 43.5% had complicated disease behaviour, 39% had perianal disease, while 56.2% of UC patients had extensive colitis. 23/19% of patients had received previous anti-TNF therapy in CD and UC, respectively. 60/51% of CD/UC patients received concomitant immunosuppressives at baseline. 49, 53, 48% and 86, 81 and 65% of CD patients reached clinical remission and response by week 14, 30 and 54, respectively. Remission and response rates were 56, 41, 43% and 74, 66 and 50% in UC patients. Previous anti-TNF exposure was associated with decreased clinical efficacy in both CD and UC. Mean CRP decreased significantly both in CD and UC by week 14, which was maintained throughout the 1-year follow-up. 31 (8.8%) patients had infusion reactions, 32 (9%) patients had infections and 1 death occurred.
Conclusion: Final results from this prospective nationwide cohort confirm that CT-P13 is effective and safe in inducing and maintaining remission in both CD and UC. Efficacy was influenced by previous anti-TNF exposure, no new safety signals were detected.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP236 EFFICACY OF HEPATITIS B VIRUS VACCINATION IN NEWBORNS EXPOSED TO ANTI-TNF ALPHA IN UTERO
A. De Lima-Karagiannis1, S. Kanis1, J.C. Escher2, C.J. Van Der Woude1

1Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam/Netherlands

2Department Of Pediatrics, Erasmus MC University Medical Center, Rotterdam, Netherands, Rotterdam/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
a.delima@erasmusmc.nl

Introduction: Neonates exposed to maternal anti-TNF alpha treatment in utero are born with clinically significant anti-TNF alpha levels that can still be detected throughout the first months of life.1, 2 Adults treated with anti-TNF alpha agents have been reported to respond inadequately to the hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine compared to adults not treated with anti-TNF alpha.3–5 Since 2011, HBV vaccination is included in the Dutch National Vaccination Programme. The efficacy of the HBV vaccination is unclear in children that have been exposed to anti-TNF alpha in utero. The objective of this study was to compare anti-HBs levels following routine HBV vaccination in anti-TNF alpha-exposed children versus non-exposed children.
Aims & Methods: We performed a cross-sectional, controlled cohort study at a single, tertiary referral center. Study enrollment took place from 2014 until 2017. Pregnant women treated with anti-TNF alpha until at least the second trimester for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) and their subsequent children were recruited from the IBD preconception outpatient clinic. Pregnant women treated with other medication than anti-TNF alpha for IBD and their subsequent children were eligible as controls. Women were not eligible for participation in case of HBV infection. Adherence to the Dutch National Vaccination Programme was mandatory for participation in this study (Routine HBV vaccination (Engerix-B Junior, rDNA vaccine) at 6 weeks, 3, 4 and 11 months). A venous blood sample was obtained from the children one month after final HBV vaccination. Anti-HBs levels were measured by ELISA.
Results: Anti-HBs levels at 12 months did not differ between the anti-TNF alpha exposed (n = 15) and the control group (n = 12) (>1000 IU/L vs >1000 IU/L, p = 0.59). All children were successfully immunised against HBV, defined as anti-HBs>10 IU/L. Median anti-TNF alpha levels determined in cord blood at birth were 2.5 ug/mL (IQR: 0.40–11.01 ug/mL). There were no differences in birth outcomes, growth and infections in the first year of life between the anti-TNF alpha exposed and the control group.
Conclusion: This study suggests that children born with detectable anti-TNF alpha levels can be effectively vaccinated against HBV.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP237 STRUCTURE AND BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY OF INFLIXIMAB PRODUCTS
C. Lee1, M. Jeong1, J. Lee1, S. Seo1, S. Cho1, W. Zhang2, O. Jaquez3

1Samsung Bioepis Co., Ltd., Incheon/Korea, Republic of

2Biogen, Inc., Cambridge/United States of America

3Biogen, Inc., Zug/Switzerland

Contact E-mail Address:
conrad.lee@samsung.com

Introduction: As biosimilars are entering the market, evaluation of the quality of these products is needed as differences in manufacturing process may lead to differences in critical quality attributes, which affect efficacy. Thus, major biological activities of reference infliximab and of two biosimilars (SB2 and CT-P13) were determined.
Aims & Methods: More than 30 structural, physicochemical, and biological attributes of the infliximab products were evaluated. Structural comparison was performed by multiple assays including peptide mapping using mass spectrometry and hydrogen/deuterium exchange (HDX). TNF-α neutralisation activity was measured by a luciferase reporter gene assay. The percentages of galactosylated, afucose plus high mannosylated, and charged glycan were determined. FcγRIIIa binding activity in surface plasmon resonance, AlphaScreen-based binding assay, and cell-based binding assay were assessed. Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) activity in a NK92-CD16a cell line and in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were determined.
Results: Analytical similarity of SB2 was demonstrated through extensive characterisation studies. For example, the primary structure and higher-order structure of the reference infliximab and SB2 were similar. In the comparison of three infliximab products, the relative potency was similar for all 3 products. In N-glycan analysis, as compared with the reference infliximab, a lower percentage of charged glycan with SB2 was noted, and a higher percentage of galactosylated glycan and a lower percentage of afucose plus high mannosylated glycans with CT-P13 were noted. The percentage of the relative FcγRIIIa binding affinity by all 3 methods was lower with CT-P13 as compared with the reference infliximab. The percentage of the relative ADCC activity in the NK92-CD16a cell line was lower with CT-P13 and higher with SB2 as compared with the reference infliximab but was similar for all 3 products in PBMCs.
Conclusion: Comparison of the three infliximab products showed that there was no difference in most quality attributes. FcγRIIIa binding and ADCC activity showed differences that were correlated with the N-glycan profile, but the differences were not demonstrated in the physiologically more relevant condition.
