## OP238 BODY WEIGHT AND RAPID CLEARANCE DETERMINE EARLY FORMATION OF ANTI-DRUG ANTIBODIES AGAINST INFLIXIMAB
W. Reinisch1, A. Eser1, S. Schreiber2, H.C. Kwon3, D.R. Mould4

1Gastroenterologie Und Hepatologie, Medical University of Vienna Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Vienna/Austria

2Uksh, Universität Kiel UKSH Medizinische Abt. I - UKSH, Universität Kiel UKSH Medizinische Abt. I; Kiel/DE, Kiel/Germany

3Celltrion Inc., Yeonsu-gu, Incheon/Korea, Republic of

4Projections Research Inc, Phoenixville PA/United States of America

Contact E-mail Address:
walter.reinisch@meduniwien.ac.at

Introduction: Anti-drug antibodies (ADA) arise during treatment with Infliximab (IFX). ADA accelerate drug clearance (CL), rendering IFX ineffective (1). Delineation of risk factors for ADA formation and early identification of ADA offer opportunities to attenuate ADA response.
Aims & Methods: A 2-part modeling approach was undertaken to 1) develop a semi-mechanistic conditional on ADA+ pharmacokinetics (PK)/pharmacodynamics (PD) model and 2) identify predictors of early ADA formation. PK data obtained from Celltrion Study 1331 (2, 3) investigating originator and biosimilar IFX in RA patients were evaluated. The PK/PD model by Chen (4), using Nonmem 7.3, was modified: 1) A 2-compartment linear model was fitted to the PK data from the first 2 doses (MOD1), 2) PK and ADA were modeled simultaneously with the PK part of the model fixed to the MOD1 estimates, 3) a zero-inflated Poisson distribution linked predicted ADA to a non-negative integer reflecting ADA levels as suggested by Bonate (5) (MOD2). ADA formation was implemented by introducing putative doses into an empirical ADA depot in a saturable fashion starting at the 3rd IFX dose. The model included a variable time lag before ADA was introduced into the central PK compartment, where it associated with IFX in a 1st order fashion to form an IFX-ADA complex, eliminated by a 1st order process, or was eliminated as free ADA. The incidence of ADA was modeled with logistic regression using baseline predictors (weight (WT), albumin, sex, methotrexate dose, presence of immunosuppressants, and serum glucose) and the estimated CL from MOD1 using Fisher scoring and SAS proc logistic (MOD3).
Results: MOD1 estimated IFX elimination half-life was 8.4 days. Predicted CL increased by 6, 10, and 1.7% as weight increased, albumin decreased, and C-reactive protein (CRP) increased by 10 kg, 1G/dL, and 5 nmol/L, respectively. Unexplained between subject variability (BSV) expressed as coefficient of variation (CV) in CL was 42%. MOD2 indicated variable time to the 1st appearance of ADA (median time = 87 days, 95% CI 74–103 days), with high BSV (CV = 144%). Rising ADA titers associated with decreasing trough levels (TL), given stable albumin, WT, and CRP. For a ADA+ patient, 5 mg/kg dosing at weeks 0, 2, 6, 14, TLs were undetectable by the 5th dose. Simulations using MOD2 suggested that appropriate dose adjustments may be able to overcome low ADA titers to restore response. The ADA formation incidence model (MOD3) identified CL and WT as the only predictors of ADA formation. The odds ratios (95% Wald based confidence intervals (CI) for 0.1 L/day and 10 kg increases in CL and WT were 1.78 (1.50, 2.12) and 1.19 (1.06, 1.33), respectively. Mean IFX CL for ADA+ and ADA- subjects were 0.364 L/day (probability (Pr) of SC = 0.67) and 0.264 L/day (Pr of SC = 0.49).
Conclusion: 3-part modeling identified baseline WT and CL as predictors of ADA formation. A transit model for the combined PK/PD from ADA+ patients described ADA titers that rose after a lag time with increasing elimination of IFX resulting in unmeasurable TLs. Strategies of early rapid CL estimates are needed to guide dosing or measures targeting reduction of ADA production.

S. Schreiber: Consultant for celltrion

D.R. Mould: President of Projections Research Inc., consulting company for the pharmaceutical industry
All other authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

2. Yoo DH, Hrycaj P, Miranda P, et al. A randomised, double-blind, parallel-group study to demonstrate equivalence in efficacy and safety of CT-P13 compared with innovator infliximab when coadministered with methotrexate in patients with active rheumatoid arthritis: the PLANETRA study. ## OP239 RELATED FACTORS TO THE QUALITY OF COLON CLEANSING
C. Mangas1, E. Santana Rocamora1, A. Suárez González2, I. Portillo Villares3, A. Seoane4, M. Ponce5, P. Diez6, E. Quintero Carrion7, M. Herraiz8, M. Pellisé Urquiza9, Á. Ferrández Arenas10, V. Hernández11, Á.E. Pizarro Moreno12, R. Jover1

1Hospital General Universitario de Alicante, Alicante/Spain

2Servicio De Aparato Digestivo, Hospital Universitario Central de Asturias, Oviedo/Spain

3Hospital Universitario de Donostia, San Sebastián/Spain

4Hospital del Mar-Parc de Salut Mar Barcelona, Barcelona/Spain

5Hospital Universitari i Politecnic de la Fe, Valencia/Spain

6Gastroenterology, Hospital Universitario Rio Hortega, Valladolid/Spain

7Gastroenterology, Hospital Univ. de Canarias, Santa Cruz de Tenerife/Spain

8Clinica Universitaria de Navarra, Pamplona/Spain

9Gastroenterology, Hospital Clinic Barcelona, Barcelona/Spain

10Hospital Clínico Universitario Lozano Bleza, Zaragoza/Spain

11Instituto de Investigación Biomédica, Xerencia de Gestión Integrada de Vigo, Vigo/Spain

12Gastroenterology, Hospital Virgen del Rocio, Sevilla/Spain

Contact E-mail Address:
cmangassanjuan@gmail.com

Introduction: An adequate colon cleansing is needed for the fullfilment of quality indicators of colonoscopy.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to evaluate which factors are related with colonic cleansing quality. A total of 6323 colonoscopies performed between January and October 2016 were prospectively included in the QUALISCOPIA project, an observational, multicenter and prospective study, developed in 12 centers in Spain. Inadequate cleansing was considered when the Boston Scale score is 0/1 in any of the segments. Variables such as indication for the colonoscopy, sex, age, type of bowel preparation, time of the examination and the time between the last dose of bowel preparation and colonoscopy have been analyzed.
Results: Inadequate cleansing was presented in the 14.1% of the patients. In the multivariate analysis (Table 1) we observed that the indication of colonoscopy influences cleanliness. Regarding the indication of the procedure, inadequate cleansing was observed in 18.4% of the patients with gastrointestinal symptoms (p-value<0.001, aOR1.7, 95%CI 1.3–2.1); 14.6% of patients with post-polypectomy surveillance (p-value<0.001, aOR2.4, 95%CI 2.0–2.9) and 10.6% of patients with direct screening (p-value=0.111, aOR1.3, 95%CI 0.9–1.8) compared with positive fecal immunochemical test, were inadequate cleansing was seen in 8.8% of colonoscopies with this indication. Moreover, inadequate cleansing was more frequently in males (p-value = 0.048, aOR1.3, 95%CI 1.1–1.5) and in patients ≥60 years (p-value = 0.007, aOR1.2, 95%CI 1.1–1.5). Regarding the length of delay between the last dose of bowel preparation and the start of colonoscopy, we observed that a delay longer than 7 h was associated with inadequate cleansing (p-value<0.001, aOR1.8, 95%CI 1.5–2.5), nevertheless, a delay longer than 4 h did not show this association (p-value = 0.174, aOR1.1, 95%CI 0.9–1.4). On the other hand, the type of bowel preparation had no effect on the cleansing quality.

 Conclusion: The indication of colonoscopy, sex, age, and time between the last dose of bowel preparation and colonoscopy longer than 7 h are factors that are independently related to the quality of colonic cleansing.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP240 IMPROVEMENT OF COLONOSCOPY PREPARATION BY AN AUTOMATED 4-DAY PATIENT GUIDANCE BY SMS; RESULTS FROM THE PERICLES-II STUDY
B. M. Walter1, P. Klare2, K. Strehle2, J. Aschenbeck3, L. Ludwig4, N. Dikopoulos4, B. Neu5, S. Delius2

1Klinik Für Innere Medizin I, University Hospital Ulm, Ulm/Germany

2Ii. Medizinische Klinik, MRI der TU München, München/Germany

3Facharzt für Innere Medizin Versorgungsschwerpunkt Gastroenterologie, Berlin/Germany

4Gastroenterologische Schwerpunktpraxis, Dornstadt/Germany

5Medizinische Klinik Ii, Klinik Landshut-Achdorf, Landshut/Germany

Contact E-mail Address:
benjamin.walter@uniklinik-ulm.de

Introduction: Participation in colon-cancer screening is still low in Europe and worldwide. Especially bowel preparation is reported to be the most unpleasant burden. Despite the fact that bowel preparation is a major cornerstone of quality of colonoscopy, in a certain proportion of patients bowel preparation is still insufficient. Problems with dietary recommendations and problems taking the purgatives are reported very often in these cases. Among our patients usage of mobile phone has increased rapidly in the last years. Therefore using this new medium for improvement of colonoscopy preparation has to be considered.
Aims & Methods: To optimize patients' guidance in colonoscopy preparation an easy-to-access solution for all mobile phones by short message service (SMS) covering the 4 days prior colonoscopy was used in a prospective, randomized multicenter study. In comparison to other approaches not only laxative intake but a complete patient guidance over the last four days before colonoscopy was served by the SMS system. 500 (250/250) participants with appointment for out-patient colonoscopy were randomized to regular colonoscopy preparation (control group) or SMS supported colonoscopy preparation. The control group received information about colonoscopy preparation orally and by a leaflet as regularly done by gastroenterologists. The SMS supported group additionally received information regarding dietary and general recommendations time axis adjusted to the colonoscopy appointment by an automated SMS system starting 4 days prior colonoscopy preparation. Level of bowel cleanliness was measured by BBPS. Patients' satisfaction with bowel preparation procedure was analyzed by a questionnaire.
Results: Participants of the SMS supported colonoscopy preparation had a significant higher BBPS score (7.6 vs. 6.1; p < 0.0001) in comparison to regular colonoscopy preparation. All regions of the colon, especially the right colon had higher BBPS scores in SMS supported patients. Overall patient satisfaction with bowel preparation was higher in the SMS supported group.
Conclusion: SMS supported colonoscopy preparation by an automated 4-day guidance improved bowel cleanliness. Patient guidance covering the last four days before colonoscopy was highly accepted by the patients. We conclude further that the usage of a simple tool as SMS for optimizing colonoscopy preparation could improve CRC-Screening participation.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP241 A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL COMPARING WATER ASSISTED AND AIR INSUFFLATION COLONOSCOPY WITHOUT SEDATION
R. Azevedo, C. Leitão, H. Ribeiro, J. Pinto, F. Pereira, A. Caldeira, R. Sousa, E. Pereira, J. Barros, A. Banhudo

Gastroenterology, Amato Lusitano Hospital, Castelo Branco/Portugal

Contact E-mail Address:
richardazevedo13@gmail.com

Introduction: Water-assisted colonoscopy is gaining increasing popularity as an alternative method to reduce patients’ discomfort and need for sedation in unsedated and minimally sedated patients. Previous studies have shown that water-aided colonoscopy is superior to air insufflation in attenuating insertion pain.
Aims & Methods: We conducted a patient-blinded, randomized controlled trial with head-to-head comparison of these two methods to evaluate the effectiveness of water-assisted colonoscopy in reducing discomfort and pain in patients without sedation and to determine its influence on other colonoscopy quality indicators compared to the conventional method. A total of 127 outpatients were randomized to either water-aided insertion and air insufflation during withdrawal [Water] or standard air insufflation during both insertion and withdrawal [Air]. The primary outcome was the improvement of patient intraprocedural pain (pain score), evaluated using a questionnaire (score 1 to 10).
Results: Baseline characteristics of the two groups were comparable; 64 patients were included in the Water group and 63 in the Air group. Patients in the Water group reported less intraprocedural pain than those in the Air group (3.52 ± 2.29 vs. 5.10 ± 2, 01 p < 0.01), despite lower levels of anxiety prior to the examination (score 1–5) in the Air group (1.89 ± 0.88 vs. 2.27 ± 1.16 p < 0.05). There were no differences in the quality of bowel preparation (median of 8 for the two arms, according to the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale), cecal intubation time and withdrawal time (15.61 ± 6.74 vs. 16.83 ± 6.55 minutes; 11.23 ± 3.42 vs. 11.90 ± 5.91 minutes, p > 0.05), as well as polyp detection rate (40.6 vs. 39.7%, p > 0.05) in the Water vs. Air group. There were no major complications in both groups.
Conclusion: Water-assisted colonoscopy seems to be a safe and effective alternative to conventional colonoscopy without sedation, being associated with less intraprocedural pain and not influencing other performing measures of colonoscopy. Based on this evidence, the use of water-assisted colonoscopy should be encouraged.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP242 NEW GENERATION FULL-SPECTRUM VERSUS STANDARD FORWARD-VIEWING COLONOSCOPY: A MULTICENTER, RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED, TANDEM COLONOSCOPY TRIAL
K. Hotta1, T. Kudo2, Y. Saito3, H. Ikematsu4, Y. Takeuchi5, M. Shimatani6, K. Kawakami7, N. Tamai8, K. Yoshimura9, H. Ishikawa10, K. Imai1, Y. Mori11, T. Matsuda3, S. Kudo2

1Division Of Endoscopy, Shizuoka Cancer Center, Nagaizumi/Japan

2Digestive Disease Center, Showa University Northern Yokohama Hospital, Yokohama/Japan

3Endoscopy Division, National Cancer Center Hospital, Tokyo/Japan

4Endoscopy Division, National Cancer Center Hospital East, Kashiwa/Japan

5Department Of Gastrointestinal Oncology, Osaka International Cancer Institute, Osaka/Japan

6The Third Department Of Internal Medicine, Kansai Medical University, Hirakata/Japan

7Second Department Of Internal Medicine, Osaka Medical Collage, Osaka/Japan

8Department Of Endoscopy, The Jikei University School of Medicine, Tokyo/Japan

9Kanazawa University Hospital, Innovative Clinical Research Center, Kanazawa/Japan

10Department Of Molecular-targeting Cancer Prevention, Kyoto Prefectural University of Medicine, Kyoto/Japan

11Northen Yokohama Hospital, Showa University Northern Yokohama Hospital, Yokohama/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
k.hotta@scchr.jp

Introduction: Standard forward-viewing (SFV) colonoscopy was proved to have more than 20% adenoma miss rate based on meta-analysis of tandem colonoscopy trials1). Previous model of full-spectrum endoscopy (FUSE) was proved to improve the adenoma miss rate compared to SFV colonoscopy by a multicenter, randomized tandem colonoscopy trial2). However, recent another randomized trial did not prove a significant efficacy of FUSE compared to SFV colonoscopy with regard to the adenoma detection rate3).
Aims & Methods: Aim of this study was to compare the new generation FUSE with SFV colonoscopy. A multicenter, randomized controlled, tandem colonoscopy trial was conducted in eight Japanese institutions between February 2016 and January 2017. Patients aged 40–75 years referred for colorectal cancer screening, positive fecal immunological test, or polyp surveillance underwent same-day, back-to-back tandem colonoscopy with the new generation FUSE (330°) and SFV colonoscope (140–170°). Randomization was stratified by gender, age, indication and institution. Primary endpoint was the adenoma miss rate via per-protocol, per-patient analysis. Secondary endpoints included the polyp miss rate and the adenoma detection rate. This trial is registered with University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN), number UMIN000020448.
Results: A total of 344 patients were enrolled and finally 319 patients were included in the per-protocol analyses: 159 (50%) were randomly assigned to receive FUSE first, and 160 (50%) to receive SFV first. Per-lesion analysis, the adenoma miss rate was significantly lower in patients in the FUSE first than in those in the SFV first: 60 (20.5%) of 293 vs 103 (30.7%) of 335 adenomas were missed (P < .0035). Per-patient analysis, the adenoma miss rates was significantly lower in patients in the FUSE first than in those in the SFV first: 11.7 (8.0–15.4) % vs 22.9 (17.5–28.3) % (P < .001). The polyp miss rate via per-patient analysis was also significantly lower in the FUSE first than in the SFV first: 13.9 (10.0–17.7) % vs 26.8 (21.3–32.4) % (P < .001). The adenoma detection rate was significantly superior in patients in the FUSE first than in those in the SFV first: 62.9 (54.9–70.4) % vs 49.4 (41.4–57.9) % (P = .018). Cecal intubation rates (%), mean cecal intubation and withdrawal time (min) of FUSE and SFV were 98.2 and 99.1 (P = .50), 7.5 and 4.7 (P < .001), 8.4 and 7.9 (P < .001), respectively.
Conclusion: New-generation FUSE improved not only adenoma miss rate but also adenoma detection rate compared with SFV colonoscopy.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

2. Glalnek IM, et al. Lancet Oncol 2014; 15: 353–60
3. Hassan C, et al. Gut 2016 Aug 9(Epub ahead of print)

## OP243 PERFORMANCE COMPARISON OF FULL-SPECTRUM VERSUS FORWARD-VIEWING COLONSCOPY: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL

Introduction: Technology of colonoscopy is constantly evolving. In the whole FUSE group 1.8 polyps per patients were found overall increasing to 1.9 with newer FUSE generation and 1. 9 with Lumos (tissue enhancement technology from Endochoice) compared to 1.8 in FVE (ns). 96 to 95% of the polyps were sessile lesions; 84.4 vs 83.7% below 5 mm of size, 12.8 vs 12.5 % between 5–9 mm and 3.2 respectively 3.8% bigger than 1 cm. 34.2 vs 34.1% were right sided, 21.9 vs 20.2% located in the tansverse colon. 48% of the extracted FUSE polyps and 50% of the polyps in the FVE group were tubular adenomas, 0.6 vs 1.2% were villous, 17.5% vs 23.6% serrated (SSA) adenomas and 15 respectively 11.8% were hyperplastic polyps. In 0.7% a CRC and in 0.02% an anal carcinoma was found in the FUSE group vs 0.8% CRCs in the FVE group. There was no significant difference in histology. Time to ileum was with 5.3 min (CI 5.0–5.5) slightly faster with FUSE (overall) even more pronounced with the at that time newest FUSE generation (gen2) and a mean time of 5.0 min (CI 4.7–5.3) compared to 5.5 min (CI 5.2–5.7) with the FVE (p = 0.02). Withdrawal time was significantly shorter with FUSE with a time of 15.8 min (CI 15.3–16.3) in FUSE and 19.1 min (CI 16.8–21.4) in FVE (p = 0.01). Time for intervention was identical in both groups (3.3 (CI 2.8–3.4) vs 3.4 min (CI 2.8–3.6); ns). Depending on FUSE generation the overall examination time gain was 3 to 4.1 min (p < 0.05).
Conclusion: Our randomized controlled trial with the largest FUSE examined patient cohort in the literature revealed significantly shorter examination time compared to conventional high definition colonoscopy with equal adenoma detection rates for both types of instruments. Due to the wider field of view (330° for FUSE endoscopes) polyps might be detected faster and easier during the withdrawal, resulting in the same high adenoma detection rate of 51 up to 52% for FUSE compared to 53% for FVE but with significantly shorter pullback time.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP244 IMPLEMENTATION OF AN OPTICAL DIAGNOSIS STRATEGY FOR DIMINUTIVE POLYPS INCLUDING SESSILE SERRATED LESIONS: TRAINING AND LONG-TERM QUALITY ASSURANCE
J. L. a. Vleugels1, M.G. w. Dijkgraaf2, Y. Hazewinkel1, P. Fockens1, E. Dekker1, O.B.O.T. Discount Study Group1

1Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam/Netherlands

2Clinical Research Unit, Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
j.l.vleugels@amc.uva.nl

Introduction: Narrow band imaging (NBI) allows real-time differentiation of diminutive (1–5 mm) polyp histology during endoscopy. Before this practice can be implemented in daily practice, guidelines endorse ≥90% negative predictive value (NPV) for neoplastic histology in the rectosigmoid and ≥90% agreement in surveillance intervals for high-confidence predictions. This study aimed to train endoscopists in optical diagnosis of diminutive polyps with NBI and to determine whether these endoscopists can achieve and maintain the prior thresholds.
Aims & Methods: In this prospective multicentre study, endoscopists accredited for colonoscopies in FIT-positives within the Dutch bowel cancer screening program were trained in optical diagnosis with our validated NICE-WASP module [1]. This module includes optical differentiation of sessile serrated lesions. Trained endoscopists were required to meet predefined thresholds in image-based and real-time tests before entering the continuation phase. In this phase, endoscopists recorded histology predictions and confidence levels of all polyps in consecutive FIT-positive colonoscopies for 1 year. Endoscopists were randomized to receive feedback or no feedback on their performance. Primary outcome was whether endoscopists could maintain a NPV ≥90% for neoplastic histology in the rectosigmoid for high-confidence predictions, either with or without regular interim performance feedback. NPV was determined by comparing predicted with actual histology outcome. Neoplastic histology was defined as adenomatous and sessile serrated lesion histology. For surveillance interval agreement, prediction was based on the combination of high-confidence predictions and histology outcome of low-confidence predictions and polyps sized >5 mm. Generalized estimated equation analyses were used and adjusted for clustering of polyps per patient and per endoscopist.
Results: Of 39 endoscopists initially attending the training sessions, 27 (69%) qualified after a median number of 3 tests (range 2–5). The pooled NPV for predicting neoplastic rectosigmoid histology during the real-time tests was 94.1% (95% confidence interval (CI) 86.1–97.6). In the continuation phase, these 27 endoscopists performed 3, 144 colonoscopies in which 4, 504 diminutive polyps were removed. Of these, 73.5% were predicted with high-confidence and 40.4% were located in the rectosigmoid. The pooled NPV for predicting neoplastic histology in the rectosigmoid at the end of the continuation phase was 90.8% (95% CI 88.6–92.6). The NPV in the feedback group was 91.7% (95% CI 88.2–94.2) and 89.6% (95% CI 85.2–92.8) in the observation group (p = 0.93). The pooled surveillance interval agreement was 95.4% (95% CI 94.0–96.6), and did not differ between the feedback and observation group (96.4% versus 94.1%, p = 0.10). Individually, 17 (63%) endoscopists achieved ≥ 90% NPV for predicting neoplastic rectosigmoid histology, 24 (89%) achieved ≥90% surveillance interval agreement and 16 (59%) achieved both. High-confidence predictions and use of high-definition scopes were independently associated with accurate histology prediction.
Conclusion: Using a validated training module including sessile serrated lesions, a selected group of endoscopists achieved and maintained a pooled NPV and surveillance interval agreement of at least 90% over the course of 1 year. Providing regular interim feedback did not lead to differences in those endpoints. This study design can be used as a template for safe implementation of an optical diagnosis strategy in daily practice (NCT02516748).

E. Dekker has equipment on loan from Olympus Europe and Fujifilm, has received a research grant from Olympus Europe and Fujifilm, and consulted for Tillotts Pharma (one time).
All other authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP245 LONG-TERM EFFECTS OF H. PYLORI ERADICATION ON MOLECULAR ALTERATIONS RELATED TO GASTRIC CARCINOGENESIS
J. Watari1, Y. Michigami1, C. Ito1, K. Hara1, T. Yamasaki1, T. Okugawa1, T. Kono1, K. Tozawa2, T. Tomita2, Y. Ohda1, T. Oshima1, H. Fukui1, H. Miwa1

1Division Of Gastroenterology, Department Of Internal Medicine, Hyogo College of Medicine, Nishinomiya/Japan

2Gastroenterology, Hyogo College of Medicine, Hyogo/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
watarij@hyo-med.ac.jp

Introduction: A meta-analysis showed that H. pylori eradication seems to reduce gastric cancer (GC). However, a study from Japan showed that even after an H. pylori infection is cured and gastric inflammation is eliminated, the risk of the development of GC remains, and the risk increases in individuals with precancerous conditions such as atrophic mucosa (AM) and intestinal mucosa (IM). Indeed, GC has occurred to some degree during a long-term follow-up in patients treated for H. pylori eradication. In addition, the roles of a number of genetic and epigenetic alterations have been reported to be involved in GC and precancerous conditions of the stomach.
Aims & Methods: To clarify the molecular changes due to H. pylori eradication, we evaluated differences in molecular alterations related to carcinogenesis in background mucosa with and without GC before and after H. pylori eradication. We enrolled 78 consecutive patients and divided them into three groups: the chronic gastritis patients with long-term follow-up (≥3 yrs) after H. pylori eradication (AG group, n = 30), the patients who developed intramucosal early GC after eradication (≥3 yrs) (GC group, n = 27), and the H. pylori-positive chronic gastritis patients (control group, n = 21). The H. pylori status was analyzed in each patient by both Giemsa staining and serum H. pylori-IgG antibody measurement. Biopsy specimens were obtained from the stomach's antrum, angulus, and corpus. DNA was separately extracted from the AM and IM via laser capture microdissection. Genetic instability was evaluated at five loci based on the Bethesda panel; we assessed the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) and the methylation status at seven tumor-related genes, including CDH1, CDKN2A, hMLH1, MINT1, MINT31, MGMT, and RUNX3, by conducting a methylation-sensitive high-resolution melting analysis. CIMP was defined as ≥3/7 methylated markers using the seven-marker CIMP panel.
Results: The mean duration after H. pylori eradication was 6.0 ± 3.1 years (range 3–13 years) in the AG group and 7.0 ± 4.5 years (3–20 years) in the GC group; thus there was no significant difference between groups. The incidence of CIMP and methylation at CDH1 (p < 0.0001), CDKN2A (p = 0.006), MINT1 (p < 0.0001), and MINT31 (p < 0.0001) genes was significantly lower in the AG group compared to the controls. H. pylori eradication was associated with a significant reduction of CDH1 (odds ratio [OR] 0.13, p = 0.02), MINT1 (OR 0.03, p = 0.002), MINT31 (OR 0.08, p = 0.006) in the AM. In contrast, no significant differences in the molecular alterations were seen in the IM between the AG and control groups. The incidence of CIMP in both the AM and IM was significantly higher in the GC group compared to the AG group (p = 0.06 and p = 0.002, respectively). The incidence of molecular alterations was significantly higher in the AM compared to the IM.
Conclusion: In the patients with ≥3 yrs' follow-up after H. pylori eradication, an alteration of molecular events (especially CpG island hypermethylation) in the AM but not the IM may be an important factor in the reduction of GC incidence. In addition, CIMP in the AM and IM may be a surrogate marker of gastric cancer.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP246 CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF HELICOBACTER PYLORI NAÏVE NON-CARDIAC GASTRIC ADENOCARCINOMA
S. Suzuki1, N. Uedo1, M. Arao1, T. Iwatsubo1, H. Nakahira1, M. Kato1, Y. Tounai1, K. Hamada1, Y. Yamasaki1, N. Matsuura1, S. Sichijo1, T. Kanesaka1, S. Yamamoto1, T. Akasaka1, N. Hanaoka1, Y. Takeuchi1, K. Higashino1, R. Ishihara1, Y. Tomita2, H. Iishi1

1Gastrointestinal Oncology, Osaka International Cancer Institute, Osaka/Japan

2Department Of Pathology, Osaka International Cancer Institute, Osaka/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
syo_suzuki@med.miyazaki-u.ac.jp

Introduction:
Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection is strongly associated with development of non-cardiac gastric cancer, and gastric adenocarcinoma occurred in patients naïve to H. pylori infection is very rare. In this study, we investigated the clinical characteristics of non-cardiac gastric adenocarcinoma that developed in H. pylori uninfected patients who underwent endoscopic resection.
Aims & Methods: A total of 2221 gastric neoplasia in 1707 patients that were removed by ESD or EMR between January 2010 and May 2016 at our hospital were included. Patients were excluded if they were not evaluated H. pylori infection status, and were diagnosed with tumors other than adenocarcinoma. H. pylori uninfection was defined as condition that fulfilled all following criteria: 1) negative result from at least one of the H. pylori test: serum antibodies (<3U/ml), urea breath test and stool antigen tests, 2) no endoscopic finding of gastric mucosal atrophy, and 3) no histological finding of grandular atrophy and intestinal metaplasias in the surrounding mucosa of the resected specimen. Clinical characteristics including age, sex, tumor location, size, macroscopic type, histological type, and depth, presence of ulceration and curative resection rate were compared between H. pylori-uninfected and –infected gastric adenocarcinoma. For differentiated type adenocarcinoma in the uninfected group, mucin phenotype was compared between the lesions in the infected group that were matched by age, sex, tumor location and size. Mucin phenotype was classified into gastric (G-), intestinal (I-), and gastrointestinal (GI-) types according to immunohistological staining with MUC5AC, MUC6, CD10 and MUC2.
Results: Finally, 1, 430 non-cardiac gastric adenocarcinoma in 1111 patients were analyzed in this study. 18 (1.3%) out of 1430 lesions were diagnosed as H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma. Mean age of patients with H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma was significantly younger than that of those with H. pylori infected gastric adenocarcinoma (63 vs. 70 years old, p < 0.001). Undifferentiated type was more frequent in the H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma (44%) than in the H. pylori infected gastric adenocarcinoma (5.8%). Among 10 differentiated type H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma, 70% (7/10) located in upper third of the stomach, while 51% (675/1330) of differentiated type H. pylori infected gastric adenocarcinoma located in the lower third (p < 0.05). There was no statistical difference for other variables. Of the 10 differentiated type H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma, 5 (50%) were G-type and 5 (50%) were GI-type lesions. Of the 30 matched differentiated type H. pylori infected gastric adenocarcinoma, G-type lesions, were only 2 (6.7%, p < 0.05) and 26 (86.7%) were GI-type and 2 (6.7%) were I-type, respectively.
Conclusion: The prevalence of H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma was low (1.3%). H. pylori uninfected gastric adenocarcinoma has different characteristics from infected gastric adenocarcinoma in terms of histological type, location of the tumor and mucin phenotype. It is important to bear these differences in mind when we make diagnosis of early gastric cancer in H. pylori uninfected patients.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP247 EPIGENETIC SILENCING OF AN AUTOPHAGY GENE BY HELICOBACTER PYLORI FACILITATES CARCINOGENIC TRANSFORMATION OF GASTRIC EPITHELIAL CELLS
J. Sualeh Muhammad1, S. Nanjo2, T. Ando2, S. Yamashita3, T. Ushijima3, T. Sugiyama2

1Biological And Biomedical Sciences, The Aga Khan University, Karachi/Pakistan

2University of Toyama, Toyama/Japan

3National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo/Japan

Contact E-mail Address:
dr.jibran@live.com

Introduction:
Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection is known to induce epigenetic silencing, that is DNA methylation of the promoter region of various genes, leading to silencing of those genes. Impairment of autophagy via methylation silencing induces DNA damage leading to genetic instability and carcinogenesis. For the first time in this study, we aimed to identify the role of H. pylori infection in inducing DNA methylation and silencing of host autophagy-related (Atg) genes. Further, it was evaluated whether silencing of specific autophagy gene will lead to impairment of autophagy leading to promotion of gastric carcinogenesis.
Aims & Methods: We obtained gastric mucosae from 41 gastric cancer patients and from 11 healthy volunteers (8 H. pylori-uninfected and 3 H. pylori-infected). Methylation microarray and quantitative methylation-specific polymerase chain reaction (qMSP-PCR) were used to assess the methylation statuses of 34 Atg genes. Further, quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) was used to analyze mRNA expression of specific Atg genes. De-methylation assay was performed using an enzyme, 5Aza-dC. Later, gene knock-down was performed by siRNA transfection. To assess tumorigenic properties, cell proliferation, migration, and invasion assays were performed using normal rat gastric epithelial cells. Western blotting of LC3 was performed to assess autophagy.
Results: We found that MAP1LC3A variant 1 (MAP1LC3Av1) and ULK2 were specifically methylated in H. pylori-infected mucosae and gastric cancer tissues, identified by methylation microarray analysis. Data from qMSP, qRT-PCR, and de-methylation assay confirmed methylation silencing of MAP1LC3Av1 in two gastric cancer cell lines. Knock-down of MAP1LC3Av1 from rat normal gastric epithelial cells, which were deprived of serum, showed inhibition of autophagy, an increased cell proliferation, increased cell migration, and increased cell invasion. Furthermore, analyses of human gastric tissue sample showed that MAP1LC3Av1 was methylated and silenced in 23.3% of gastric cancerous mucosae and 40% of non-cancerous mucosae with H. pylori infection.
Conclusion: MAP1LC3Av1 is an essential gene for normal function of autophagy and H. pylori-induced methylation silencing of MAP1LC3Av1 impairs autophagy, promoting a carcinogenic transformation of gastric mucosa. Results of this study highlight how H. pylori-associated epigenetic changes in infected host cells, such as methylation silencing of Atg genes, are likely to play a significant role in gastric cancer development and the progression of the precancerous cascade. Therefore, in future chemoprevention may be achieved against H. pylori-associated gastric cancer with by using de-methylating agents.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP248 THE EPITHELIAL-MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION PROCESS OF NORMAL EPITHELIUM INFECTED BY HELICOBACTER PYLORI. ROLE OF FIBROBLASTS AND CANCER-ASSOCIATED PROTEINS
G. Krzysiek-Maczka, A. Ptak-Belowska, A. Targosz, M. Strzalka, U. Szczyrk, T. Brzozowski

Physiology, Jagiellonian University Medical College, Cracow/Poland

Contact E-mail Address:
gracjana.krzysiek-maczka@uj.edu.pl

Introduction: Major human gastrointestinal pathogen Helicobacter pylori (Hp) colonizes the gastric mucosa causing inflammation and severe complications including gastroduodenal ulcers, MALT lymphoma, or even cancer but the role of fibroblasts in the pathogenesis of Hp in the stomach has been little studied. Normal stroma contains few fibroblasts, especially myofibroblasts, but their number rapidly increases in the reactive stroma surrounding inflammatory region and neoplastic tissue. The interaction between Hp and fibroblasts and the contribution of Hp-infected fibroblasts to the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) process of gastric epithelium in Hp-infected mucosa has been little explored.
Aims & Methods: We determined the effect of co-incubation of cultured rat gastric fibroblasts with alive Hp strain expressing cagA+, vacA+ compared with Hp (cagA-, vacA-) strain on the transdifferentiation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts associated with Hp-induced inflammation and neoplasia. We also attempted to examine whether differentiated fibroblasts possess characteristics of cancer associated fibroblasts (CAF) able to induce epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) of normal rat gastric epithelial cells (RGM-1 cell line). Gastric mucosal samples were harvested from 8-week-old Spraque-Dowley rats and cultured to obtain the sub-confluent fibroblasts. The isolated fibroblasts were infected with 1 × 109 per dish of live Hp (ATCC 700824, cagA+, vacA+) or for comparison, with Hp (cagA-, vacA-) and incubated in humidified atmosphere for 3 h, 24 h and 48 h. At respective times, Hp (cagA+ vacA+) increased mRNA expression of α-SMA, collagen I, HSP-70 and Hif1α. After co-incubation with live Hp, fibroblasts were harvested for determination of the protein expression for α-SMA and HSP-70, by Western Blot analysis.
Results: We found that fibroblasts co-cultured with Hp (cagA+, vacA+) strongly upregulated protein expression α-SMA and HSP-70. In clear contrast, the co-incubation with Hp (cagA- vacA-) failed to significantly alter the expression of mRNA for α-SMA, collagen I, HSP-70 and Hif1α. The extension of the time of incubation of fibroblasts with selected Hp (cagA+ vacA+) strain up to 72 h revealed a strong signals for the mRNA expression of CAFs markers including α-SMA, FAP, Fsp, SDF, IL-6, IL-8, HGF, THFβ, collagen I and III and tenascin C. Interestingly, after insert co-culture of differentiated fibroblasts with RGM-1 cells from 24 h up to 96 h, the E-cadherin mRNA expression was significantly decreased starting from 48 h. The parallel increase in the expression of Twist and Snail mRNAs was observed already after 24 h, along with the overexpression of TGFβRII, HGFR and FGFR mRNA. The increased expression of mRNA for N-cadherin, vimentin, α-SMA, Fsp, Fap VEGF and integrin β1 has been observed in RGM1 cells after insert of co-culture of differentiated fibroblasts.
Conclusion: We conclude that 1) the Hp strain encoding for cagA+ vacA+ cytotoxins, but not Hp strain (cagA-vacA-) increased the differentiation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts mediated by an overexpression of HSP-70 protein, and 2) Hp strain expressing cagA+, vacA+ may induce the differentiation of fibroblasts associated with expression of CAFs markers, likely to initiate at least, partial EMT process in RGM-1 cell line with insert co-culture.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP249 HELICOBACTER PYLORI INFECTION IS AN INDEPENDENT RISK FACTOR OF EARLY AND ADVANCED COLORECTAL NEOPLASM
S.J. Lee, S.H. Kim, T.J. Kim, E.R. Kim, S.N. Hong, D.K. Chang, Y.H. Kim

Internal Medicine, Samsung Medical Center, Seoul/Korea, Republic of

Contact E-mail Address:
puhaha78677867@gmail.com

Introduction: The role of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) in the development of colorectal neoplasm remains controversial. We examined the association between H. pylori infection and colorectal neoplasm in a large sample of healthy participants who underwent screening colonoscopy.
Aims & Methods: A cross-sectional study of 8916 men, who participated in a regular health screening examination that included an H. pylori-specific immunoglobulin G antibody test and colonoscopy, was conducted to evaluate the association between H. pylori and colorectal neoplasm.
Results: Multivariable analyses adjusted for age, body mass index, smoking status, alcohol intake, regular exercise, regular aspirin use, and family history of colorectal cancer showed that the odds ratio (OR) [95% confidence interval (CI)] for any adenoma and advanced neoplasm was 1.32 (1.07–1.61) and 1.90 (1.05–3.56) in participants with H. pylori infection and without H. pylori infection, respectively. The association persisted after further adjustment for inflammatory markers or metabolic variables including fasting blood glucose, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol. Regarding the location, a positive association was confined to cases with proximal adenomas, and was observed similarly in all the evaluated subgroups.
Conclusion: In a large-scale study, carefully controlled for confounding factors, involving asymptomatic participants without a history of colonoscopy, H. pylori infection was significantly associated with the risk of any colorectal adenoma and advanced colorectal neoplasm. Prospective studies are necessary to determine whether H. pylori eradication can reduce this risk.

## OP250 HELICOBACTER PYLORI INFECTION ALLEVIATES THE ALLERGIC SYMPTOMS OF ATOPIC DERMATITIS IN A MOUSE MODEL VIA GENERATION OF CD4+CD25+FOXP3+ T CELLS

xueqian0719@163.com

Introduction: Increasing attention was paid to the protective function of Helicobacter pylori (H.pylori) on some allergic diseases. Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a kind of chronic inflammatory skin disease associated with allergy and inheritance tendency. The clinical manifestations include pruritis, xerosis and eczematous dermatitis, which affecting the quality of life seriously. The atopic dermatitis is usually accompanied with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Whether H.pylori infection had the similar protective effect on AD was unknown. CCR4 is an important skin-homing marker. We found H. pylori infection and atopic dermatitis could induce CCR4+CD4+CD25+Foxp3+Tregs expansion in gastric lymph nodes, spleen, blood, MLN and cervical lymph nodes synchronously by time.
Conclusion:
H. pylori infection could alleviate AD symptom by inducing the amplification of CD4+CD25+Foxp3+Tregs cells in peripheral blood, and did increase the expression of IL-10, TGF-β and inhibite the expression of IL-4 in dermal tissue. Atopic dermatitis may chemoattracte CCR4+ Tregs cells migrating to the skin.

## OP251 INCREASING MORTALITY FROM PANCREATIC CANCER IN PORTUGAL – AN EPIDEMIOLOGICAL ANALYSIS OF 25 YEARS
P. Marques Da Costa1, R.T. Marinho2, H. Cortez-Pinto1, L. Costa3, J. Velosa1

1Gastroenterology And Hepatology Department, Hospital de Santa Maria, Lisboa/Portugal

2Gastroenterology Clinic, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisboa/Portugal

3Oncology Department, Hospital de Santa Maria, Lisboa/Portugal

Contact E-mail Address:
pedroavmcosta@gmail.com

Introduction: Pancreatic cancer is the 5th leading cause of death by cancer in Europe. With a mortality that mostly overlaps its incidence, this cancer type is predicted to become increasingly prevalent as a result of population aging and high prevalence of known risk factors (e.g. smoking, alcohol, obesity).
Aims & Methods: We aimed at describing the mortality trends through the past 25 years in the Portuguese population (around 10.3 million habitants). For this purpose, we analysed the data published by the Portuguese National Statistical Institute, regarding the cause of death attributed to malignant pancreatic neoplasia (ICD10-C25; ICD9/8 -157) from 1991 to 2015. Data were further sub analysed by sex, age, and geographic area. Crude mortality rates (MR) represent deaths per 100.000 habitants. Age-standardised rates (ASR) were calculated using the revised (2013) standard European population. Logistic regression with jointpoint analysis was used to predict expected mortality rates by 2030.
Results: A total of 25,449 deaths from malignant pancreatic neoplasia were recorded between 1991 (n = 701) and 2015 (n = 1415). The number of deaths displayed an average annual percent change (AAPC) of 2.8 (CI:2.6–3.1, p < 0.0001). Overall, crude MR demonstrated an exponential growth (AAPC = 2.7 CI:2.3–3.0; p < 0.001) between 1991 (MR = 7.5) and 2015 (MR = 13.68). A higher annual percent change (APC) was recorded from 2006–2015 (APC = 3.8 CI:3.0–4.6); in relation to 1991–2006 (APC = 2.0 CI:1.5–2.4). As for ASR, a 29.5% increase was observed from 1991 (ASR = 6.1) to 2015 (ASR = 7.9). Assuming growth trends remain similar through the next 15 years, mortality from pancreatic cancer is predicted to reach 2131 annual deaths by 2030, corresponding to a 35.5% increase. Virtually all deaths (99%) occurred in patients over the age of forty. People aged 70–74 exhibited the highest ASR (ASR70–74 = 1.09). ASR increased equally among all age groups. Male patients showed a higher mean ASR when compared to females (9.49 ± 3.2 vs 5.18 ± 0.4 p < 0, 001). They also displayed an ASR growth rate that was approximately 5 times higher than females (AAPCmale = 4.5 CI:3.9–5.1 Vs AAPCfemale = 0.9 CI:0.6–1.2, p < 0.001). Regional differences were observed: the two provinces of Alentejo (ASR = 12.8 ± 2.9) and Azores archipelago (ASR = 17.05 ± 3.0) demonstrated significantly higher ASR.
Conclusion: In Portugal, pancreatic cancer mortality increased 29% throughout the past 25 years. This seems unrelated to population aging and may reflect an impressive rise in incidence. Sex and regional differences were noted with male patients and habitants living in Alentejo and Azores provinces exhibiting significantly higher mortality from pancreatic cancer.

 Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP252 ADHERENCE TO FOOD GUIDELINES OF THE WORLD CANCER RESEARCH FUND & AMERICAN INSTITUTE FOR CANCER RESEARCH AND PANCREATIC CANCER RISK
J. Fest1, R. Ruiter2, M. A. Ikram2, C. H.j. Van Eijck1, J. C. Kiefte-De Jong3, B. H. Stricker2

1Surgery, Erasmus Medical Centre, Rotterdam, Rotterdam/Netherlands

2Epidemiology, Erasmus Medical Centre, Rotterdam/Netherlands

3Global Public Health, Leiden University College The Hague, Rotterdam/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
j.fest@erasmusmc.nl

Introduction: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most lethal cancers, it has an increasing incidence and limited treatment options. Prevention of this cancer might be the key in lowering the burden of this disease. Two well-known modifiable risk factors are smoking and BMI. For other lifestyle factors, such as diet, there is limited or inconsistent evidence for the association with pancreatic cancer. The World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF) and American Institute for Cancer Research (AICR) have developed guidelines for the prevention of cancer in general. It is known that adherence to these guidelines results in a lower risk of colorectal and breast cancer, however to what extend this applies to pancreatic cancer is unknown.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to assess whether adherence to the WCRF & AICR guidelines is associated with a lower risk of pancreatic cancer. This study was embedded in the Rotterdam Study, a longstanding, prospective and population-based cohort study. Data on dietary intake were collected at baseline, through a frequent food questionnaire and interview by a dietician. We constructed an adherence score, based on the WCRF/AICR recommendations on weight management, foods and drinks that promote weight gain, plant and animal foods, alcoholic drinks, and use of dietary supplements. A higher score corresponds with greater adherence and an hypothesised lower risk of pancreatic cancer. We used Cox Proportional Hazard Models to estimate the association between the adherence score and pancreatic cancer risk.
Results: For 9778 (65.5%) participants dietary data was available. During a median follow-up time of 11.9 years, 77 patients developed pancreatic cancer. Adherence to the WCRF/AICR recommendations was analysed continuously and after stratification into quartiles. Greater adherence was associated with a reduced risk of pancreatic cancer, however not significantly (HRcontinuously: 0.82, 95%CI: 0.64–1.04). Stratified analysis showed a significant effect for the third quartile (HR: 0.44, 95%CI: 0.22–0.88) with a P-value for trend over the quartiles of 0.028. This effect persisted after excluding all participants with less than two years of follow-up, ensuring the effect was not due to yet undetected disease. Further analysis of the separate recommendations showed that the overall effect was driven by refraining from taking dietary supplements (HR: 0.54, 95% CI: 0.34–0.84).
Conclusion: Greater adherence to the World Cancer Research Fund and American Institute for Cancer Research guidelines for diet and lifestyle might be associated with lower risk of pancreatic cancer. Promoting these recommendations to the general population could help reduce pancreatic cancer incidence. However definitive results should follow from pooled analyses of multiple, large and longstanding prospective cohorts to secure more power.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP253 SURVEILLANCE FOR PANCREATIC CANCER IN HIGH-RISK INDIVIDUALS: FIRST-ROUND SCREENING RESULTS OF A MULTICENTRIC ITALIAN PROGRAM
S. Paiella1, G. Capurso2, G. Butturini3, R. Pezzilli4, S. Carrara5, M. Falconi6, M. Signoretti2, M. Di Leo5, I. Frigerio3, C. Bassi1, A. Zerbi7

1General And Pancreatic Surgery Department, Pancreas Institute, University of Verona, Verona/Italy

2Digestive & Liver Disease Unit, Ii, Medical School Univesity “Sapienza”, S. Andrea Hospital, Rome/Italy

3Hpb Unit, Clinica Pederzoli spa, Peschiera del Garda/Italy

4Sant'orsola Malpighi Hospital, Pancreatic Unit, Bologna/Italy

5Department Of Gastroenterology, Humanitas Research Hospital, Endoscopic Unit, Rozzano/Italy

6San Raffaele University Hospital, Pancreatic Surgery Department, Milan/Italy

7Humanitas Research Hospital, Pancreatic Surgery Department, Rozzano/Italy

Contact E-mail Address:
salvatore.paiella@univr.it

Introduction: The early diagnosis of cancer can help reduce mortality. Surveillance programs on high-risk individuals (HRI) proved to be able to detect premalignant lesions or early pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Currently, surveillance programmes on HRI are based on findings from endoultrasonography and/or MRI. These imaging techniques proved to be able to diagnose malignant or pre-malignant both on syndromic and familiar cases. The aim of our study was to provide the first registry-based Italian experience on HRI enrolled in a surveillance program for pancreatic cancer.
Aims & Methods: The multicentric surveillance program includes: individuals with familial pancreatic cancer (FPC) defined as those with 3 first-, second- or third-degree relatives with PDAC or individuals with 2 relatives with PDAC with at least 1 first-degree relative; BRCA 1/2 or p16 mutation carriers with at least 1 first- or second-degree relative diagnosed with PDAC; subjects suffering from hereditary pancreatitis or Peutz-Jegher syndrome. The surveillance program consists of an annual magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP).
Results: Seventy-eight subjects were enrolled from September 2015 to February 2017, by six high-volume pancreatic Institutions. The mean age was 50 years (range 26–79). Sixty-seven (86%) subjects had FPC, 9 were syndromic HRI (11.5%) and 2 (2.5%) subjects suffered from hereditary pancreatitis. MRCP detected pancreatic cysts in 14 HRI (17.9%, 12 FPC- and 2 syndromic-HRI) and features of chronic pancreatitis in 2 (2.5%). Twelve branch duct-IPMNs (mean diameter 9 mm, range 3–16) and 1 serous cystadenoma were identified. Of note, a patient with a MD-IPMN with high-grade dysplasia (Figure) has been considered for surgical resection. Two suspected solid lesions were identified at MRCP, not further confirmed at endoultrasonography.
Conclusion: At the time of the first-round screening program in Italy, the rate of diagnosed malignant or pre-malignant lesions on HRI is lower than expected. MRCP diagnosed pancreatic cystic neoplasms in 17.9% of subjects. This might be due to the low rate of syndromic HRI and/or to a low mean age compared to other series and/or to the less strict criteria of definition of FPC. The diagnostic yield for lesions with an indication for surgery is currently 1.2%.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP254 THE ROLE OF CYSTIC PRECURSOR LESIONS IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF PANCREATIC DUCTAL ADENOCARCINOMA IN CDKN2A-P16-LEIDEN MUTATION CARRIERS
I. Ibrahim1, M. Wasser2, Y. Wu3, A. Inderson1, W. De Vos Tot Nederveen Cappel4, H. Morreau2, F. Hes2, R.A. Veenendaal1, H. Putter2, S. Feshtali2, A. Van Mil2, N. Gruis2, R. Tollenaar5, W. Bergman2, B. Bonsing2, H. Vasen1

1Gastroenterology, Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden/Netherlands

2Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden/Netherlands

3West Suffolk Hospital, Bury St. Edmunds/United Kingdom

4Isala Clinics, Zwolle/Netherlands

5Surgical Oncology, Leiden University Medical Centre, Leiden, Netherlands, Leiden/Netherlands

Contact E-mail Address:
isaura_ibrahim@hotmail.com

Introduction: CDKN2A-p16-Leiden mutation carriers have a 15–20% risk of developing pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Surveillance of these carriers increased the survival but did not prevent all cancer deaths. Understanding of the natural course of PDAC might further improve the surveillance program.
Aims & Methods: The aim of the study was to evaluate the role of cystic precursor lesions (PRL) and the growth rate of PDAC. Since 2000, a large cohort of CDKN2A-p16-Leiden mutation carriers has participated in the annual MRI-surveillance program. We compared the frequency of cystic PRL in this group with that of controls who underwent MRI-scanning for symptoms of liver-biliary tract disorders. We also evaluated whether cystic PRL increase in size and develop into PDAC. Finally, we calculated the growth rate of screen-detected PDAC.
Results: Cystic PRL were found in 52 (25%) of 205 mutation carriers compared to 19 (19%) of 100 controls (P = 0.22). Growth of PRL was observed in six mutation carriers (12%). Five (9.7%) of 52 mutation carriers with PRL and eight (7.0%) of 114 mutation carriers without PRL developed PDAC (P = 0.56). The growth rate of PDAC was 21 mm per year. A reduction of the surveillance interval to 6 months would increase the detection of early tumors from 58% to 92%.
Conclusion: Cystic PRL play a minor role in the development of PDAC in CDKN2A-p16-Leiden mutation carriers. More intensive surveillance is only recommended for patients with large cystic PRL. Independent of the presence of cystic PRL, the surveillance interval may be reduced to 6 months, if studies show this approach to be cost-effective.

## OP255 CHARACTERIZATION OF GENETIC ALTERATIONS IN PANCREATIC CANCER HIGH-RISK POPULATION
G. Rosner, E. Scapa, E. Santo, M. Ben-Yehoyada

Gastroenterology, Tel-Aviv Sourasky Medical Center, Tel-Aviv/Israel

Contact E-mail Address:
guyr@tlvmc.gov.il

Introduction: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Despite modern treatment, 90% of patients die within one year of diagnosis. At early stages, surgical treatment is most beneficial, however, early diagnosis is rare, and most PC cases are confirmed as being locally invasive or metastatic. Inherited predisposition to pancreatic cancer is prevalent in 10% of PC cases. These include characterized genetic conditions such as the hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC), Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome (FAMMM) and hereditary pancreatitis (HP). However, about 85% of PC cases with strong family history are still uncharacterized.
Aims & Methods: We have recruited 120 high-risk PC individuals for genetic screening and clinical surveillance. Forty individuals fulfilled criteria for familial pancreatic. For all individuals, germ line DNA was extracted from whole blood and analyzed for the BRCA1 and 2 mutations. Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) technique (Illumina HiSeq platform) was used to screen families with high prevalence to PC for pathogenic germline mutations. Candidate genetic variants were analyzed for their pathogenic potential through familial genetic segregation analysis. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) was used to correlate the genetic findings to the clinical phenotype.
Results: We screened 10 informative families and performed segregation analysis. Out of these families we have discovered several possible pancreatic cancer candidates' point mutations in well-established as well as in unreported genes. Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed wide variety of genetic changes in cancer related genes including KLLN, HMMR, GATA5, MSR1 and KDR genes.
Conclusion: PC development is relatively slow, making it ideal for screening of high-risk individuals. Therefore, identifying this high-risk population is crucial for better surveillance and early detection of pancreatic cancer.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP256 DETECTION OF PANCREATIC CANCER BY URINE ELECTRIC NOSE ANALYSIS, A PROOF-OF-CONCEPT STUDY, 80 CASES
S. Nissinen1, A. Roine2, L. Hokkinen3, T. Rantanen4, N. Oksala2

1Gastroenterology, Kuopio University Hospital, KYS/Finland

2Surgery, Tampere University Hospital, Tampere/Finland

3Technology, University of Tampere, Tampere/Finland

4Surgery, Kuopio University Hospital, KYS/Finland

Contact E-mail Address:
samuli.nissinen@kuh.fi

Introduction: The prognosis of early stage pancreatic cancer has improved yet there is no feasible screening tool in clinical use. Recent studies have shown that an electronic nose can detect volatile organic compounds from urine and can discriminate between cancer patients and healthy controls.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this study was to determine if pancreatic cancer can be detected non-invasively from a urine sample by an electric nose (FAIMS, Field Asymmetric Ion Mobility Spectrometer). Pancreatic cancer patients were recruited in two centers, Seinäjoki Central Hospital and Kuopio University Hospital, between January 2014 and June 2016. Cancer patients provided a urine sample at the time of the diagnosis. Controls were patients undergoing hernia reparation or cholecystectomy and were recruited in the same centers during the same time period. They provided a urine sample before their operation. 100 ml of midstream urine was stored in −70C and thawed and warmed up to room temperature for analysis in random order with FAIMS. FAIMS analyses volatile compounds released from the sample, producing an ion mobility spectrum. The resulting spectrums were analyzed by linear discriminant analysis and cross-validated by leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV).
Results: 80 patients with pancreatic cancer, 40 with acute pancreatitis, 16 with chronic pancreatitis and 14 patients with suspected pancreatic lesion and 44 controls were recruited. The mean age of the pancreatic cancer patients was 70. 49% were females, 29% had stage IB-IIB, 71% stage III-IV cancer and 26% underwent the Whipple procedure or radical pancreatectomy. Patients who died had 16.9 months mean survival time and the mean follow-up time for survivers was 57 months (25–87 months). FAIMS signal data was identified to detect differences between cancer and control samples. The test detected pancreatic cancer with 81% sensitivity and 68% specificity. We combined patients with pancreatic cancer and premalign pancreatic lesions into one group and compared it to controls. Sensitivity was 83% and specificity 63%.
Conclusion: We found that the urine of pancreatic cancer patients has distinct volatile compounds that can be detected by FAIMS, which can distinguish pancreatic cancer patients from controls. It may also be able to detect premalign pancreatic lesions. This investigation was the first to test the ability of electric nose detect pancreatic cancer from urine samples. Measurement is quick and easy to perform, its costs are low and most importantly it is non-invasive. FAIMS has potential to be a screening tool for pancreatic cancer.
Disclosure of Interest: A. Roine: Owner of Olfactomics ltd, a company that develops clinical applications of eNose technology
N. Oksala: Owner of Olfactomics ltd, a company that develops clinical applications of eNose technology
All other authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP257 HINOS PROMOTES A CD24+CD133+ LIVER CANCER STEM CELL PHENOTYPE AND TUMOR PROGRESSION THROUGH A TACE/ADAM17 DEPENDENT NOTCH SIGNALING PATHWAY

R. Wang

Department Of Gastroenterology And Hepatology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan/China

Contact E-mail Address:
1765106711@qq.com

Introduction: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is closely associated with chronic inflammation caused by viral hepatitis, alcoholic or non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and other conditions leading to chronic inflammation and hepatocyte regeneration1. These long-term processes include an accumulation of genetic and/or epigenetic changes, alterations of the liver tumor microenvironment, and generation of liver cancer stem cells (LCSCs)2. Growing evidence supports the concept that tumor initiation can be driven by cancer stem cell (CSCs) subsets that are responsible for tumor relapse, metastasis, and chemotherapy-resistance3. Therefore, identification of CSC markers as well as signaling pathways activated in LCSCs could advance the development of liver cancer diagnosis and treatment strategies. The inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is associated with more aggressive solid tumors, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Notch signaling in cancer stem cells promotes cancer progression and requires Notch cleavage by ADAM (a disintegrin and metalloprotease) proteases. We hypothesized that iNOS/NO promotes Notch1 activation through ADAM17/TACE activation in liver cancer stem cells (LCSC) leading to a more aggressive cancer phenotype.
Aims & Methods: Primary human HCC were subjected to immunohistochemistry (IHC) for the expression CD24, CD133, iNOS, activated ADAM17/TACE or activated Notch. CD24 + CD133+ cells isolated from HCC cell lines or from human tumors were assessed in vitro and in vivo (Xenograft tumor model in mice) for stem-like properties and growth characteristics. Lentiviral-based short hairpin RNA (LV-shRNA) and LV-iNOS were used to knockdown or overexpress hiNOS in LCSCs, respectively. Activation of the Notch signal pathway was detected by a CSL-luciferase reporter in CD24 + CD133+ cells after iNOS overexpression, or the inhibition of iNOS (1400W) or TACE (TAPI-2). Immunoprecipitation experiments were carried to assess the interaction between TACE and iRhom2 or TACE and Notch intracellular domain (NICD). We evaluated the relationship of hiNOS and NICD with clinic-pathological features using a liver cancer tissue microarray (TMA).
Results: Expression of stem cell markers, CD24 and CD133 in the tumors of patents with HCC was associated greater iNOS expression and worse outcomes. The expression of iNOS in CD24 + CD133+ liver cancer stem cells (LCSC), but not CD23-CD133- LCSC, promoted Notch1 signaling and stem-ness characteristics in vitro and in vivo as well as accelerated HCC initiation and tumor formation in the mouse xenograft tumor model. Lentiviral-based short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated iNOS knockdown or iNOS activity inhibition using BYK191023 significantly suppressed CD24 + CD133+ LCSCs stem-ness characteristics in vitro and in vivo. Furthermore, up-regulation of iNOS expression in LCSCs led to TACE and iRhom2 phosphorylation in a cyclic GMP (cGMP)/protein kinase G (PKG)-dependent manner. Immunoprecipitation experiments show that the physical binding between TACE and iRhom2 increased significantly when iNOS was overexpressed. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that high hiNOS and NICD expression were significantly associated with aggressive behavior of HCC and decreased survival in patients.
Conclusion: These findings link iNOS to Notch1 signaling in CD24 + CD133 + LCSC through the activation of ADAM17/TACE and identify a mechanism for how iNOS contributes to progression of CD24 + CD133 + HCC.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.
References
1. Grivennikov SI, Greten FR, Karin M. Immunity, inflammation, and cancer. Cell 2010;140:883–99.
2. Magee JA, Piskounova E, Morrison SJ. Cancer stem cells: impact, heterogeneity, and uncertainty. Cancer Cell 2012;21:283–96.
3. Ishizawa K, Rasheed ZA, Karisch R, et al. Tumor-initiating cells are rare in many human tumors. Cell Stem Cell 2010;7:279–82.

## OP258 AUTOPHAGY INHIBITS PROTUMORAL EFFECTS INDUCED BY COLIBACTIN-PRODUCING COLORECTAL CANCER-ASSOCIATED ESCHERICHIA COLI
C. Lucas1, G. Dalmasso1, M. Bonnet1, P. Sauvanet1, D. Pezet1, N. Barnich1, P. Rosenstiel2, R. Bonnet3, H. T.T. Nguyen1

1Université Clermont Auvergne, Inserm U1071, INRA USC2018, M2iSH, Clermont-Ferrand/France

2Institute Of Clinical Molecular Biology, University of Kiel, Kiel/Germany

3Laboratoire Bacteriologie, CHU Hopital G. Montpied, Clermont-Ferrand/France

Contact E-mail Address:
cecily.lucas@uca.fr

Introduction: The mucosa of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) is abnormally colonized by Escherichia coli strains, which frequently harbor the pathogenic pks genomic island responsible for the synthesis of the genotoxin colibactin. Colibactin-producing E. coli induce DNA damage and enhance tumorigenesis in CRC mouse models. Autophagy, cellular process allowing the degradation of cytoplasmic contents via the lysosomal pathway, plays a crucial role in the maintenance of homeostasis and is implicated in various human diseases including cancer.
Aims & Methods: This study aimed at investigating the role of autophagy in host responses to infection with the CRC-associated E. coli strains. mRNA expression levels of autophagy genes in the colonic mucosal biopsies from CRC patients were determined by qRT-PCR. Autophagy induction was assessed by Western blot and immunofluorescent labelling of LC3. DNA damage was assessed by Western blot analysis and immunofluorescent labelling of phospho-H2AX. Recruitment of the DNA repair protein RAD51 into the nucleus, which is required for DNA damage repair, was examined by Western blot analysis of nuclear extract and immunofluorescent staining. Intestinal epithelial HCT116 cells, APCMin/+ mice deficient for Atg16l1 in intestinal epithelial cells (APCMin/+/ATG16L1ΔIEC) and the control mice (APCMin/+/ATG16L1f/f) were infected with the pks-harboring E. coli strains (pks+ E. coli).
Results: mRNA expression levels of many autophagy genes were increased in the tumors compared to the adjacent mucosa from CRC patients. In particular, their expression was higher in the mucosa colonized with pks+ E. coli compared with those colonized with E. coli strains without pks island (pks- E. coli). Infection of HCT116 cells with the pks+ E. coli strains resulted in autophagy activation, and this was dependent on the presence of the pks island. Using autophagy-deficient HCT116 cells infected with the pks + E. coli reference strain 11G5 or its isogenic mutant defective for pks, we showed that autophagy was required to decrease colibactin-induced DNA damage by recruiting RAD51 into the nucleus and thereby activating the DNA damage repair. Autophagy deficiency increased colonic tumorigenesis induced by infection with the pks+ E. coli 11G5 strain in APCMin/+ mice.
Conclusion: Autophagy is induced in intestinal epithelial cells infected with the CRC-associated pks+ E. coli strains, and a functional autophagy is necessary to limit the protumoral effects of pks+ E. coli on infected cells.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

## OP259 INTERPLAY BETWEEN CD80 SIGNALLING AND MISMATCH REPAIR GENES EXPRESSION IN THE EARLY STAGES OF COLONIC CARCINOGENESIS
A. Kotsafti1, M. Scarpa1, M. Fassan2, S. Morgan3, A. Porzionato4, C. Marchiori5, P. Brun4, I. Angriman6, M. Rugge7, C. Castoro8, I. Castagliuolo2, M. Scarpa1

1Esophageal And Digestive Tract Surgical Unit, Regional Centre For Esophageal Disease, Veneto Institute of Oncology (IOV-IRCCS), Padova/Italy

2University of Padova, Padova/Italy

3Barnsley Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Barnsley/United Kingdom

4Dept. Of Molecular Medicine, University of Padova Dept. of Molecular Medicine, Padova/Italy

5Department Of Molecular Medicine, University of Padua, Padova/Italy

6Dept. Of General Surgery, University of Padova, Padova/Italy

7Pathology, Medical School of the Padova University, Padova/Italy

8Venesto Institute of Oncology, Padova/Italy

Contact E-mail Address:
andromachi.kotsafti@iov.veneto.it

Introduction: Several studies and meta-analysis demonstrated that patients with mismatch repair (MMR) genes deficient colorectal cancer (CRC) have a more favourable stage-adjusted prognosis. A possible mechanism is that in tumor with MMR defects T-cells, macrophages, and natural killers, infiltration might be increased enhancing immune surveillance mechanisms [1]. In fact, a higher density of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes was associated with better disease free survival in cases with defective versus intact MMR [2, 3]. CRC with MMR genes deficiency showed a higher CD80 expression, and in vitro silencing of MSH2, MLH1 and MSH6 significantly increased CD80+ cell rate [4]. However, the precise role of CD80 signalling and its effect on MMR genes expression colonic carcinogenesis remain unclear.
Aims & Methods: The aim of this work was to investigate whether the modulation of CD80 signalling may influence the expression of MMR genes in a mouse model of early colorectal carcinogenesis. C57BL/6 mice received azoxymethane (AOM) i.p. at a dose of 10 mg/kg body weight weekly for 6 weeks to induce dysplasia and then sacrificed four or six months after the first AOM injection to perform histology, flow cytometry analysis and immunohistochemistry of colonic mucosa. Some WT mice received i.p. a monoclonal antiCD80 or antiCTLA4 antibody following AOM administration. Immunohistochemistry for MLH1, MSH2 and MSH6 was carried on. Non parametric statistics was performed.
Results: Low-grade dysplasia (LGD) extension was to about 20% of the colon mucosa at 4 and 6 months after AOM treatment in the AOM group and in the AOM-antiCD80 antibody while it dropped at less than 5% in the AOM-antiCTLA4 group (p < 0.001). High grade dysplasia (HGD) extension peaked in AOM-antiCD80 group (p = 0.018). The frequency of mice with low expression of MLH1 was significantly lower in the AOM-antiCD80 group (23.1%) compared to the AOM one (78.5%) (p = 0.007). Similarly, the frequency of mice with low expression of MSH2 was significantly higher in the AOM-antiCD80 group (30.7%) compared to the AOM one (85.7%) (p = 0.006) Curiously enough, the frequency of mice with low expression of MSH6 was significantly higher in the AOM group (71.4%) compared to either AOM-antiCD80 (0%) or AOM-antiCTLA4 (0%) groups (p < 0.001). (p = 0.014).
Conclusion: Lack of functional CD80 in colonic mucosa is associated to extended LGD and to the presence of HGD whereas enhancing CD80 function with antiCTLA4 antibody drastically decrease LGD extension and make HGD disappear. CD80 inhibition is associated to a high expression of MLH1, MSH2 and MSH6 suggesting a possible interplay between CD80 and MMR genes expression. Unexpectedly, MSH6 expression seemed enhanced even in case of CD80 stimulation suggesting a more complex regulation.
Disclosure of Interest: All authors have declared no conflicts of interest.

2. Dolcetti R, Viel A, Doglioni C, Russo A, Guidoboni M, Capozzi E, Vecchiato N, Macrì E, Fornasarig M, Boiocchi M. High prevalence of activated intraepithelial cytotoxic T lymphocytes and increased neoplastic cell apoptosis in colorectal carcinomas with microsatellite instability. Am J Pathol. 1999;154:1805–1813.
